capabilities.notes: Not a Vega input format

A `url` dataset is fetched through a host-supplied `DataLoader`, read as `json`, `csv`, `tsv` or `dsv`, with `format.property` reaching into a document and `format.parse` giving a tabular column its type. **Denied by default**: a specification is data, often pasted data, and a URL in it asks this process to fetch an address the specification chose — so the host opts in and says what to. `topojson` is decoded too — `format.feature` for one feature per geometry, `format.mesh` with an optional `interior`/`exterior` filter for the shared borders — which is data and not geography, so it stands on its own. What a map still needs beyond it is a projection

The shape nearly every published Vega specification uses. `FallbackDataLoader` tries loaders in order, and `VegaDataLoaders.directoryThenNetwork` is the useful arrangement: read from a directory if the file is there, fetch from the base URL if it is not, and — with `cacheDownloads` — write it to that directory so the second run is offline. The default base is `https://vega.github.io/vega/`, the site the gallery is served from, so a relative path under it is the file the example was written against rather than a lookalike. It is a default for *reaching* the data, never for whether to: `DenyLoader` is still what a compiler gets unless a host passes something else. The base URL's host is the allowlist by default, because a specification chooses its own URLs and an unrestricted loader following a relative path is a request-forgery primitive one redirect away

capabilities.feature: The demo loading a pasted example's data
capabilities.tests_text: `DemoActivityTest` (on an API 37 emulator, over a real socket)
capabilities.notes: The demo opts in with `VegaDataLoaders.directoryThenNetwork(cacheDir, cacheDownloads = true)`, so pasting a gallery example whose data is a relative URL draws the chart rather than an empty pair of axes, and the second paste of the same example needs no network. The allowlist is the one host the base URL names, which is the whole safety argument: this screen compiles text a *user pasted*, and an unrestricted loader would let that text aim the process at any address it liked. Private addresses are refused too, so the allowed host cannot be rebound onto loopback. The device test is where this can be proved at all — the JVM tests use a fake transport, and a missing `INTERNET` permission would show up nowhere earlier

capabilities.feature: Passing a loader to the chart
capabilities.notes: `VegaChartController(loader =...)`. Until this existed the engine had a loader and no host could opt in to it, which is the same as not having one

Ported from the Go loader in `mgilbir/aster`, with the same controls: an allowlist of domains, a base URL for relative references, blocking hosts that resolve to private/loopback/link-local addresses (including the cloud metadata endpoint), and a response-size cap that fails rather than truncating. The policy is re-applied to **every redirect hop**, which a check on the first URL alone misses. `sanitize` is separate from `load` so the decision can be tested without I/O, and is required to be idempotent

All of it is common Kotlin in `vega-runtime`, including the URI parser and RFC 3986 reference resolution, so the rules cannot drift between platforms. The only seams are `HttpTransport` (one GET, no redirects) and `HostResolver`; `vega-loader` supplies the JVM ones

capabilities.feature: Pasting a specification into the demo
capabilities.notes: The demo's "Paste your own" entry compiles a specification from the clipboard or from an editable field, and shows the diagnostics beneath the chart — the only place they are aimed at a user rather than at a contributor. Three outcomes are worded apart on purpose: it did not compile (the previous chart stays, and saying so matters or the app looks like it ignored the paste); it compiled but something could not be drawn (the chart is not what was asked for); or a property was merely ignored (it very nearly is). Reading the clipboard needs foreground focus on Android 10 and later, so the null path is real and is reported

Parses and compiles the subset below, including signals, expressions, all 51 of upstream's 51 documented data transforms, nested group scopes, group `layout`, legends and titles. Loaded through `VegaChartController.setSpec`, or `setSpecAsync` to compile off the calling thread

`VegaLiteCompiler` compiles Vega-Lite to Vega in Kotlin, and the emitted specification is compared **property by property** against upstream's own compiler on every fixture — not only the picture it draws, because Vega-Lite's whole value is in the defaults it supplies and each of those is one property of the output. A single view, a `layer` of views, or a grid of them faceted by `row` and `column`; see the Vega-Lite section below for the channels and marks, and for what is reported instead of approximated
Numbers are always `Double`
Malformed paths resolve to null rather than throwing

The guide blocks: `axis` with its `axisX`/`axisY`, `axisTop`/`axisBottom`/`axisLeft`/`axisRight` and `axisBand` variants, `legend`, the `guide-label` and `guide-title` styles, and `background`/`padding`/`autosize`. Precedence runs style → axis → dimension → side → band → the guide's own properties, verified by setting one property at every level and seeing which drew. A `style` block names its properties the way a **mark** does, so `fill` becomes `labelColor` on the way through — without that the form every Vega-Lite theme uses would set nothing. Also the mark blocks: `config.mark`, the per-mark-type blocks, and named `config.style` blocks a mark opts into through its own `style` property. `config.mark` sits **below** the engine's built-in per-type defaults and `config.{marktype}` sits above them, because upstream's default configuration is itself written into those per-type blocks — so `config.mark.fill` never recolours a rect and `config.rect.fill` does. `config.range`, `config.group` and `config.projection` are reported by name

`SpecCompiler`, `VegaLiteCompiler`, `VegaLiteInput.toVega` and `VegaChartController` take a `config` block from the **host**, and the specification's own beats it key by key — a theme is a default and a stated value overrides it. `Config` was internal and built from the specification alone, so an app drawing a server's chart on a dark surface had no way in at all. The merge is `vega-util`'s `mergeConfig` transcribed: a block merges property by property, an object inside a block overwrites, `legend.layout` and each `style` entry recurse one level further, `signals` merge by name, and the prototype keys are dropped at every level. **Two things it cannot reach**, both Vega-Lite's own precedence: a mark's own encoded property beats every configuration block, and `Normalize.pointOverlay` uses a `point` object verbatim as the overlay mark's definition — so a specification hard-coding `mark.point.fill: "white"` keeps its white point, and a host that must change that is rewriting the specification anyway

A responsive width cannot come from the specification — `"container"` means "ask the page" — so `SpecCompiler` and `VegaChartController` take the surface's size from the **host**, and `containerSize()` answers with it. A compile input rather than a draw-time one, because Vega-Lite compiles `"container"` into a signal and every scale range and axis extent below is resolved from that; the controller's property recompiles when set, keeping the signal values a reader has changed. With nothing supplied the chart takes `config.view.continuousWidth`, 300, which is what upstream falls back to outside a browser and what the differential fixtures compare against — so the default is load-bearing rather than a placeholder

Each parser names the properties it *consumes* and reports the remainder, rather than keeping a list of what is missing. Covers axes, scales, legends, titles, marks and encode channels, so a property nobody anticipated — including one upstream adds later — is a diagnostic rather than a silence. Where there is something specific to say about what gets drawn instead, it is said by name: `limit`, for instance, draws the text past the width it was told to stay inside

`background` on the specification beats `config.background` — a theme's default is what a stated one overrides — and a top-level **`view`** block paints the *plotting area* rather than the surface around it, so it becomes an `encode` on the chart's own group. The two are different colours in the same chart

capabilities.feature: Field names with dots in them
capabilities.notes: The rule is about **who wrote the string**: a column an *encoding* aggregate reads is a reference this compiler derived and its dots are escaped, where a column named in a `transform` the specification wrote is left exactly as written. `escapePathAccess` escapes a bracket, a dot and both quotes **inside** a path step as well as between steps: a column called `source.reco` is a name and not a path, and writing it unescaped tells Vega to look one level into a `source` that is not there

The theme reaches the compiled Vega, which is the only way a restyled chart survives the compiler. Three things happen on the way, all upstream's: Vega-Lite-only keys are dropped (some already applied — `background` became a top-level property), a per-mark-type block is **redirected into `config.style`** because Vega-Lite's `bar` and `rect` are the same Vega mark, and `config.title` becomes the `group-title` style with `color` rewritten as `fill`. A **style** block outranks every other configuration of a mark property — `getMarkConfig` puts it ahead of the per-mark block and `config.mark`, over the mark's own type followed by whatever its `style` names, the last one that answers winning — which is how a theme turns a chart's ticks on their side. And every axis property is read from the whole block chain (`config.axisX` as much as `config.axis`), not only the ones Vega has never heard of; what a theme settles there is used to decide what follows from it, such as which way a label is aligned, and then left where it is rather than written back onto the axis, Vega applying the configuration itself. Anything unrecognised passes through untouched, since Vega has configuration this compiler never reads

`VegaLiteInput.toVega` routes on `$schema` and, where a specification has none, on its shape — only Vega-Lite has a top-level `mark`, only Vega has `marks`. It reports which way it went rather than deciding silently, because a Vega-Lite specification read as Vega fails with a complaint about a missing `marks` array, which reads like nonsense to whoever pasted a working chart. **On every host**, which it was not until `:vega-lite` stopped being a JVM module: nothing in the compiler touches the JVM — it emits a specification, it does not execute one — so a specification pasted into the Android demo drew a chart while the same text on iOS could not be read at all, for no reason but a build file. The module is now built for all five targets and exported to the framework, so Swift reaches `VegaLiteInput` directly; the iOS demo's paste screen converts through it and says which grammar it took the text for, as Android's does

The `arc`, `bar`, `point`, `circle`, `square`, `tick`, `line`, `area`, `trail`, `rect`, `rule` and `text` marks, given as a name or as a mark definition. `filled`, `orient`, `size`, `thickness`, `binSpacing` and the mark's own graphic properties are honoured; `orient` is derived from the encoding the way upstream derives it, which is what decides whether a bar grows upwards or sideways

Scales, axes and legends are shared across layers unless `resolve` says otherwise: domains union, and the axis title becomes `"b, Mean of b"` the way upstream joins them. A layer **inside** a layer works to any depth — its names simply run deeper, `layer_1_layer_0_marks`, which is what a composite mark inside a layer already produced — and what the nesting has to keep hold of is the name of the *outermost* member, that being the child a top-level `resolve` speaks about. A layer may name its own `data`
`x`, `y`, `x2`, `y2`, as field, `datum` or `value` definitions

A scaled non-position channel like any other, mapped onto the mark's own `angle` — which is how a radial histogram turns each of its labels to face outward. It takes a scale and **no legend**: `LEGEND_SCALE_CHANNELS` does not list it, a key of rotated swatches saying nothing a reader could use

An arc that states its own `outerRadius` is not measured from the plotting area — a donut naming its own reach means it — and still takes an inner radius of zero, Vega drawing nothing where neither is given. An arc over *categories* takes a **band** on its polar positions, a slice spanning an angle rather than sitting at one, and spanning it uses the branch of `positionAndSize` for a channel with no size channel: Vega has no `thetaWidth`, so the far angle is the near one plus the extent, written as an `offset` on the same reference. An arc is a rectangle in polar coordinates, which is how upstream compiles one too: the same rect rules serve both, and `theta`/`theta2`/`radius`/`radius2` are written as Vega's `startAngle`/`endAngle`/`outerRadius`/`innerRadius`. An arc stacks by default, in polar coordinates, and a chart with no Cartesian position is styled `view` rather than `cell` — it has no plotting area to draw a border around. A polar position **bucketed** by a bin takes those Vega names too, and takes no half-unit nudge with them: that nudge is the *axis's* translation, and an angle is not drawn against a ruler. An arc may also state its bounds on the mark rather than in the encoding — four sliders driving one arc — and `positionRef` reads the encoding first, the mark's own value only as a fallback

An offset scale is **not always a band**: it divides a band between the marks nested in it, and how it divides follows the mark — a bar takes a band of its own inside the group, a point sits at a place in it. That settles the offset scale's type, its `paddingOuter`, the step expression that counts its entries (`bandspace` counts *bands*, and a point scale has only places), and whether the position's offset is centred in a lane. A *position* with an offset nested in it is a band whatever the mark, a point scale having no span to divide. An offset with **no position** beside it has no band to sit inside and spans the whole plot from the middle, `[-width/2, width/2]`; a *continuous* position bucketed by a time unit does have one, a bucket wide, measured through the scale and inset by half the nested padding at each end. An offset encoding also takes a rect **off** its bucket's edges, so the bucket is no longer what the rect spans and the banded positioning applies — with the band being the *offset's*, which is what makes the width `bandwidth('xOffset')` rather than the five units a lone continuous rect takes. Otherwise: The channel that puts bars side by side within a band. Four things follow from it and all four are upstream's: the offset is a band scale of its own, the outer band takes the wider `bandWithNestedOffset` paddings, the bar's width comes from the *inner* scale, and the outer step becomes `20 * bandspace(domain(offset), 0, 0) / (1 - paddingInner)` — as many marks as the group holds, divided by what the padding takes

`getSort`: an `order` channel names the drawing order outright and the mark is sorted by that column rather than by its position — a line running through the years rather than left to right, which is the whole of what a connected scatter plot is. A **stacked** mark is the exception, where `order` says how the segments stack
A `DateTime` in a scale's domain becomes the expression that builds the instant, wrapped in `{data: …}` so Vega reads it as one *datum* of the domain rather than a list to be spread

`color`, `fill`, `stroke`, `opacity`, `fillOpacity`, `strokeOpacity`, `strokeWidth`, `size`, `shape`, `text`, `detail`, `order`, and **`href`** — a link the mark carries, written the way a text channel is, with the **pointer** beside it, since nothing else about a linked point looks clickable. `color` resolves to `fill` or `stroke` by the mark's `filled`, which is why a hollow point's legend is hollow too. **`strokeDash`** tells two series apart by their *pattern* rather than by colour, for a reader who cannot rely on colour or a chart that will be printed in one ink: an ordinal scale whose range values are the five dash arrays upstream carries itself (Vega has no `range.strokeDash` in its own configuration), and a legend whose every swatch is drawn in its own pattern

`rangeMin`/`rangeMax` **replace the ends** of whatever range the channel would take and are not emitted themselves — how a radial chart says "start the rings at twenty" without writing out the expression for the other end. A stated `scheme` is the scale's **range** — `parseScheme` — and not a property beside one: written as a property it sat next to the `"category"` range this would otherwise default to, and Vega reads the range, so a chart asking for `category20` got the ten-colour scheme. Otherwise, type from the field's type, the channel and the mark — a nominal field is a `band` under a rect-shaped mark and a `point` under anything else — with `zero`, `nice`, `padding`, `paddingInner`/`paddingOuter`, `bins`, `interpolate` and the range defaults, each gated by whether the scale type takes that property at all

`{"step": 50, "for": "position"}` hands the step to the **outer** band rather than to one mark inside it, so the step signal takes it outright and the offset divides whatever band it produced. A stated `scale.padding` likewise settles a band's two ends at once and passes through as it stands, the derived inner and outer paddings being for a scale that said nothing. A discrete position has no width of its own, so the chart is *derived* from a step per category and `width` becomes a signal: `bandspace(domain('x').length, 0.1, 0.05) * x_step`. A continuous position takes `config.view.continuousWidth`, 300. Only a **band** scale has a real inner padding there: a **point** scale counts as 1, because n points have n−1 steps between them, and its `padding` is the outer one — vega-scale builds `point()` as `pointish(band().paddingInner(1))`

`aggregate` (including `count`, whose output field is the reserved `__count`), `bin` — as `true`, as parameters, or `"binned"` — and `timeUnit`. A column that arrives **already bucketed** — written either as `bin: "binned"` or as an object saying `binned: true`, both of which `isBinned` accepts, and reading only the string bins it a second time — takes the bucket's far edge from the secondary channel rather than from an `_end` column nobody computed, — and only where something is drawn *between* the two edges: `isRectBasedMark(mark) || bandPosition`, so a label beside such a rect, placed at a single position, computes neither the far edge nor the interpolated ones a `bandPosition` asks for, and names neither in its domain. That form requires an `x2`; the same edge is what the row is announced by and what groups the stack beside the start. Two layers aggregating one table are folded into **one** aggregate where they group by the same fields, upstream's `MergeAggregates`, and the union is a union of *measures*: the order follows each field's first appearance, which puts a `count` after every measure of a column. Field naming follows upstream's `vgField`, so `mean_b`, `bin_maxbins_10_v` and `sum_yield_end` are the names the transforms, the scale domains and the mark encodings all use — and the *signal* a `bin` publishes its chosen boundaries as is named through the view, so a binned field inside a facet is `child_bin_maxbins_10_v_bins` on both sides of the reference

A stacked path mark's **imputation** happens within `facetby.concat(stackby)`, so a gap in a trellis is filled from the cell's own rows rather than across the cells; and a path mark split into series reads the *cell's* partition rather than the whole table, which had been drawing every cell's series in every cell. Upstream's rules, which are asymmetric on purpose: with a measure on both axes the aggregated one stacks, and with neither aggregated a bar or an area falls back to its orientation. A stacked *path* mark imputes the gaps to zero first, or the band above a gap would step into it

`values`, `url` with a format, `name` — a **named** root keeps that name and does not consume a `source_n`, and the rows a top-level `datasets` block holds are written out beside it, that hand-off being what the name exists for — and **`sequence`** — the one data source that is a *transform*: the dataset holds a `sequence` transform instead of values, the flow does not fork below it (a generator being nothing Vega might overwrite), and its column is derived, so nothing parses it. **Every table the chart reads is a root**, in the order it was first asked for, because that order is the numbering — a layer or a plot with its own `data` gets a source of its own, without which its marks are drawn against the first view's rows, which is a wrong chart rather than a missing one — and a `lookup`'s joined table is a root too. Then `assembleRootData`'s last step: a dataset that derives from nothing and does nothing moves to the front, Vega having to hold a handed-over table before whatever joins against it. The dataset naming (`source_0`, `data_0`, …) follows upstream's flattening walk, because whether a view's transforms land on `source_0` or on a derived `data_0` decides what every scale domain and mark reads from. A `format.parse` the specification states over rows it **wrote out** is not the loader's work — Vega has already ingested them — so it joins the flow's own parse and becomes a formula, and an explicit parse wins over an inferred one (`Split(explicit, implicit)`). The implicit **parse** follows the same walk, and every case is a comparison that would otherwise be made between strings: a temporal field before a time scale sorts it, a `min`/`max` aggregate before it answers with the alphabetically smallest, and a path mark's own dimension before it draws a line through 1, 10, 2 in that order. Where several views share a dataset the parse is hoisted above the fork and *every* branch re-parented onto it — upstream's `MergeParse` — which is what puts a layer's own transforms after the shared parse rather than beside it. Three more of upstream's optimizers decide the same shape and so the same names: identical sibling branches fold into one (`MergeIdenticalNodes`), sibling aggregates grouping by the same fields fold into one (`MergeAggregates`), and a fork with a bare *output* branch in it collapses, because an output is a name and nothing else and everything at the fork belongs below it (`MergeOutputs`). Identical *sibling* branches fold together on the same basis upstream compares them — every node's `hash`, over the transform it emits and, for a stack, over the whole component: two stacks that segment the column differently, or whose dimension is quantitative in one plot and ordinal in another, are two questions from one transform. Time units fold by their own rule, which keeps the **last** sibling where the general one keeps the first, and which of them survives is which branch the walk meets first and so how the datasets are numbered. The whole sequence runs again until nothing moves, at most five times, because one fold makes the next one's siblings: two layers bucketing an instant are not sibling aggregates until their time units have been folded together

capabilities.feature: A bucket a rect is drawn over
capabilities.notes: `offsetedRectFormulas`: a `bandPosition` other than the middle moves a bucketed rect *within* its bucket, and the two ends it is drawn between are then interpolated — between the previous bucket's start and this one's, and between this one's start and its end — into two columns a formula writes, which the scale reaches and the mark is drawn between. At `bandPosition: 0` a band marking a gap sits **over** the missing point rather than after it

The `timeunit` transform, a scale domain over the bucket's start *and* end, an axis labelled by the `timeUnitSpecifier(...)` Vega chooses at render time — beside a `formatType` saying to read that specifier as a *time* one, which the scale implies only where it is itself temporal, so a band of month names would otherwise be labelled with its milliseconds — and a `tickMinStep` of one bucket — expressed as the difference between two dates in a deliberately non-leap year, because no constant says how long a month is. A field is an instant when it is typed temporal **or** carries a time unit — `isFieldOrDatumDefForTimeFormat` — so a month bucketed onto an *ordinal* scale is parsed as a date, spoken as a date and labelled as a date, on its axis and in its legend alike; reading only the type announced the bucket's raw milliseconds. A `utc` unit carries `timezone: "utc"` on the transform, without which a midnight instant is bucketed against the viewer's calendar. The bucket's *end* joins the scale domain only for a mark that occupies the span, which upstream decides by whether the mark has a `timeUnitBandPosition`; and an axis over a cyclic unit — month, hours, day, quarter — asks for no tick count at all, since twelve months want twelve ticks rather than seven

capabilities.feature: Chart size with no scale on a channel
capabilities.notes: `defaultUnitSize`: a channel with **no scale at all** is not a continuous one — it falls to the *discrete* size, which is a step — so a strip of ticks or a single total is twenty units deep rather than three hundred. `config.view.discreteWidth`/`discreteHeight` replaces the step outright where a theme states one

capabilities.feature: A rect filling part of its band
capabilities.notes: Two numbers rather than one: the mark fills `band * bandwidth(scale)` and starts `(1 - band) / 2` in, so the gaps either side of it match. `cornerRadiusEnd` rounds the two corners at the **far** end of a bar — Vega has four corner properties and no notion of which end a bar grows from, so it resolves into two of them by orientation — and `xOffset`/`yOffset` on a *mark* are plain nudges that fold into the position's `offset`

capabilities.feature: A rect filling part of its bucket
capabilities.notes: `{"width": {"band": 0.7}}` on the mark: both edges move in by half of what is left over, `(1 - band) / 2` and its complement. The interpolation happens in **data** space and the scale is applied to the result, which is not the same as interpolating two scaled positions once the scale is not linear

One value with two opposite readings, both upstream's. `assembleTitle` writes `titleString ? {title} : {}`, so an axis titled `""` has **no** caption; the tooltip and the description read `fieldDef.title || defaultTitle(...)`, an `||`, so the same empty title falls through to the field's own name there

Written the way `String(n)` writes one — the shortest text that reads back as the same double. `max(4.0, …)` and `max(4, …)` are the same instruction and a different string, and a specification is compared as text; the display canonicaliser is not the answer either, since it rounds, and `0.15000000000000002` is not `0.15`

capabilities.feature: A rect's size on a continuous scale
capabilities.notes: `getBandSize` asks the scale's kind first: a rect-based mark against a quantitative axis takes `continuousBandSize` — five units for a bar — and only a *discrete* domain reaches `discreteBandSize` or a step. Using the step made a bar nearly four times too wide

A Vega mark property, not a Vega-Lite-only one, so it is emitted rather than stripped, and the runtime applies it to a non-group mark as upstream does: the mark's items are drawn under a clip of `(0, 0, group.width, group.height)` — the *enclosing* group's extent, not the mark's own bounds — and the same rectangle is intersected with its bounds. It is a paint-time cut and not a filter, so an item outside it is still in the scene and still announced — but it is **not** under a finger placed where it would have been drawn, because upstream's `pick` returns from a clipped group before testing its contents at all

What a chart does with a value no scale can place. Upstream's default, `break-paths-show-path-domains`, is a macro for two behaviours — a path **breaks** at the gap and keeps the row, everything else **drops** the row — so the mode is normalised once per view and the mark's `defined` and the data flow's filter both read it: filtering a row the path was going to break at removes the break along with the row. `filter`, `break-paths-filter-domains` and `break-paths-show-domains` all compile. `defined` is asked once per **scaled** channel rather than once for x and y, so a line coloured by a continuous field breaks where that colour is missing, and a channel whose scale has a discrete domain is never invalid — a null is another category. Under **`show`** — written as `invalid: null` — the value is *drawn*, at the scale's own output for one: the channel becomes a production rule whose first arm tests for it and answers with `config.scale.invalid` where a specification named one, and otherwise with the same zero-or-minimum a bar measures from. Every other mode has already dealt with the row, so `show` is the only one that reaches the encoding

capabilities.feature: A field named through a path
capabilities.notes: `record.high` is a path into a nested object in Vega-Lite and a column's *name* in Vega. Each nested field gets a formula flattening it — guarded step by step, so a row missing the outer object yields nothing rather than failing — and `format.parse` names only the top-level columns, Vega having no path syntax there. The property is written even when it comes out empty, which is what upstream's node does. Beside it, the *derived* rule from `data/parse.ts`: a column a transform computed is never parsed, having the type its transform gave it and never having been seen by the loader

A line whose thickness follows the data, and two rules that are not the ones they look like. Its `size` is Vega's own `size` — a width that varies point by point — rather than one `strokeWidth` for the path, and so `size` does **not** split it into one trail per value the way it splits a line. Its legend names two channels differently from every other mark's: colour goes on the `stroke` however the mark is filled, since the swatch is a short stroke, and `size` becomes `strokeWidth`. The **runtime** draws a `strokeWidth` legend at the symbol's size rather than the scale's stroke width, so the fixture states `legend: null`

`defaultType`, which is read off the *definition* and not off the data — nothing has read a row when it runs. A latitude is quantitative and a shape, facet or `strokeDash` nominal whatever they carry; `order` is ordinal; a `sort` written as a **list** makes the field ordinal; a `timeUnit` makes it temporal; a `bin` or **any aggregate except `argmin`/`argmax`** makes it quantitative; a stated `scale.type` answers by category (numeric and discretizing → quantitative, time → temporal); and only then does it fall through to nominal, with a report. Falling straight through instead turns a summed measure into a category per distinct total, and draws a bar chart as a scatter of squares along a diagonal

Both fields reach the scale domain and both names reach the axis title (`start, end`), and the secondary channel takes its type from the channel it bounds — `{"x2": {"field": "end"}}` is how every ranged mark is written

**`"-x"`** — a shorthand naming another *channel*, with the minus for descending, which is how most sorted bar charts are written: the categories are ordered by the aggregate of that channel's field, computed from the pre-aggregation table. Read as an unrecognised string it became the default alphabetical order, a chart sorted the wrong way rather than one that failed. Beside it, `"sort": "descending"`, a **written-out list** of values, a sort object over an aggregate of another field, or sorting by another channel's encoding. An aggregate sort reads the *pre-aggregation* table, which is named in the output for it, so the ordering is computed independently of the aggregation being drawn. A list is not a comparator Vega has: each row's *place* in it is computed as a column and the domain sorts on the smallest place a category carries, so a value the list never names falls past the end and lands last. A sort with no `op` takes `min`, or `sum` where the sort field is not one of the stack's own dimensions — sorting by a field each category has once means the smallest is the value, and sorting by a field the stack accumulates means asking which column is tallest

`calculate`, `filter`, `aggregate` — whose `groupby` is a **set**, a column named twice being grouped by once, unlike a `joinaggregate`, which Vega takes as written — `bin` and `stack`, which are the same nodes their channel-written counterparts produce with everything stated rather than derived (`makeFromTransform`, where only the `as` has a rule of its own: one name becomes the pair of edges), `joinaggregate`, `window`, `fold` and `flatten` — both of which always write their output names, filling in `key`/`value` and each field's own, since those names are what everything downstream groups and scales by — `pivot`, `sample`, `extent`, `quantile`, `density`, `regression` and `loess`, and `impute` — as a transform of its own, naming its field, key and grouping, or on a position channel, either way taking a `keyvals` written as a **sequence**, and either way three transforms rather than one where the method is not `value`: Vega's `impute` fills a gap with a *constant* and nothing else, so the gap is filled with null, a `window` averages over the frame (which belongs to the window), and a formula writes the result back over the nulls, which becomes a `sequence(...)` signal — the *other* position is its key and a path mark's series fields are its grouping, so one series' gaps are filled from its own rows; a method other than `value` becomes a `window` beside it written back over the nulls,. A `filter` takes an expression or a **predicate object** — `equal`, `lt`/`lte`/`gt`/`gte`, `range`, `oneOf`, `valid`, over `and`/`or`/`not` — compiled to the expression upstream chose rather than an equivalent of it — including the two rules a **date** brings with it: a month or quarter written as a *number* is one-based to the reader and zero-based to `datetime()`, where one written as a *name* has already been resolved and must not be shifted again; and a **binned** time unit needs no bucketing on the way into the comparison, the column already holding the bucket — and a predicate also settles the *type* of the column it compares, which a CSV would not otherwise know. `lookup` joins a second table: its data stands *beside* the view's source rather than below it — a join reads a second table, it does not derive from the first — and is named in the same sequence. Both grammars say `fields` and mean different things, which is the one thing to get right: Vega's `fields` are the rows' own columns to match on and its `values` are what to bring across, where Vega-Lite's `lookup` is the first and `from.fields` the second. A lookup naming a **parameter** rather than a dataset joins against the rows that selection has picked: the selection is materialised as a table of its own — a filter on it hung off the view's main output, `materializeSelections` — and with no `from.fields` the whole matched row is nested under a name, which for a parameter lookup falls back to the parameter's own. Only the selections a lookup actually names are materialised, an output nobody reads still costing a dataset name; and the join's `from` is corrected after the flow has been walked and named, since the dataset that output node turns out to be is not known before then

Gridlines and axis emitted as the two guides upstream emits, with `gridScale`, `tickCount` following the plot size (`ceil(width/40)`, or `ceil(width/10)` when binned), `labelFlush`, `labelOverlap`, the 270-degree label angle a nominal horizontal axis takes, and a `zindex` that paints a heatmap's axes over its cells. An axis given explicit `values` is asked for no tick *count*: it has been told how many. A **conditional** axis property — `gridDash`, `tickColor`, any of the pairs `CONDITIONAL_AXIS_PARTS` names — moves onto the `encode` block of the part it paints, and its `test` is a *predicate* in a `filter`'s grammar compiled through the same function, so a gridline dashed everywhere but January says so as an expression Vega reads. A theme may write those, and `labelExpr`, in `config.axisX` as much as in `config.axis` — Vega has no name for either, so they are resolved onto the axis here rather than left in the configuration; the blocks are searched most specific first, the scale-named ones (`axisTemporal`, `axisXBand`) outranking the rest

Not a Vega axis property at all: `assembleAxis` destructures it out and writes `encode.labels.update.text` from it, on the axis that draws labels and not on the gridline axis beside it. Passed through as a property it was silently ignored. Where an encode block already states the text, `datum.label` in the expression means *that* text rather than the axis's own, so the two compose

The same rule as the axis's, which is upstream's: `assembleLegend` destructures it out of the component and writes `encode.labels.update.text` from it. Passed through it survived into the emitted Vega and the *Vega* parser reported it as an unknown property two stages later, while the labels were drawn from the scale's domain at full length — and the untruncated labels are what the legend's width is computed from, so a chart overflowed whatever held it with no way for a host to compensate. Applied after the encode parts are assembled, so where a block already states the labels' text `datum.label` means *that* text and the two compose

capabilities.feature: A baseline over an unknown domain
capabilities.notes: `domainHasZero` has three answers, not two — `definitely`, `definitely-not` and **`maybe`** — and the third is the common one, a domain read from a column not being known until the data is. The `maybe` case decides nothing here and hands the question to Vega, which has the data: `scale('y', inrange(0, domain('y')) ? 0 : domain('y')[0])`. Reading `maybe` as "no" put a baseline at the bottom of the data rather than at the origin whenever the column straddled it

`varName`, run over every name a model hands out. A column called `IMDB Rating` gives a bin signal `bin_maxbins_10_IMDB Rating_bins`, which is not a name Vega's expression language can read — every scale domain, extent and axis mentioning it was a parse error waiting to happen. Anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]` becomes an underscore, and a leading digit takes one in front of it

`assembleTitle` splits on the kind of model. A **unit or layer** anchors its title to the *group*, which keeps it over the plotting area when an axis widens the drawing to its left; a **composition** takes `anchor: "start"` instead, having no one plotting area to sit over. A plot inside a concatenation is still a unit, so it frames its group while the concatenation above it anchors to the start

A stated `labelAngle` turns the caption to face its cell, `defaultHeaderGuideAlign` and its baseline twin both opening with "if the angle is stated": a **row**'s captions run down the side of the grid, right-aligned against the cells and centred on them. A stated `spacing` is the gap between cells and beats the configured twenty. `assembleHeaderProperties`: a header names its properties `titleFontSize`/`labelFontSize` where a Vega title names them `fontSize`, so each part is a rename. Without it a header's whole styling was read and dropped

`mergeValuesWithExplicit`: a value the specification **stated** beats one derived from a field, and only where both are derived — or both stated — does the tie-breaker join them. One field encoded as both a colour and a size, titled on one of them, is titled by the one that was written; and an axis whose **guide** names a title keeps it rather than gaining every layer's field name after it

capabilities.feature: A bucketed column read through a scale
capabilities.notes: `interpolatedSignalRef`: a bucketed column is read at its bucket's **middle**, through every scale and not only a position — `scale("size", 0.5 * datum["bin_a"] + 0.5 * datum["bin_a_end"])`. It matters for the legend as much as for the mark: a size legend's swatches are drawn from the scale, and a mark placed at a bucket's near edge would be a size the legend never shows. At a band position of 0 or 1 the interpolation is skipped and Vega scales the column itself. The runtime draws such a legend as one swatch per **bucket**, labelled with the interval it covers, rather than one per boundary

A facet channel is lifted out of the encoding before the scales are built — it says nothing about what a cell *looks like* — but the column it breaks the chart down by may still need bucketing, and upstream does that on the facet's own model, above the cell's. So a trellis broken down by `year(date)` buckets the year before it buckets the quarter. A cell's caption goes through the same rule a mark's text does (`formatSignalRef` with `expr: "parent"`), so a bucketed instant is captioned as a date with the specifier Vega picks at render time

capabilities.feature: A stacked bar with rounded corners
capabilities.notes: `getGroupsForStackedBarWithCornerRadius`: the radius belongs to the *stack*, not to the segment at its end, so the stack is faceted into a group that carries the radius and clips, and the segments are drawn inside it with none. The group's extent along the stack is the min and max of every segment's two ends in **pixels**, the accumulation being in data space and the rounding not; the inner group undoes the outer one's translation. The test is truthy, so a stated radius of zero leaves a plain rect, and a bar with a `size` encoding is left alone — its segments would no longer fill the group's thickness

`extractTransformsFromEncoding`: a **time unit** on a composite mark's channel becomes a transform of its own, the summary coming after the bucketing — one interval per bucket, not one per instant — and a channel that is not itself temporal is then told to read the column as a time. The grouping is every channel but the continuous axis, colour included, and a field named on two channels is named twice; a tooltip is taken out before the grouping is read and only the part of it asking for an aggregate is put back. The tooltip keeps each channel's own title

capabilities.feature: A binned field on a discrete scale
capabilities.notes: `binRequiresRange`: an ordinal channel has no numbers left to derive labels from, so the bin writes them out into a `_range` column, and the scale's domain, the mark's position and the aggregate's grouping all read it. The domain sorts by the bin's own **start**, labels not sorting into numeric order. The spoken *description* still reads the bin's range where upstream reads the raw column — one difference, on the accessibility text alone

`autoMaxBins`: ten along an axis, **six** on a colour, a size or a facet, and four on a stroke dash. The number goes into the field's own *name*, so reading ten everywhere renamed every column a binned colour scale produced

capabilities.feature: A column bucketed before it arrived
capabilities.notes: `binnedyearmonth` and its kin say the *data* did the bucketing, and almost every rule reading a time unit has to know it: there is no `timeunit` transform, only a formula computing where the bucket ends (`timeOffset('month', datum['date'], 1)`); the field keeps its own name, `vgField` skipping the prefix; the title is the field's own, there being no derivation to announce; and the stack groups by the bucket's start alone

`isContinuousToContinuous` includes the two time scales, so a temporal colour scale is a **gradient** legend and not a row of square swatches, and its labels take the configured date format outright — `omitTimeFormatConfig` is true for an axis and false for a legend. It compiles exactly as upstream compiles it, and the runtime draws it: `ScaleResolver` routes `time` and `utc` to `buildSequentialColor` the moment the range holds colours, exactly as it routes `linear`. This row said the runtime could not, which was true once and left behind by the code with nothing checking it.

`getMarkPropOrConfig` reads the mark, then the style blocks it names, then the mark type's configuration. Reading only the mark wrote `align: "center"` beside a label styled `{align: "left"}` — the default overriding the very thing the style was for. The runtime honours a style block's `align`, `baseline`, `dx` and `dy` too, which it had been reading only from the encoding

An aggregate that answers with a whole **row**: `{"aggregate": {"argmax": "US Gross"}, "field": "Production Budget"}` asks for the production budget *of* the highest-grossing row. The three parts play different roles — the aggregate is taken over `US Gross` and names its output column after it, the `field` is a path *into* the row and is appended unescaped since it is a real step into a real object, and the default title reads `Production Budget for max US Gross`. Every field definition contributes to the aggregate too, not only the channels' own, since a `tooltip` written as a list may be the only thing asking for one

capabilities.feature: A size scale over binned positions
capabilities.notes: `sizeRangeMax` reads a *step*, and a binned position has none until the bin transform has chosen its boundaries — so the largest mark is an expression reading the signal the bin published, not a number. A scale that maps a continuum onto **buckets** takes `interpolateRange` instead, Vega having no way to interpolate a discretizing range itself: the sequence is written out as an expression

Legends are grouped by the **field** they encode rather than by the scale, as `assembleLegends` groups them: one field encoded twice, as a colour *and* as a size, is one key to the reader and one legend whose swatches carry both, where keying by the scale gave two side by side saying the same thing. The scale's own prefix stays in the key, so a composition resolving its legends independently still gets one per plot, and so does the discreteness — a ramp and a set of swatches cannot be the same legend

`scale`, `axis` and `legend`, per channel. A shared channel keeps its plain name and one scale takes every view's domain; an independent one is named for the child that owns it — `layer_1_y`, which is the whole of what makes a chart **dual-axis**, or `concat_0_color`, which puts a key inside each plot instead of one beside the chart. The resolve governs the **outermost** composition and nothing below it, as upstream's per-model resolve does, and the child it names is a composition child rather than an expanded view: a line that draws its own points is two views under one layer, and naming from the view would give them a scale each. `parseGuideResolve` then forces an independent guide wherever the scale is independent, one axis being unable to label two scales; two independent axes on a channel are moved onto opposite sides, counting the side each *asked* for, and only the first rules gridlines

A **variable** parameter is a Vega signal and little else: a `value`, an `expr` computing it from the others, and a `bind` describing the input that sets it — `assembleParameterSignals`, emitted after the layout's own signals since a parameter may read a size. `{"value": {"expr": …}}` on a channel is **not a literal**: the expression becomes a `signal` in the same value ref, so a `datum` written that way still passes through its scale. A **selection** parameter — one carrying `select` — compiles too, as its own row below

Symbol and gradient legends, the symbol type the mark implies (`stroke` for a line, `square` for a bar), and a swatch built from the mark's **own** colour encoding with what it cannot say taken away: the channel this legend explains, and any colour that is a scaled field, since a swatch has no datum to scale — a stroke is dropped and a fill becomes black at the mark's opacity. Building the swatch from the mark's *default* colour instead looks identical whenever the mark has no colour encoding, and paints a size legend's swatches in the default blue on every chart that does. Several views encoding one channel get **one** legend between them, merged property by property: a bar fills its swatch and a point strokes one, so the merged key carries `fill` and `stroke` alike, and where the two disagree the first view's answer stands except that a circle wins over any other glyph and two titles are joined. What comes out of the symbol encoding is then decided by the *merged* legend's own channels — a point's `fill: transparent` is right alone and blanks every swatch beside a scaled `fill`

Three forms, and they produce different things: a **list** of fields becomes an object of title-to-value pairs, which reads as a small table; a **single** field becomes that field's own value, formatted the way its guide would format it; and `tooltip: true` on the mark definition asks for every encoded field. An array of values is joined with *line breaks* here and with spaces in the spoken description, a tooltip being a table and a description a sentence. `{"content": "data"}` shows the whole row

The `description` signal upstream builds from every encoded field, formatted the way that field's own guide would format it, and `ariaRoleDescription` for a mark whose Vega type does not name it. The name each field is announced by is the **field's** own title, not its guide's: hiding an axis title with `axis: {title: null}` is a restyling, and reading the guide's title there dropped the whole channel out of what a screen reader says. A definition's own `format` is honoured wherever a value is read as text, and the value a **normalized** stack announces is the share it takes — `end - start` through `config.normalizedNumberFormat` — not the quantity behind it

The `longitude` and `latitude` channels and the projection that turns them into pixels: a `geojson` transform gathering each pair into a feature collection, a `geopoint` asking the projection where it lands, and the mark reading the two columns it wrote rather than a scale. A fitted projection is given the plotting area and the collections to fill it with; one stating its own `scale` or `translate` takes the middle of the area instead. `equalEarth` is the default type, and a layer whose members agree about the projection has **one**, named for the layer and fitted to everything they draw. The **`geoshape`** mark has no position at all: the projection draws it, through a transform hung below the mark that runs after the encoding, naming the column the outlines are in where the rows carry them. `{"sphere": true}` is one row saying so — the whole globe as a feature — and `{"graticule": true}` a transform drawing the globe's grid, which is **not filled**, filling it having painted over the map beneath. A projection is handed down as the data is, a property written as an expression is a signal, and a merged projection carries only what its members specified, so a layer saying nothing about the kind of map it wants writes nothing where a single view falls back to `equalEarth`. A **second** coordinate pair is a second place, projected into a second pair of columns, and a mark spanning two places reads both ends from what the projection wrote — a rule between them has no `x` or `y` at all. All four geographic channels default to quantitative. A table a chart both joins against and draws from is given a named point of its own, so the join reads the table bare rather than the drawing's own steps. A geoshape is always reachable, a click on a map being a click on a country. A `lookup` naming no `from.fields` brings the whole matched record across under a name, which is how a column of outlines arrives; such a column is a feature collection of its own — the rows with nothing to draw dropped first — has no scale, and is one object in a spoken description rather than a list. A **facet** merges its cells' projections as a layer does, so a grid of maps is drawn at one scale. Fitting works, composites included, and every fixture here is checked against upstream's drawing as well as its compiler. A fit published by **two** datasets that each read it back has no ordering that resolves each dataset once, and does not need one: the fit is **eventually consistent**, refitting as each collection arrives

capabilities.feature: A `repeat` or a `facet` inside a concatenation
capabilities.notes: A repetition is a concatenation of its copies, so one nested in a `vconcat` is normalised where it stands and the ordinary nesting takes it. A **facet** there is a grid belonging to the plot that holds it: its group has no plotting area — no style, no `encode`, a title anchored to the start — the size its name carries is one cell's, its cells resolve their scales as a facet's do rather than as a concatenation's, and its values stand beside the table they are drawn from. A facet inside a **facet** is still reported: a grid whose every cell is itself a grid needs a second level of cell groups

A picture placed where a point would be. Positioned exactly as a rect is — a stated width and height centre it, a channel pair spans it — with its `url` read as text the way `href` is. Not painted: `baseEncodeEntry` ignores colour for an image, so no fill is written. The centring is a general rule rather than a rule about pictures: with no second position but a size the mark states outright, the extent is that size and the position becomes an aligned one, `vgAlignedPositionChannel` centring it by default

A chart animated frame by frame. The channel is a **band** scale over the column the frames run through, stepped at `config.scale.framesPerSecond`, drawn with nothing and read by the signals that advance the frame: `anim_clock`, `last_tick_at` and `is_playing` at the top of the chart, and per view the domain's start, the range's extent and the value the elapsed time inverts to. What advances is the time *elapsed* since the last tick, so a paused chart keeps its place. The frame is a table of its own — the selection's filter is lifted out of the view's main table onto a `<name>_curr` beside it — so the scales still measure the whole column while the marks read one frame

Either channel or both, compiled the way upstream compiles it and drawn where upstream draws it: a cell group faceted from the data — *crossed* when both channels are present, so a combination no row carries still gets a cell and the grid stays rectangular — a `<channel>_domain` dataset per channel for the layout to count and the headers to title from, a `layout` block with the `offset` that keeps a heading clear of the captions beneath it, `child_width`/`child_height` sizes, the facet fields joining every grouping so a stack stays inside its cell, and the axes split: gridlines in each cell, the labelled axis in a band drawn once. Which of the four bands a shared axis lands in follows the **axis's own orientation** — top or left is a header, bottom or right a footer — and the facet channel decides only whether that band is one group per cell or a single group; choosing the band from the facet's *direction* instead is what drew a row-faceted chart's x axis above the chart. A channel's `sort` orders the *cells* — it lands on the group mark that makes them and on the header bands beside it. A bare `"ascending"`/`"descending"` is honoured, and so is an **aggregate** of another column on a facet gridded one way: the key is computed twice under two names, as `sum_amount` on the domain dataset for the header bands to sort on and as `sum_amount_by_era` on the cell's own `from.facet.aggregate` for the cells, suffixed with the faceted field so the two cannot collide (`DEFAULT_SORT_OP` is `min`, not `sum`). A sort by a written-out **list** is honoured too, and by the same route it takes upstream: `parseAllForSortIndex` writes each row's place in the list onto it as a `<channel>_<field>_sort_index`, and the grid then orders itself by the *greatest* of each cell's, which is the only one a cell has. An aggregate sort on a facet gridded **both** ways works too, and that is what the writing-first is for: a cell of a crossed grid is one row-value and one column-value together, so its group is keyed by both, while a sort ordering the rows is keyed by the row field alone. The two cannot be one aggregate, so `makeJoinAggregateFromFacet` computes the key over its own grouping and writes it onto every row; the cell then takes the *greatest* of what its rows already carry, every row of a cell holding the same number. Where a cell's chain cannot be hoisted above the facet — a domain sorted by an aggregate needs the pre-aggregation table, which is a named point the scales read and where `moveFacetDown` stops — the chain stays **below** it and is computed once per cell, over the rows that cell was handed, while a copy of it with the facet's fields added to every grouping is hung beside the facet for the scales to measure (`cloneSubtree`). The cell's datasets are then assembled by a second walk rooted at the *partition* rather than at the table the facet reads, emitted in the group mark's own `data` and numbered in sequence with the outer ones; the `*_domain` datasets move to where the facet is; and the group's `sort` reads the key the cell measured for itself. However many layers a cell draws, they share the one partition, and a later layer rebuilds only its **own** steps below it — what an ancestor wrote is the facet model's and stands above the partition already, and so is the sort index a facet listed by hand. The two formulas a crossed grid needs are written in the order the facet was **declared**, `forEachFieldDef` walking a model's encoding as it stands, while everything else about the grid stays ordered row-before-column. A scale or a guide resolved independently belongs to the *cell*, which is the facet's one child — never to the layers inside it, so a trellis of layers measuring its `x` per cell has one `child_x` and one axis over the picture; where the flow splits, that scale reads the cell's own tables, and an axis in the cell drawing its grid across no other scale aliases the `width` or `height` it falls back to. Which axes go in a band and which stay in the cell is `parseGuideResolve`'s answer rather than the scale's alone: an independent scale forces an independent guide, and `resolve: {"axis": {"x": "independent"}}` asks for one on its own, leaving the grid with no band to draw and so no `*_domain` dataset for one to read. Where the cells size themselves **and** the grid is faceted both ways, the counting happens once per cell in a `cross_<column>_<row>` dataset grouped by every facet field and each band takes the greatest of its own — counting along its own direction only, a row band being as tall as a cell and knowing nothing of how wide one is. `align` and `bounds` are still reported: cells are gridded the way `align: "each"` does, which differs from the `"all"` Vega-Lite asks for only where the cells are not all one size

`defaultScaleResolve` settles which channels a composition shares and which it gives each child, and a stated `resolve` overrides it — but only for channels that *can* be shared. Where the children ask for scale types of different families — a colour ramp over counts beside a pair of named colours — `parseNonUnitScaleCore` switches the channel to independent before merging anything, since there is no one scale that is both, and the layers get `layer_0_color` beside `layer_1_color`. The families are upstream's own, including its written-out exception: an ordinal *position* can stand for instants

A nested concatenation contributes upward only the dimension it shares **as a whole**: a column of plots has one width and its `childHeight` is one cell's, so a row of columns must not merge on it. The plain name is what says which of the two a level settled. A nested concatenation may also carry a title of its own, and being a composition it anchors to the start. One construct, as it is upstream (`ConcatModel`), differing only in `columns`. Each plot keeps its **own** position scales and axes — `defaultScaleResolve` makes `x` and `y` independent — so `concat_0_x` stands beside `concat_1_x` while one colour legend covers both; the marks and axes move into a group per plot and the top level keeps the data, the shared scales, the legends and a `layout` placing the groups. `columns` decides which sizes merge: a row shares a height and a column shares a width, so the merged size is called `height`/`width` along that axis and `childHeight`/`childWidth` across it, and the merge is abandoned outright when the plots disagree or any is sized by a step. A plot may have its own `data`, and may itself be a **concatenation**: the names compose (`concat_0_concat_1_x`), the sizes merge per level innermost first — a nested one contributing upwards only what its own children agreed on — and the layout signals come out in tree order, each level's own before it recurses. A nested concatenation's group carries a `layout` and nothing else, being a place rather than a plotting area

Not a compiler construct: upstream normalizes it away into a concatenation of the same view with `{"repeat": …}` replaced by a real column name in each copy, and so does this. All three forms — a **list** laid out under `columns`, **`row`/`column`** crossed into a scatter-plot matrix whose width is the number of columns rather than `columns`, and **`layer`**, which stays a layer. Each copy names itself (`child__amount`, `child__row_amount_column_score`) and a spec's own name beats the one its parent offered it, which is why the scales read `child__amount_x`; the grid takes `align: "all"` where a plain concatenation takes `each`, the copies being one view drawn several times

Two constructs under one name. A **`row`/`column`** operator is the same chart as the same channels written in the view's encoding — upstream's two outputs are byte for byte identical — so the channels move down and nothing else changes; `columns` beside it is reported and dropped, as upstream's `columnsNotSupportByRowCol` does. A **wrapped** facet, `{"facet": {"field": …}, "columns": n}`, is a layout of its own: with one list and a number to wrap it at, the grid's rows and columns are *computed* — `ceil(length(facet_domain) / columns)` and `min(length(facet_domain), columns)`, as two `sequence` datasets — and the shared axes are drawn once per position rather than once per value. The caption moves to the cell, there being no band of column headings to name it in

A production rule *ends* in the mark's own value: `color(model, {filled})` hands it to `nonPosition` as the `defaultValue`, and a rule with no unconditional arm drew every mark the condition did not catch in Vega's default rather than the chart's. A condition on a **`test`** compiles: the channel becomes a Vega production rule, an array of `{test, …}` entries tried in order with the unconditional one last, and each entry is built by the same reference builder as the unconditional part — so a condition may name a value, a `datum` or a field just as freely. The test itself is a `filter`'s grammar, an expression or a field predicate, through the same compiler, which is what keeps `oneOf` spelled `indexof(…) !== -1` in one place. A condition naming a `param` is refused *by itself*, leaving the rest of the definition standing

Both kinds compile in full. A point selection on a **bucketed** field remembers the bucket — its two edges — rather than the raw column, so the test asks whether a row falls between them and a click picks the bar rather than the row. A projection is keyed by the **field**, so a column bound to both channels is remembered once under the channel that reached it first — the diagonal cell of a scatter-plot matrix — while a scale-bound selection is still panned and zoomed in both directions, its anchor following the view's scales rather than its projection, and the signal it is read through at the top names every field any copy is scaled by. Either kind may be **projected** onto channels or onto bare fields, which is what decides what a picked row is remembered by: a click that projects onto `x` remembers the date under the pointer rather than the row, and records the channel it came from so a test knows what the value was compared against. A **point** selection is a store dataset of the tuples a reader clicked, an `identifier` transform giving every row a `_vgsid_` to be remembered by, and the signals that write the store — `_tuple`, `_toggle`, `_modify` — beside the `unit` each tuple records itself against. An **interval** is a drag, which is more: a pixel extent and a data extent per projected channel, each answering to six streams — the press that starts it, the move that drags it, the scale change that rewrites it, the double click that clears it, and the pan and zoom that move it — a `_scale_trigger` that fires when a scale it reads is rebuilt, and the brush drawn as **two** rects, a background under the marks so the data stays legible through it and an outline over them so it can be grabbed. What each projection stores follows the scale: a **range** over a continuous one, since that is what a drag names, the covered **categories** over a band or a point scale, since there is nothing between two categories — which is also why such a scale's change clears the brush (`[0, 0]`) rather than moving it. A selection belongs to the **unit** that declared it, not to the chart: its tuples record that view's name, its machinery is written inside that plot's group, and its brush is drawn around that plot's marks, which is what makes one plot of a concatenation filter another. A stated `value` opens the chart already brushed — a row in the store and an `init` on the signals. `empty: false` withdraws the empty store's blanket pass; it does not negate the test. Inside a **facet** the machinery belongs to the cell: every signal in it reads the pointer against one cell's scales, and so does the brush rectangle, which is dragged across one cell's rows. What stays outside is what a cell cannot own — the store, the signal it resolves into, and whatever a control writes, a widget being part of the page rather than of the drawing; a scale-bound selection keeps its per-channel signals in the cell and pushes them outward to bare ones declared at the top. The cell then carries a `facet` signal naming the cell the pointer is in, and a picked tuple records the cell as an expression rather than a name. A selection bound to controls is bound to them alone unless it asked for the pointer by name. Selections can be read from a `{"param": …}` condition, from a `filter` transform, and — as a *table* of the rows they have picked — from a `lookup`. A stated starting `value` is a row already in the store, keyed by the **channel** first and the field second, so a selection projected through `x` is initialised as `{"x": …}`; an instant written there becomes the millisecond it names rather than a `datetime(…)` call, a store being data and not an expression. A selection **bound to the scales** — `"bind": "scales"` — is a pan and a zoom rather than a brush: no rectangle is drawn, each channel keeps only its data signal, and the scale reads the drag back through `domainRaw`, which is why the pan divides by the plot's size rather than by the brush's span and the zoom anchors at the *inverted* pointer. A log, a power or a symlog scale is panned and zoomed by its own function, with its base, exponent or constant passed along. A scale domain may also name a selection, `{"domain": {"param": …}}`, which does not replace the computed domain — the selection is assembled to `domainRaw` beside it — and does not suppress `nice`, a stated domain doing that only when it is an array. Either way the mark is **clipped**, a pan past the data otherwise drawing the rows outside the plot. The events a selection reacts to are **parsed**, not passed through: Vega's event-selector grammar — a source before a colon, a mark name after an `@`, bracketed filters, a throttle in braces, a `!` for consumption, and a `[start, end] > during` window — is ported from `vega-event-selector`, so `on`, `translate` and `zoom` may each be written as a selector and a chart may carry two brushes distinguished by a modifier key. A brush's own `mark` block splits between the two rects it is drawn as, the fill below and the outline above, and the brushes nest rather than queue. `nearest: true` compiles to a **voronoi** overlay — one transparent cell per point, each covering the ground closest to it — which the selection listens on instead of the marks. `bind` may also name **controls**, one per projected field, and then the controls are the interaction: each projection gets a signal of its own at the top of the chart, the tuple becomes an expression over them rather than a listener, and the click, the clear and the toggle come off the selection unless the specification asked for them by name — so the marks stop showing a pointer too. `bind` to a **legend** makes the legend the control: its swatches, labels and rows are named so the selection's signal can listen on them and made interactive so the click lands, the picked categories are drawn solid and the rest at `unselectedOpacity`, and the signal walks the scene graph to the symbol's datum because a legend entry carries no tuple of its own. Direct manipulation goes as it does for an input binding, but the toggle stays, so shift-clicking adds to the picked set

capabilities.feature: A path that draws its own points (`point`, `line`)
capabilities.notes: `{"type": "line", "point": true}` is two marks written as one, and upstream normalizes it into a **layer** before compiling anything — the pass now exists here too. The base keeps everything but `point`/`line`; an area with no opacity of its own fades to 0.7 first, so what is drawn over it stays legible; the overlay takes the base's stack offset, because a `point` does not stack of its own accord and would otherwise sit at the raw value rather than on its band; and `x2`/`y2` are dropped, because a line given a second position becomes a rule and draws a bar out of every point. `point: "transparent"` asks for points that are there and invisible, and a `shape` channel on a path mark asks for points at all

A whisker runs along the **measured** axis, and saying so is what centres it on the other: a boxplot with no discrete channel has nothing to span, so its parts sit in the middle of the plot rather than filling it edge to edge

`errorbar` and `errorband` are one rewrite with different parts drawn from it: a summary of one continuous field per group, then a layer per part over that summary. The **extent** chooses the aggregates and the distinction matters — `stderr` and `stdev` are a *width* measured from a centre, so they aggregate the centre and the width and then add and subtract, while `ci` and `iqr` are two *positions* and so two more aggregates. Which parts are drawn is configuration: `config.errorbar` is `rule: true, ticks: false`, so a plain error bar is one rule per group. An `extent` of `ci` compiles but does not draw — `ci0`/`ci1` are a bootstrap over a thousand random resamples, which the runtime declines by name because a scene has to be reproducible. **`boxplot`** is a *layer of layers*, and has to be, because its parts read different tables: the quartiles are found first and joined back onto every row, which is what lets a row be compared with its own group's box; the flow then forks, one branch keeping the rows outside the whiskers and drawing them as points, the other keeping the rows inside and taking their extremes as the whisker ends. `extent: "min-max"` is the older, simpler form — whiskers to the extremes and no outliers, because with the whiskers there nothing can be outside them. An error bar or band over rows that **already carry** their interval is summarised by reading rather than aggregating: `x2` beside `x` names both ends outright, and `xError` names a width measured from `x` — one arm where the interval is symmetric, two where `xError2` gives the other, upstream *signing* the second rather than subtracting it. Nothing is grouped, since nothing is being collapsed

Every mark lands exactly where upstream puts it; the surface around them still comes out between half a unit and a unit small in each direction. Since nothing drawn has moved, the shortfall is in a guide *extent* — the one input the mark comparison cannot see, because text bounds are excluded by design (docs/adr/0006). The test asserts the shape of the difference rather than tolerating it silently
One container per datum, translated by its `x`/`y`, painting its fill and stroke over its declared `width` × `height`. `clip` narrows it. Nests to any depth

`groupby` only, on one or more fields. Cells appear in first-appearance order and each cell's datum is the groupby fields plus `count`, matching the `aggregate` transform upstream inserts. Pre-faceted `facet.field` and extra `facet.aggregate` measures are reported

Every value reference accepts all four, applied after the scale in upstream's order — `round(pow(v, e) * m + o)` — and each is itself a value reference, so an offset can be read from the datum: `{"field": "y", "offset": {"field": "height", "mult": 0.5}}` centres a label in a band whose height only the row knows. They had been read on a *scaled* channel only, so `{"field": "x2", "offset": -5}` placed a label at the end of the bar instead of just inside it, with nothing reported

capabilities.feature: A mark drawn from another mark (`from.data: "<mark name>"`)
capabilities.notes: Marks and datasets share one namespace in Vega, so a mark may be drawn from the *scene items* an earlier named mark produced — which is how a radar chart labels each vertex of its line and closes the ring its rules describe. Each item is the mark's resolved channels plus `datum`, the row behind it, so a label reads `datum.x` for the vertex and `datum.datum.value` for the number. `x` is derived from `xc` or `x2` the way upstream's `adjustSpatial` derives it, and a `rule` is exempt from that as upstream exempts it. Only marks declared **before** the reader are visible, which is upstream's order too; a name that resolves to neither a dataset nor an earlier mark says so in those words

It does not place ticks; it caps the *count* — `count = min(count, floor(span / minStep || 1) + 1)` — so a span holding one minimum step allows two ticks whatever the axis asked for. A plain numeric scale then keeps shrinking the count while the step d3 would choose is still under the minimum; a binned, logarithmic or temporal one does not, their steps not shrinking monotonically with the count. Vega-Lite writes it on every bucketed axis as one bucket's duration, and without it an axis over two months offered sixteen ticks

The fields are **field accessors on the scene item**, not expressions: Vega hands them to `vega-util`'s `field()`, so `x` and `y` name where the item ended up and `datum["era"]` is the path `datum` → `era`, naming a column of the row the item was bound to. A faceted group sorted by its own facet key is the case that matters — it is what decides which cell of a trellis goes where — and a chart whose categories already arrive in order hides the difference entirely. A path neither reading can resolve leaves the order alone rather than inventing one

Every *combination* of the grouping values gets a cell, empty or not, so a trellis crossed by two fields stays a rectangle — without it the cells after a gap slide into it and every header beside them names the wrong one. Crossed only where there is more than one dimension to cross, and the missing cells are **added after** the ones the rows made rather than the order being rebuilt. An empty cell then draws **nothing at all**, not even its gridlines: Vega instantiates a faceted group's subflow only for keys that rows arrived under, so a cell `cross` invented is a group with no contents

d3's SI prefix. An axis shares **one** prefix, chosen from its largest tick as `tickFormat` pins it, so the labels read `−1.0k` beside `0.0k` rather than `0` beside `−1.0k`; the decimals come from `precisionPrefix`, which counts what is needed to tell one step apart *after* the division. A bare `format(x, "s")` with no axis around it chooses per value, as d3 does

Marks with `zindex: 0` paint first in specification order, then the rest sorted by `zindex` and declaration. That is upstream's rule and not the obvious one: a **negative** `zindex` raises a mark above its neighbours rather than sinking it, because `zorder` partitions on `if (item.zindex)` instead of sorting the whole list. Encoding order is unchanged — a mark reading back another mark's items still needs it built first. Per-*item* `zindex`, from an encode channel, is still reported

capabilities.feature: A mark drawn from a **group** mark
capabilities.notes: The same namespace, and the item is the group's own encoded channels plus `datum` — its facet tuple. That is how a trellis titles each cell: a text mark drawn from the group reads `width` for the centre, `y` for the row and `datum.site` for the name, none of which any dataset holds. A group placed by a `layout` reports the position it encoded rather than the one the grid gave it, which is a known difference and the only case where the two disagree

capabilities.feature: Guide `encode`: a legend label read through a scale
capabilities.notes: `encode.labels.update.text` with `{"scale": "label", "field": "value"}` — how a cluster's id becomes its name, resolved against the entry as its datum. There is no `legendLabelText` property to fold that into, and `symbols.*.fillOpacity` is the same case: upstream's `symbolOpacity` fades the outline with the swatch, and this fades only what is inside it

`encode.labels.update.x` resolved against the tick as its datum, so `{"scale": "x", "field": "value"}` moves every label to the start of its band. **`update` only**: a guide writes its own text and position into `update` on every pass, so a specification's `enter` is overwritten before anything is drawn — verified upstream, where a label given `enter: {text:...}` still reads its tick's own text. An `enter` block naming one of those is reported as changing nothing rather than as unimplemented, because the rule is Vega's and not this engine's

An axis's `grid`, `ticks`, `domain`, `labels` and `title` blocks, and a legend's `symbols`, `labels` and `title`, folded into the properties they are another spelling of — `encode.grid.enter.strokeDash` **is** `gridDash` upstream, which builds each part from an encode block and extends it with the specification's. Folding rather than overlaying is what makes the block participate in *measurement*: a legend symbol resized through `encode` moves every label beside it. Only constants fold; a `signal`, a `field` or a conditional needs the guide's own datum, which does not exist until the guide is laid out, and each is reported by name along with any part or channel with no property behind it

A nested definition shadows a same-named one outside.
