Two upstream behaviours are reproduced rather than corrected: `parent` is the group's datum, not the group item, so `parent.width` is undefined; and `width`/`height` are inherited, so a nested `"height"` range spans the whole chart unless the group declares its own `height` signal

An `offset` moves the axis away from the plot and the gridlines **back**: upstream gives every gridline endpoint an offset of `sign * axis.offset`, cancelling the translation the axis group carries. Without it a gridline is dragged along with its axis and floats clear of the data it measures

Automatic row and column placement with per-direction padding, at the top level or on a group, and the four bands of labels around it — row and column headers, footers, and a title over each. Every cell in the scope goes on **one** grid whichever group mark produced it, which looks the same whenever there is only one — as every trellis fixture had — and is the difference between two side-by-side plots and two plots on top of each other. Cells are measured by how far their contents reach, not by their declared size, so a trellis whose axis labels hang off to the left leaves room for them. The bands are placed by a port of upstream's `layoutHeaders`, and two of its rules are the ones a reasonable implementation gets wrong: a band's margin is the cells' edge rounded **outwards** to a whole unit and taken against zero as well — so a header clearing a stroked cell border at −0.5 goes to −1, and every guide inside it moves with it — and a *footer* is aligned with the last row or column rather than the first. `layout.offset` is honoured; `align`, `bounds`, `center`, the header and title bands and an `end` title anchor are reported

Encoder handles x/x2/width and y/y2/height pairs, band offsets, fill, stroke, opacity, and all five corner-radius channels — one radius or four independent ones, where a per-corner value of zero squares off that corner alone. A rounded rect is drawn as a **path** in both renderers, not as SVG `rx`/`ry` or `drawRoundRect`: neither can express four radii, and both draw a true arc where Vega draws a Bézier approximation of one at an offset of `1 - 0.448084975506`. The clamp is one limit for all four corners — `min(width, height) / 2`, of the *signed* extents, so a rectangle with a negative extent comes out square. A mark that encodes **either** paint channel gets neither default, as upstream does, so a rect given only a stroke draws as a hollow outline rather than picking up the built-in blue

A missing `x2`/`y2` defaults to `x`/`y`, as upstream. Bounds expand on both axes, which is what upstream does too — verified on `stack-diverging`, where a 1-unit rule spanning the plot bounds to half a unit past each end

`strokeDash`, `strokeCap` and `strokeJoin` as encode channels. A dash pattern with a negative or non-finite entry is dropped rather than half-applied, because SVG and Canvas disagree about what such a pattern draws. `strokeDashOffset`, `strokeMiterLimit` and `strokeOffset` are reported

One `PathNode` per series where upstream emits one item per datum; the harness normalizes both to a point list. A `null` in the data does **not** break the line — upstream reads the coordinate as `item.y \|\| 0` and draws through zero — and the `defined` channel is what breaks it. A line is stroked by default but is **also filled** when the mark encodes a `fill`, which is what shades the inside of a closed radar polygon. All seventeen interpolation methods are implemented, ported from d3-shape and pinned to its own path strings in `CurvesTest`: `linear`, the step family, `basis`, `cardinal`, `catmull-rom`, `bundle`, `monotone` and `natural`, the *open* variants `basis-open`, `cardinal-open` and `catmull-rom-open`, and the closed `linear-closed`, `basis-closed`, `cardinal-closed` and `catmull-rom-closed`. `monotone` is two curves — Vega picks d3's X or Y form from the mark's `orient` — so a horizontal series is monotone in *y*. The closed splines are not the open ones with a `Z` on the end: they wrap their control-point window round the join and emit no `Z` at all past two points. The **open** ones are not the end-pinned ones minus their ends: below three points they draw nothing at all, and at exactly three they draw a single position. `tension` applies to three of the families and means something different in each — a cardinal stiffness, a Catmull-Rom distance exponent, a bundle blend — each with its own default (0, 0.5, 0.85); and a Catmull-Rom spline at exponent 0 is not a degenerate Catmull-Rom but d3's cardinal curve, which is a different shape at the ends

Both orientations, via the (x, y) and (x2, y2) boundary pairs, and a band between two data fields rather than a baseline. Stacking comes from the `stack` transform. `defined` and interpolation as for `line`

All 12 of upstream's shapes, pinned by reference vectors. Sized upstream's way, from `sqrt(size) / 2`, **not** d3-shape's area convention — the two differ by 13% on a circle. A `shape` that is not one of the twelve names is read as an SVG path string, written in a unit box and scaled by the same reference length, so a custom outline sizes with `size` exactly as a built-in one does
Align, baseline, font, size, weight, style, angle and `dx`/`dy`. Metrics are platform metrics, not browser metrics

Annular sectors, so pie and donut charts draw. Angles run clockwise from twelve o'clock. `padAngle`, `padRadius` and `cornerRadius` are d3-shape's own geometry, ported. Neither is what its name suggests: a pad angle is a gap measured at a pad **radius** and converted back to an angle separately for each edge, so the sides of a gap stay parallel rather than splaying; and a corner radius is clamped by where the slice's own edges would meet, so a thin slice rounds less than a fat one and one too small to round loses its corners rather than folding inside out

`align` and `baseline` move the **whole image** rather than text inside a box, so `x` is its left edge, middle or right edge — the opposite of `rect`, where `x` is always the left edge. They are held on the node and applied at paint time, as upstream does, so the scene keeps the `x` the specification gave and two images at different anchors stay distinguishable. `aspect` (default true) letterboxes; `false` stretches. A `width` or `height` left out is taken from the image's own pixels upstream, which the compiler cannot know — the mark is placed with a zero extent and that is reported. An unresolvable URL leaves a gap **and a diagnostic**, never a silent one. Both public views take a `resolveImage` — `VegaChart(resolveImage =)` and `VegaChartView(resolveImage:)` — which the draw targets had taken from the start and neither view could reach, so a chart with a remote image drew every other mark and a hole. Following a URL is the host's decision, the same one `DataLoader` makes about data, so nil resolves nothing by default. On Compose the decode cache is `ImageCache`, remembered across frames: a target is built per draw, so a raster used to be re-decoded on every frame and a resolver asked on every frame. **Refusals are cached too**, on both renderers — a URL that failed was otherwise handed back to the resolver every frame — which is what makes `onUnresolvedImage` on both views a report a host can act on rather than a per-frame stream; `ImageCache.clear()` and `CoreGraphicsTarget.clearImageCache()` give a recovered host another go

The whole SVG path grammar, including implicit repeated commands — where a repeated `M` means `L` — numbers run together without separators, the `S`/`T` control-point reflections, and the elliptical arc converted from its endpoint form. The outline is in its own coordinates and the mark's `x`/`y` place it, with `scaleX`, `scaleY` and `angle` transforming it about that anchor. A string that cannot be read through stops where the reading did and is reported

A **filled** run of capsules, one per segment, overlapping at the shared points — not a stroke, since a stroke has one width. Its `size` is a **width**, halved to a radius, where a symbol's is a squared extent. Compared by the extent it covers rather than by its outline: the caps are semicircles, so this engine's cubics and upstream's true arcs differ in the last decimals, the same way an arc's do

The mark a projected geometry is drawn as: the `geoshape` transform writes the outline and the mark draws it, so it takes the same path as a `path` mark with its `shape` channel read instead of its `path` one
Domain, range, ticks and `nice` match d3 and upstream exactly. See the `zero` row below for when it widens to the origin — it is not what "data-driven" suggests

Rounds every *output* to a whole unit, so a bar's edge lands on a pixel. Not the same `round` a band scale has, which rounds the step and the band width and so moves where every band starts: here nothing about the scale changes. Upstream cannot call `round` on a continuous d3 scale — there is no such method — so it swaps the range interpolator for `interpolateRound`, which is why `invert()` still reads back the unrounded value. It had been parsed and dropped for every continuous type, silently, leaving every bar in the chart a fraction of a unit wide

Flips the **range**, leaving the domain alone, for every scale type. Reversing the domain instead maps every value to the same place, so the chart looks right and the ticks, labels and domain line all come out backwards

Ticks land on calendar boundaries from d3's own table; `nice` widens to one of them; each label is written at its own granularity, so a monthly axis reads "2026" every January and "February" otherwise. A day is a calendar day, so a daily tick holds midnight across a daylight-saving change. Locales and explicit axis format strings are not implemented

`format.parse` with `date`, `number`, `string` and `boolean`. ISO 8601 only: a bare date is UTC and one carrying a wall-clock time is local, matching JavaScript. Anything else is reported rather than guessed at, because upstream falls back to the host's parser and that differs between browsers

Both forms: by the domain value, and by an aggregate of a field the domain never mentions — which is how a bar chart is ordered by a total no row carries. Upstream *groups* the dataset on the domain field rather than listing its values, so the default order is first appearance, an aggregate sort has a grouping to ride on, and ties hold their group order. An object naming neither `op` nor `field` sorts by the value, so `{"order": "descending"}` is the only spelling of a reverse-alphabetical domain; a `field` with no `op` names an aggregate output that was never computed and changes nothing, which is reproduced and reported. A domain over several fields runs field by field, and accepts only `count`, `min` and `max`, being the operations that survive folding twice. A **union** — `{"fields": [{data, field}, …], "sort": true}` — orders the *combined* set rather than each part: upstream counts each part, aggregates the counts together and only then sorts, so laying sorted parts end to end is a different answer, and it shows the moment two plots of one table share a colour scale

How a specification positions something *between* two scaled values — a label at a bin's midpoint, a rule at the middle of a band — which no encoding channel can say, since a channel scales one field and stops. Available to mark encodings, axes and legends; **not** to a signal's own `update` in the *same* scope, because a scale there is built *from* those signals; a **group's** signals may read the enclosing scope's scales, which were built long before the group was reached, and that is how a trellis cell takes its height from one band of the outer scale. Reported with the reason rather than resolving to null, and the three failures are told apart: asked too early in this scope, asked too early at the top level, and no such scale. `invert()` on a **band** or a point scale answers with a *value* rather than a number — the domain value whose band the position falls in, `scaleBand.invertRange` — and with nothing where the position falls in the gap between two bands or outside the range; that is what a chart animated by a clock reads its frame from. An ordinal or a binned scale still has no inverse and is reported. Upstream's third argument, selecting a scale from another group's scope, has no equivalent here and is reported

`{"data": "clusters", "field": "name"}` — the mirror of a data-driven domain, and how an ordinal scale becomes a lookup table the data itself defines: `id` in, `name` out, both read from the same rows. Distinct values in first-seen order, so a domain read the same way from the same rows lines up entry for entry

`{"url": {"signal": "..."}}`, which is how a control chooses the file a chart reads. Resolved when the data is, so the signal has to be one that does not itself depend on data — the same rule every other pre-data signal follows. An address that resolves to nothing is named rather than fetched blindly

capabilities.feature: A channel holding a Vega null
capabilities.notes: Resolves to *nothing*, not to the four letters that spell it. Upstream's `textValue` is `line == null ? '' : (line + '').trim()`, so a text mark with no text draws nothing and a trailing space is trimmed before measuring. Stringifying the null instead printed "null" wherever a label was empty — which no mark comparison can see, because a text mark is compared by its anchor rather than its content

capabilities.feature: A stroke on an invisible mark
capabilities.notes: Does not widen the mark's bounds. Upstream's `boundStroke` tests the **item's** own opacity as well as the stroke's, so a mark at `opacity: 0` reaches exactly as far as its geometry. It shows wherever an invisible mark sits at the edge of a chart — a layout laid out with debug rectangles left switched off enlarged the surface by the width of a stroke nobody could see

capabilities.feature: A mark that names no position at all
capabilities.notes: The origin, not a reason to drop the mark: upstream reads `item.x || 0` in every mark's draw path, so a heading written as `{"y": -5}` and nothing else is drawn hard against the left of the group it is in. `text` and `symbol` dropped such a mark silently; every other encoder already defaulted this way. Distinct from the row below, which is about a channel that *is* declared and resolves to nothing

capabilities.feature: A mark channel that resolves to nothing
capabilities.notes: A channel the specification *declares* whose value comes back null leaves the mark in the scene with a zero extent, painting nothing — which is what upstream does, where the scene property is simply never set. A brush `rect` positioned from a signal that is empty until someone drags depends on it: the item has to exist to be dragged. A channel the specification names nowhere is still a malformed mark and still reported

A legend swatch's `opacity` resolved against the entry it is drawing, so `[{test:..., value: 0.7}, {value: 0.15}]` dims the series that are not selected. `symbolOpacity` says the same thing as a constant and cannot express a rule, which is why the `encode` block wins

The boundaries a scale's ticks land on, written out, described as `{start, stop, step}`, or held in a signal — which is the form the `bin` transform publishes. `start` is pulled up to the first whole step inside the domain and `stop` down to the last, so a binning computed over a wider extent than the axis shows does not hang ticks off either end. Setting it also drops the `zero` a linear, pow or sqrt scale would otherwise include, which is upstream's `includeZero` test and not obvious from the documentation. The boundaries are never thinned, because upstream raises the tick count to their number first

capabilities.feature: A scale domain's `field` from a signal
capabilities.notes: `{"data": "flights", "field": {"signal": "measure"}}` — the *name* of the column comes from a control, which is how a chart offers a measure picker over one scale. Upstream's `Scope.fieldRef` takes a string or a signal here and errors on anything else, and the signal supplies the name, so it is **one** lookup and not the two the same object makes under a mark's `field`. It is also an edge in the dependency order: the scale cannot be built before the signal that names its column. The other reference forms need a datum or an enclosing group, neither of which exists where a scale is built, and are reported
`{"domain": {"signal": "..."}}`, which is how a specification points a scale at what the `extent` transform published. A signal that produces nothing is reported rather than defaulted to `[0, 1]`
Step, bandwidth, padding, align and round match d3-scaleBand exactly
Implemented as a band scale with paddingInner 1, as d3 does

An explicit range array, a column of the data, or a scheme. A **categorical** scheme is the range and cycles when the domain outruns it; a **continuous** one is a function, and upstream samples it once per domain value instead — sixteen categories over `blues` give sixteen shades, not the same eleven and then five again

Configurable base; a domain spanning or touching zero is reported rather than adjusted. Ticks are the powers and their multiples, falling back to linear spacing when that is too sparse, and crowded labels are blanked as d3 does
`pow` defaults to exponent 1, i.e. linear, as upstream; `sqrt` is exponent 0.5. Negative domains handled by sign
`sign(x) * ln(1 + abs(x) / constant)`; handles zero and both signs
An explicit colour range interpolated in RGB or Lab, clamped at both ends as upstream does

All three upstream accepts: a name, a signal holding a name — how a chart offers a palette picker — and the stops written out inline, which is a scheme in every respect except that nobody named it. Generates rows rather than reading them, so it replaces whatever reached it and is only ever a pipeline's first stage. `stop` is **exclusive** — `{start: 0, stop: 5}` is five rows — and the field is named `data` unless `as` says otherwise. Steps are multiplied out from the start rather than accumulated, so a fractional step does not drift

With `values`, the named fields are copied out of the matched row and `as` renames them; without `values`, the whole matched row goes into the one field `as` names. An unmatched row takes `default`, or null. A duplicated key in the lookup table resolves to the **last** row carrying it, as a map built by insertion does

Adds the rows a series is missing so a line does not jump the gap. The key domain is the union across the **whole dataset**, not per group — a group is missing a key precisely when another group has it — and `keyvals` replaces that domain, so a series can be padded past where its data reached. `method` is `value` (the default, with a value of 0) or any aggregate, computed over the group's existing rows. New rows are **appended** rather than merged into position, and carry only the group's fields, the key and the filler

Every row paired with every row. Each output row holds the two originals **whole**, under `a` and `b` unless `as` renames them — not their fields merged, which would lose a column whenever both sides share a name — so an expression reaching into one writes `datum.a.value`. `filter` is applied as the pairs form, which is how a specification takes half a matrix

Turns rows into columns. The names come from the data and are sorted **alphabetically** before `limit` takes the first few, so limiting a pivot drops whatever sorts late however often it occurs. Cells are summarised with `op`, defaulting to `sum`, since two rows can land in one cell. A column no row in a group reaches is absent rather than zero

Counts words in a text column. The pattern defaults to `[\w']+`, so an apostrophe holds a word together. `stopwords` is anchored to the whole token and matched case-insensitively, so `the\|on` drops those two words and not every word containing them. Counts come out in first-appearance order rather than sorted

Samples a distribution at evenly spaced probabilities. With no `probs`, the sample points are the **midpoints** of `step` equal intervals — `(i + 0.5) / step`, so 100 steps run 0.005 to 0.995 and never reach either extreme. The quantile itself interpolates linearly between the two neighbouring order statistics, d3's `quantile` rather than a nearest-rank rule, so a median of an even count is the mean of the middle pair

All seven methods — `constant`, `linear`, `log`, `exp`, `pow`, `quad`, `poly`. The two straight ones come back as the fitted line's **two endpoints**; the curved ones are handed to the adaptive sampler, so their row count follows the data rather than a parameter. `params` swaps the points for `{coef, rSquared}`, in each method's own form: `pow` reports a multiplier and an exponent, the polynomials their terms from the constant upward. A group with no more points than the fit has parameters is skipped with a warning rather than fitted exactly through its own data. `exp` is fitted with residuals weighted by y rather than by taking logarithms, which is a different answer, not a rounding of the same one

A separate tricube-weighted straight line per point over its nearest neighbours, with three robustness passes re-weighting by residual against the median so an outlier stops dragging its neighbourhood. Output is one point per **distinct x**, rows sharing one being averaged. `bandwidth` is a fraction of the data, 0.3 by default — and with few enough rows that window falls to two points, where a local line passes through both and the smoothing silently does nothing

A Gaussian bump over every observation, added up: the smooth curve a histogram approximates, and one that depends on the bandwidth rather than on where bin edges happen to fall. An unset `bandwidth` comes from Scott's rule. `cumulative` gives the distribution function instead, `counts` scales a probability by the group's size so unequal groups compare by area, and `resolve: "shared"` puts every group on one domain and a **uniform** grid — adaptive sampling would give each its own x positions and leave nothing to stack. The support is taken unfiltered, as upstream does, so a null in the column turns the density into NaN rather than silently narrowing it

Samples a named distribution rather than estimating one: `normal`, `lognormal`, `uniform`, a `kde` over a field, or a weighted `mixture` of any of those, as `pdf` or `cdf`. The normal CDF is West's (2009) rational approximation, transcribed rather than derived — there is no closed form. `extent` is required, since a distribution has no data to take one from; a `kde` distribution is the exception and may read its own

Wilkinson's dot-plot stacking, which is **not** a histogram with round marks: there are no fixed bin edges. A stack opens at the first value that did not fit within `step` of the one before, and every dot in it sits at the midpoint of that stack's first and last value, so stacks land where the data is dense. `step` defaults to a thirtieth of the **whole field's** extent rather than the group's, so faceted dot plots stay comparable. `smooth` runs the variance-reducing swap pass, which moves dots away from their own value in exchange for a less jagged outline. Alone among these, it adds a field to the existing rows rather than replacing them, so the output keeps the input's order

Reads a parent-child structure out of two columns. The output is the **input, unchanged and in order** — the tree is carried to the layout after it and never reaches a mark, which is why no part of the data model had to learn about trees. The tree belongs to the **dataset**, not to the pipeline run: a dataset that sources from this one inherits it, which is how Vega's own tree examples put `treelinks` in a `links` dataset of its own, and how upstream reaches it as `source.root`. Two roots, a parent key naming no row, a duplicated key or a cycle are each reported and stop the pipeline: a tree assembled from ambiguous links is a different tree, not a smaller one, and every layout drawn from it would be silently wrong

Builds a tree by grouping where `stratify` builds one from links; each key adds a level. The interior nodes are invented and appear in the output only under `generate`, which emits them level by level from the root — not in the pre-order the layouts walk. Upstream also nests each group's own rows under a `values` column, a tree inside a field with no equivalent here; that omission is reported

All six tilings. `squarify` (the default) makes each rectangle as near square as it can, because area is what a reader judges and a sliver's cannot be — at the cost of scrambling sibling order, which `dice`, `slice`, `slicedice` and `binary` all keep. Half the inner padding comes off each side of a parent, so a gap between two siblings is one padding rather than two. `resquarify` exists upstream to hold rectangles still while data animates; nothing animates here, so it tiles as `squarify` and says so

An icicle plot: every level of the tree gets an equal band of the height whatever its values, and each node dices its width among its children. Spends one axis on depth where a treemap spends both on quantity, so the same tree through the two reads like two different datasets

Nested circles. A leaf's radius is the **square root** of its value so that area carries the quantity, as with a treemap; unlike one, circles cannot tile, so a pack always leaves gaps and reads as grouping rather than as proportion. Siblings are packed by a front chain and enclosed by Welzl's algorithm over a *seeded* shuffle, so the same data packs the same way every time. `radius` is resolved against the **layout node** rather than the row — upstream's own behaviour — so naming a data column gives every circle a radius of zero; matched rather than corrected, and reported

Both methods. `tidy` is Reingold-Tilford in Buchheim's linear-time form, which guarantees that identical subtrees are drawn identically wherever they appear; `cluster` is a dendrogram, putting every **leaf** on the last row whatever its depth, because in a clustering result the leaves are what is being compared. `separation: false` packs cousins as tightly as siblings. `size` fits the diagram to a box, `nodeSize` fixes the spacing per node and lets the diagram be whatever size follows

Turns a tree back into a row per edge, each holding the two rows **whole** under `source` and `target` — not their fields merged, since both ends carry the same column names. Edges come out **breadth-first**, the order `d3-hierarchy`'s own iterator walks, which is the order they are painted in. The output replaces the input, so a `links` dataset holds edges rather than nodes, and the tree stops there. A node whose row is no longer present emits no edge, as upstream's tuple lookup does; and because transforms here copy rather than mutate, a node is matched to its row by position, so a transform that adds or drops rows between the two is reported instead of guessed at

All twelve shape and orientation pairings upstream defines. `line`, `arc` and `curve` are symmetric in x and y, so a Cartesian `orient` falls through to the bare shape; `orthogonal` and `diagonal` bend towards the axis the tree grows along and exist only per orientation. Under `radial` the four accessors are **angle and radius** rather than x and y, and the path is emitted around the origin for the mark's own `x`/`y` to place. Numbers go into the path text the way JavaScript concatenates them, so the string is upstream's character for character. `require` names a signal that should re-run the transform; nothing re-runs here, and that is reported

All 51 of upstream's documented data transforms are now implemented; this was the last one. The layout is upstream's, ported: the sort, the archimedean and rectangular spirals, the board bitmap, the bitmask collision test, the bounding-box compaction rule, the blank-row trimming, and the order the random draws come off the generator. **Checked to the pixel**: `oracle-js/src/record-wordcloud.mjs` runs upstream's own `cloudSprite` against the pinned `vega@6.3.1` and records each word's glyph mask together with where upstream then placed it; `CloudLayoutTest` hands those masks back and requires all eighteen words at exactly upstream's coordinates. Every word's position depends on the board the words before it left, so one wrong bit moves all seventeen after it — it passes completely or fails obviously. The **difference** is the mask itself: upstream reads it back from a canvas, and nothing in common Kotlin rasterises glyphs, nor should it, since a font is the host's. A host that can rasterise supplies masks through `CloudSprites` and gets upstream's packing; everything else measures each word and treats it as a filled rectangle — same words, same sizes, same order, more air between them. Upstream's compaction rule is skipped in that case because it cannot be satisfied by solid boxes: it requires a word to *overlap* the bounds of what is already placed while missing its ink, which measured one word placed of ten before the rule was made conditional. Deterministic where upstream is not, since the generator is the chart's seeded `RandomStream`.

This row said a `projection` parameter was *refused*, which would tell an adopter this engine cannot draw a map; it is applied, and checked against d3-geo's arithmetic worked by hand rather than read off the output.

Upstream calls these post-encoding transforms and runs them over the scene *items*, writing straight onto each. They run over the items here too — the mark's channels resolved, with the row under `datum` — because both halves are read: `{"field": "datum.contour"}` reaches for the row and `{"force": "x", "x": "xfocus"}` reaches for a channel the encoding produced. Whatever a transform writes becomes an `update` channel holding the resolved value, so it wins over the encoding exactly as writing onto the item does — which is the entire point of a `force` layout. Getting the datum half wrong is invisible in the diagnostics and visible in the picture: `contour-plot`'s three densities all came out the same colour

A two-dimensional kernel density over a grid. The blur is upstream's, arithmetic included: three box passes per axis through a **float32** buffer, ping-ponged between two arrays, with the radius computed by `shiftRight` — a truncation toward zero before the shift, which is not what an arithmetic shift of a negative does. Carried in doubles instead, the grid is subtly denser and every contour drawn from it moves. `bandwidth` defaults to Scott's rule over the sample

A raster grid painted as an image. Upstream writes RGBA into a canvas; this engine has none, so the image is carried as `{width, height, pixels}` with each pixel packed `0xAARRGGBB` and `ImageNode` takes it as a raster, which the SVG renderer encodes as a PNG data URL. Two details are upstream's: with no `opacity` the default is `$value / $max`, so an empty cell is transparent and the densest opaque; and the alpha is `~~(255 * opacity)`, truncated rather than rounded, which moves half the levels of a gradient by one. An expression naming none of `$x`, `$y`, `$value` or `$max` is evaluated once **per row** rather than per pixel — per row, because a constant across one grid is still a function of that grid's datum

The raster an `image` mark carries has to reach an SVG as a data URL. Written here rather than taken from a platform: the core is KMP-portable and `java.util.zip` is not. Deflate **stored** blocks — a valid zlib stream that compresses nothing — so the file is larger than upstream's and decodes to the same pixels, which is the only property that matters to a comparison that hashes them

The indexing pair an interactive cross-filter is built from. `crossfilter` records one bit per dimension whose range query a row falls outside; `resolvefilter` keeps the rows whose verdict is zero once its `ignore` mask is cleared, which is how a delay histogram shows everything the time and distance brushes admit *including* the bars its own brush excludes. Two things are upstream's and not obvious: the range is half-open, `[lo, hi)`, because upstream bisects a sorted index with `bisectLeft` at both ends; and a set bit means **rejected**, which is why the test is for zero. Upstream's sorted indices and previous/current bitmaps exist to avoid rescanning 200,000 rows when a brush moves a pixel, and none of that is observable in a single compile. The verdicts ride on the rows rather than in a side table, because these transforms copy rather than mutate and there is no stamped `_index` to key one by

A force simulation, ported from d3-force with the quadtree underneath it: `center`, `collide`, `nbody`, `link`, `x` and `y`. Deterministic, which is the whole reason it can be a fixture — d3 seeds a fixed LCG rather than reaching for `Math.random`, and a node with no position starts on a phyllotaxis spiral. Three things are upstream's and none is guessable: a **running** simulation contributes exactly the one tick Vega takes at initialisation, before it hands over to a timer a headless render never lets fire; a `static` one runs `iterations` ticks and nothing else; and an omitted force parameter falls to **d3's** default rather than the one Vega's schema documents, because Vega only passes on the parameters a specification actually wrote — `collide` strength is 1, not the documented 0.7, and every node lands somewhere else if you believe the schema

The format decoded back to GeoJSON, ported from `topojson-client`. Three things are easy to get wrong and each changes the map: coordinates are **deltas** on a quantized grid, so a point is a running sum that restarts at every arc; a **negative** arc index means walk that arc backwards, which is how two countries share one border; and a mesh emits its runs in the order the *index* releases them rather than the order they were built, so a fragment whose endpoint another later claimed is orphaned out and re-emitted alone at the end. `format.filter` picks the shared arcs (`interior`) or the unshared ones (`exterior`)

The d3-geo pipeline, ported whole: rotation, antimeridian pre-clipping on the sphere, **circle** pre-clipping for the projections that need it, adaptive resampling, and a rectangular post-clip in projected space. Every type **Vega itself ships**: d3-geo's fifteen plus `mollweide`, the one projection `vega-projection` imports from `d3-geo-projection`. So `albers`, `albersUsa`, `azimuthalEqualArea`, `azimuthalEquidistant`, `conicConformal`, `conicEqualArea`, `conicEquidistant`, `equalEarth`, `equirectangular`, `gnomonic`, `mercator`, `mollweide`, `naturalEarth1`, `orthographic`, `stereographic`, `transverseMercator` — each with the defaults its *name* carries: the clip angle `orthographic` needs to hide the far side of the globe, the parallels and centring that make `albers` a map of the United States, the quarter turn that makes `transverseMercator` transverse. `albersUsa` is three projections at once, each clipped to its own rectangle. `mollweide` is the only one whose forward direction is iterative: its auxiliary angle solves `theta + sin theta = pi sin phi` by Newton's method, capped at thirty steps the way upstream caps it. A type this engine does not have — the rest of `d3-geo-projection`, which a host has to register for itself — is refused by name rather than substituted, which is what upstream does with them too: Vega's own `projections` example fails on the pinned oracle with `Unrecognized projection type: airy`. Three parts of it are places to be quietly wrong. The pre-clip and the post-clip are **different** clips in different spaces, and mercator needs both — the second is what stops a polygon touching a pole from running to infinity. `polygonContains` decides whether the *invisible* part of a boundary is inside, on a sum of thousands of nearly-cancelling terms, so it needs Shewchuk exact summation rather than `+=`; get it wrong and a continent is a hole. And resampling recurses on the first point of every line with a **NaN** chord length, which `!(d2 > delta)` stops and `d2 <= delta` does not — the difference is the first vertex emitted sixteen times

capabilities.tests_text: `BitmapTest` (upstream vectors for the bit algebra and the pixel scaler), visual inspection of `labeled-scatter-plot`
capabilities.notes: Places a text mark's items beside the marks they annotate and drops the ones that would collide. Everything is upstream's — the eight anchors and their two-bit arithmetic, the diagonal offsets scaled by `1/sqrt(2)`, the one-pixel-wide trial that avoids measuring a label that cannot fit, the bit-vector occupancy bitmap and its pixel scaler — **except the one step that decides what is occupied**. Upstream draws the avoided marks into a `<canvas>` and reads the alpha back; there is none under Node and its own transform throws there, so there is no reference to compare against. The occupancy is computed from the marks' geometry instead: a pixel is taken as occupied when the shape overlaps its square. The two answers agree except on pixels a shape barely grazes, and one pixel is enough to move a label to a different anchor or to drop one a crowded chart would otherwise fit — so **every use of the transform reports this**, and it is the only place in the engine that carries such a warning

limit.test: LabelOccupancyLimitTest.every use reports that the occupancy is geometric rather than rasterised
limit.claim: The occupancy bitmap is computed from the avoided marks' geometry rather than from a canvas raster, because there is no canvas under Node and upstream's own transform fails in the same place — so there is no reference to compare against. Every use of the transform reports it.

capabilities.notes: The item under the pointer is redrawn from its mark's `hover` set layered over `update`, and restored when the pointer leaves. It was parsed and carried through the compiler and never applied before, because a mark's effective encoding is `enter` overridden by `update` and nothing consulted the third set — so hovering a mark did nothing at all. Applied by a **node swap**, not a recompile: each item is encoded twice at compile time with the id allocator rewound between the two, so the pair share an id and the hit index, the selection and the accessibility tree all keep pointing at the same thing. A **tap** hovers as well, because a touch screen has no pointer and a browser synthesises `pointerover` from a touch before it reports the click. Two things a swap cannot do: a `zindex` in a hover block does not raise the item above its neighbours, and a `cursor` is not applied to the host view

Paint order **within** a mark, which is not the same channel as a mark's own `zindex` (that orders whole marks and was already there). Items are sorted stably at compile time, so ones sharing a `zindex` keep the order the data gave them; and when a hover swaps an item in, only the run of children from that same mark is re-sorted — a raised bar draws over its neighbours and still under the axis, which shares the group with it

Published on the interaction state rather than applied, because what a cursor *is* differs by platform. `VegaChartView` maps the CSS name to one of Android's system `PointerIcon`s — twenty-three names correspond — and a name Android has no icon for leaves the pointer alone rather than resetting it to an arrow. The SVG renderer writes it into the element's `style`, sharing the one attribute with a blend mode, because an element carrying `style` twice is invalid and a browser silently drops one

Scales and centres a projection so the geometry fills a rectangle, `d3-geo`'s `fitExtent` ported. The only projection property that is **data** — `{"signal": "data('states')"}` — so it is resolved in the scope that declared it and a fitted projection cannot be built until what it fits has loaded. Three details are d3's and none is arbitrary: the measurement is taken at the reference scale **150** and the answer is a multiple of it; the factor is the *smaller* of the two ratios, so the geometry fits inside the box rather than spilling out; and the user's `clipExtent` is removed for the measurement, since a clip in screen coordinates would cut the geometry to a rectangle the fit has not chosen yet

Both had been implemented on `Projection` since the geographic family was ported and neither was passed through, so an `orthographic` globe drew its far side and every conic stood on its family's default parallels. `parallels` rebuilds the raw formula rather than tuning it: the same projection on `[10, 60]` and on `[40, 45]` is a different map of the same world

The radius a `Point` or `MultiPoint` geometry draws as, since a projected city has no extent of its own. The mark's own `pointRadius` wins; otherwise the projection's, which is where upstream keeps it

A mercator clips to the square its own scale makes one full turn of the world, and that square is recomputed whenever the scale or translation moves. Kept separate from a specification's own `clipExtent`, which is intersected with it — d3's `reclip`. Without the distinction a `fit` put the stale square back over the recomputed one and clipped the whole map away, and a user `clipExtent` did not survive a recentre

`"values": {a FeatureCollection}` with `"format": {"property": "features"}` — how a specification writes a map with no data file — and the TopoJSON equivalent. The parser read `values` as an array of rows or not at all, so such a dataset was silently empty; upstream applies `format` to inline values exactly as to a loaded file

Compared for the first time. The harness measured `symbol`, `arc` and `path` marks by their outline and a `shape` mark not at all — and a `geoshape` mark carries no `x` or `y`, so the entire geographic family had only its fill and stroke checked. Three real findings came out of adding it: the path string was rounding the *model* rather than the output, a `fit` was destroying a mercator's automatic clip, and a `shape` mark with no outline was measuring as a point at its group's origin where upstream measures nothing

Starts the dash pattern part-way along, so the same array can be drawn with its gaps where another draws its marks. Compared as part of the dash pattern on both sides, since it is not a separate decoration

How far a sharp join may extend past its vertex before it is cut square. Not visible in the scenegraph comparison — it changes only the drawn join — so it is evidenced by the exported SVG. Note the engine's *default* is 4 rather than SVG's 10, which is the allowance upstream reserves when it measures a stroked path; an explicit value now flows to both the measurement and the join

A `path` mark's own channels, scaling its outline about its anchor. **Not** a symbol's: upstream reads them in `marks/path.js` alone and draws a symbol unscaled, so a specification putting them on a symbol gets nothing, here as there. The fixture asserts both halves

`lineBreak` splits one string into lines on a separator of the specification's choosing; `lineHeight` sets the gap between them, defaulting to `fontSize + 2` rather than to a ratio. `lineBreak` stays on the run rather than being folded into the text, so the scenegraph still reports what the data said — which is what a screen reader announces and what the comparison checks. A limit truncates **each line**, trimmed, which is upstream's `textValue` and was previously applied to the joined string, cutting a two-line label's first line to nothing

Right-to-left runs keep their **tail** when truncated, with the ellipsis in front, because the end of an RTL string is where its meaning starts. The direction decides this, not the sign of `limit`: a limit of zero or less is no truncation at all

`aspect: false` stretches the image to its box instead of letterboxing it inside; `smooth: false` asks for nearest-neighbour sampling. Both were read by the encoder and invisible to the comparison, which checked an image's box, url and anchor only

`strokeForeground` draws the group's outline after its children rather than before, which is the whole difference where a child reaches the border. `strokeOffset` is the half-pixel nudge that puts a thin outline on a pixel boundary; null is **not** "no offset" — upstream shifts a group stroked between 0.5 and 1.5 units wide by `0.5 - |width - 1|`, so the commonest case comes out crisp rather than grey on both sides

capabilities.tests_text: `encode-channels-tail` fixture (which leaves the rotation out), STATUS.md
capabilities.notes: Upstream's renderer rotates the outline about the item's own `(x, y)`; its *bounds* code rotates the already-placed points about the **origin**, because the context it measures with defines no `translate` or `rotate`. For a square at `(250, 40)` scaled by `(2, 0.5)` and turned 20 degrees it reports a top-left 70 units below the shape it drew. This engine reports the box it painted. Reproducing the quirk would make chart size agree under `autosize: pad` and would put every hit target for such a mark in the wrong place

limit.test: RotatedScaledPathBoundsTest.the bounds are the painted extent and no larger
limit.claim: Upstream's bounds code rotates the already-placed points about the origin, reporting a box far from the shape it drew. This engine reports the box it painted, because reproducing the quirk would put every hit target for such a mark in the wrong place.

capabilities.notes: On both `rect` and `group` marks. Each falls back to `cornerRadius`, and the fallback has to be *distinguishable from zero*: `cornerRadius: 6` with `cornerRadiusTopLeft: 0` is a bar rounded on three corners, so the overrides are nullable rather than defaulted. The harness was strengthened to compare them — a rect used to be compared by `x`, `y`, `width` and `height` alone, in which four differently rounded corners were invisible, and they are now checked both ways so a radius invented here counts as much as one missed

The slack in a curve, on `line` and `area`. Applies to three of the seventeen families and means a different quantity in each: a cardinal stiffness, a Catmull-Rom distance exponent, a bundle blend — with defaults 0, 0.5 and 0.85. Recorded in the comparison as well as applied, because two families can happen to draw the same outline for one series

Places a label at a distance and an angle from its anchor rather than at an offset from it — `theta - π/2`, so zero is up. Upstream keeps both on the item and offsets at paint time, where this engine's scene holds the anchor already offset; the harness folds the offset in, the same equivalence it applies to `dx`/`dy` and in the same order Vega applies them, so a rotated label turns about the offset point

The mark-level form of what the guides have always done. The scenegraph keeps the **whole** string — as upstream's does — and only the drawn lines and the measured width shrink, so the datum a tooltip shows is still what the data said

All sixteen CSS `mix-blend-mode` values, on every mark type. Exported SVG carries all sixteen; an Android canvas needs API 29 for the eleven above `lighten` and reports the rest rather than approximating them

`clip` is both a mark property and an encode channel, and real specifications use the channel — `overview-plus-detail` writes `clip: {value: true}` into `enter`, and it is what keeps the detail view's line inside its own panel. Evidenced by the exported SVG rather than by the comparison: upstream's scenegraph still holds the items its renderer hides, so clipping is one of the few things the differential cannot see

What a tooltip says, when the specification would rather say it than show the whole row: `{"signal": "'bar ' + datum.c"}` gives one line. With no channel the item carries its datum, which is upstream's behaviour too

The controller publishes the hovered datum as `interactionState.tooltip` with an anchor and emits `TooltipChanged`; **`VegaChartView` now draws one**. Vega itself draws no tooltip — it hands the datum to the host, which in a browser is the separate `vega-tooltip` library — and that division is right, but it still left this view showing nothing for a specification that asks for a tooltip. So there is a plain default (one `name: value` line per field, flipped to stay inside the view) and `tooltipsEnabled = false` for a host that wants its own. Drawn outside the scene transform, because a tooltip is chrome: it does not scale with a pinch or move with a pan

The region of the plane nearest to each point, as an outline. Ported from `d3-delaunay` over `delaunator` over an exact `orient2d`, and the exactness is the point: a Delaunay triangulation is a sequence of "is this point left of that edge?" decisions, each of which decides the shape of everything after it, and airports along a coastline are nearly collinear. One wrong sign does not perturb the diagram — it produces a different one, or sends the hull walk into a loop. So the cross product is a floating-point **expansion** (Shewchuk's adaptive predicate) extended only as far as the sign is in doubt. The insertion order is upstream's quicksort exactly, median-of-three included, because a triangulation is not unique on cocircular points. Clipping a cell to a box is not clipping its edges independently: where a cell leaves one side and returns through another, the **corner** between belongs to it, but only if the cell is the nearest one to that corner — a nearest-point query. Almost always drawn transparent, as a pointer target, and compared outline by outline regardless

Upstream's items are property bags, so a mark encoding `strokeWidth` and no `stroke` carries a width and paints no outline — its own SVG renderer emits neither attribute. A scene node here holds what a renderer needs, so it holds no stroke at all. The comparison accepts that one equivalence and nothing wider: a reference carrying a stroke *colour* still demands a stroke of that width

limit.test: StrokeWidthWithoutStrokeTest.a width with no colour leaves the node with no stroke
limit.claim: A scene node holds what a renderer needs, and a stroke with no colour paints nothing, so there is no stroke to hold a width on. The comparison accepts that one equivalence and nothing wider.

capabilities.notes: A fixed row height for a symbol legend, so entries with very different symbol sizes still line up. It applies **vertically only**: the rows are that tall and a bigger symbol overflows its row, while the horizontal anchor still comes from the widest real symbol, so the labels clear the biggest circle. The legend is then sized as though nothing had overflowed

Upstream's `LegendScales` order decides which scale a legend takes its entry *values* from, and it is **size, shape, fill, stroke, opacity** — not fill first. A legend encoding both `size` and `fill` is ticked on the size scale and coloured from those values; reading `fill` first gives the right number of entries at the wrong values. The caption reads its channels in the same order

A discretizing scale's legend is neither a symbol legend nor a smooth ramp: it is a bar cut into bands as wide as the ranges they stand for, with the cut points written beside the cuts. Upstream's `legendType` chooses it for any `quantize`, `quantile`, `threshold` or `bin-ordinal` scale carrying a single colour channel, and chooses it again when a specification asks for a `gradient` over one. Two details are upstream's: the lowest band's label is **absent** — that bucket reaches to negative infinity and there is no number to write at its foot, which is not the same as an empty label and the comparison can now tell them apart — and the bands are measured against the scale's *input* extent, so a quantile scale's bands come out uneven, which is the whole point of one. The label precision comes from the narrowest interval rather than the whole span

Where a shape balances, and a point on the page read back to a place on the globe. The centroid is area-weighted where there is area, length-weighted where there is only a line, and a plain mean of points otherwise — which is why a label on a country lands on its mainland rather than out at sea between it and an island. `invert` undoes the placement, the formula and the rotation, in that order; clipping and resampling are not functions and are not undone, so it is exact for a point and meaningless for a shape. A projection whose formula has no closed-form inverse says so

A GeoJSON feature drawn through a projection, and the grid of meridians and parallels under it. Upstream writes a path *generator* onto the item and lets its renderer call it; the path string is written instead, which is what that renderer would have produced. `graticule` is a generator — it ignores its input and publishes one row holding every line, so the whole grid is one geometry and one mark
The twelfth mark type, and the last one without an encoder. It is a `path` mark reading a different column: whatever outline `geoshape` put on the item

Wilkinson dot placement, with the `smooth` pass that swaps dots between neighbouring stacks within a quarter step. Both passes pinned against upstream for all 48 points of Vega's own dot plot: a single misplaced dot changes one column's height and nothing else, so nothing short of the whole vector would catch it

The ends of a 95% confidence interval on the group's mean, by **bootstrap**: a thousand resamples drawn with replacement, then the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of their means. Not a summary statistic in the sense every other operation is — it is a property of the draw sequence as much as of the data, which is why it could only be pinned once both engines shared a generator. The two ends come from **one** run, as upstream caches it on the cell: asking for both does not resample twice, and the group after depends on this one having consumed exactly 1,000 x n draws and no more

`argmin`/`argmax` return the **whole tuple** at the extreme rather than the value, which is what makes them useful: a chart labels a point by aggregating with one and then reading any column of the row that came back. `stderr` is `sqrt(dev / (n * (n - 1)))`, upstream's arrangement

Each publisher must publish before *any* reader runs, and a walk that resolves a dataset once has to pick one to go first — so there is no order to find. Previously the two datasets waited on each other and the compile reported a cycle; with the wait alone removed, the first layer landed at x=0 where upstream has 80. Upstream has no knot because its operators are per transform. Here the fit is made eventually consistent instead: a publisher no longer waits for its fit's other publishers, and the datasets that read such a fit are resolved a **second time** once every publisher has published — which is what upstream does by re-pulsing

capabilities.feature: A lookup or group key across types
capabilities.notes: Upstream indexes and groups through `fastmap`, which is object-backed, so JavaScript coerces every key to a string: the integer `1001` and the string `"1001"` are one key. This engine tagged them apart — `"s:1001"` against `"n:1001"` — which **split what upstream merges**. It showed as a join that matched nothing: a TSV column of `"22051"` against TopoJSON's integer `22051` drew an empty map with no error, because delimited cells are strings and nothing had said to parse them. Verified both ways — upstream merges the two into one aggregate group and matches them in one lookup

`fitExtent` lived on the concrete projection rather than the interface a composite implements, so `build()` set an `albersUsa`'s scale, translate and precision and returned without offering it the fit. A fitted composite drew at the family's unfitted default — x at 431.97 where upstream has 85.26 — silently. It is the projection Vega-Lite reaches for by default on any United States chart. The fix is the same arithmetic a plain projection uses; a composite needs nothing special, since its three pieces are driven from one `k`, `tx` and `ty`

The geometry under a brush selection: `intersectPoint`, `intersectRule` and Liang–Barsky's `intersectBoxLine`, in `MarkIntersect`, clean against upstream's 39 vectors first time. A **point** mark is tested by its centre alone, so a symbol whose edge overlaps the brush and whose middle does not is not caught — reproduced rather than improved, because a selection that disagrees with the one a reader dragged is worse than a strict one. `intersectPath` is left out: upstream rasterises into an offscreen canvas and walks pixels, which is a renderer's answer, and returns `true` when it has no context

A field is reached through `datum.name`, so the identifier grammar decides which columns an expression can see. This engine tested for a letter or digit; ECMA-262 uses `UnicodeIDStart`/`UnicodeIDContinue`, so upstream reads `datum.café` with a decomposed acute, a name starting with `Ⅷ`, and one carrying a zero-width non-joiner, and this read none of them. Reading Unicode categories directly still missed **86 characters** — `Other_ID_Start`/`Other_ID_Continue` sit on top of the categories and move with the Unicode version — so the lexer asks `ktecma262` once per character and remembers

`trim` is a Vega function — from `vega-expression`'s codegen whitelist rather than `functionContext`, which is why it does not appear in the registry — so it is JavaScript's and carries **ECMA's** whitespace set. This engine used Kotlin's, and they disagree at both ends: ECMA trims **U+FEFF**, a byte-order mark, and Kotlin does not; Kotlin trims U+001C–U+001F and ECMA does not. Two of the fixture's six codepoints were wrong before. `parseFloat` and `parseInt` skip the same set and went with it

capabilities.feature: A grey's hue in Lab and HCL
capabilities.notes: `toHcl` already had d3's rule — a hue is undefined when both Lab opponents are zero — but it never fired, because `toLab` never produced exactly zero for a grey. d3 does it deliberately: `if (r === g && g === b) x = z = y` reuses the luminance rather than recomputing, so `a` and `b` are literal zeros instead of last-bit dust. Without it `#ccc` had a hue of **158°**, and since an HCL interpolator holds the other endpoint's hue when one is undefined, `red → grey` would have swung two thirds round the wheel and gone through green instead of desaturating. The 174 vectors behind this were filed as "a colour space this engine does not model"; the spaces were modelled, the adapter was not

capabilities.tests_text: `ramp-through-grey.vg.json`; 185 fixtures with `font` and `fontWeight` no longer excluded
capabilities.notes: Reviewing what the harness was told to ignore. d3 blanks a transparent colour's channels to NaN and its interpolators hold the other endpoint's channel constant, so `red -> transparent` stays red and fades; this engine read the parsed zeros and faded through **black**. A transparent endpoint now contributes only its opacity. Separately, comparing the `font` channel found a `style` block's family leaking from a title into its **subtitle**, which upstream never allows from any source, and found `fontWeight` had never been mapped into the comparison at all — excluded *and* absent

capabilities.feature: A colour ramp over a constant column
capabilities.notes: d3's `normalize` answers `constant(0.5)` when a domain's ends coincide, so a colour scale over a column that turns out constant paints the **middle** colour — the one reading "nothing to compare" — not an extreme. This engine gave three different answers between its own methods: `position` 0, `fraction` 0, and `colorAt` a special case returning the *last* colour. Found by replaying `scaleSequential`, which with d3's default identity interpolator *is* its own normaliser and so checks the arithmetic every ramp runs on. `scaleIdentity` and `scaleSequential` had both been filed as "no equivalent scale here" when the engine had had both all along

d3's log `tickFormat` labels a tick only when its mantissa is within `base × count / ticks.length`, so a four-decade axis shows the powers of ten alone while a single-decade one labels all nine. Already correct here; the fixture exists because it had never been checked, and a correct implementation nothing verifies is one refactor from an incorrect one. Its 51 vectors cannot be replayed — `tickFormat` returns a formatter, which a vector records as `{$: function}`

Upstream's `invert()` falls through to `invertExtent` when a scale has no continuous inverse, answering the stretch of domain a range value covers — how a clicked legend swatch becomes a data range. This engine reported "invert() needs a continuous scale" and refused. The four scales differ only in what bounds their outermost buckets: **quantize** by its declared domain, **quantile** by the samples, **bin-ordinal** by the outermost bin edges, and **threshold** by nothing at all — a cut point at 10 says nothing about how far below it the first bucket reaches, so upstream answers `undefined` there. An unmatched range value answers `[NaN, NaN]`, not nothing

No specification names one: Vega's `scaleKey` prefixes `diverging-` onto a continuous colour scale with a **three-point domain**, so `{"type": "linear", "domain": [-10, 0, 20], "range": {"scheme": "blueorange"}}` is a diverging scale. This engine interpolated between the first and last values, so zero came out a third of the way along the ramp and still blue where upstream gives the near-white midpoint — the whole point of that chart being that neutral sits at zero. The two halves scale independently. The gradient **legend** stays linear over the extent, because upstream's `scaleFraction` strips the prefix and the gradient already carries the asymmetry in its stops

Upstream expands a mark's bounds by `(cap === 'square' ? √2 : 1) × sw/2`, raised to `miterLimit × sw/2` where a join can occur. This engine had the miter half and the **square cap nowhere**, so every square-capped rule and line measured short by √2 — and bounds drive layout, autosize and clipping. The miter branch was a bare product rather than upstream's `max`, so a miter limit below one would have pulled bounds *inside* the stroke. Found only after fixing the recorder, which encoded arguments **after** the call and so recorded this in-place mutator's answer as its question

capabilities.feature: `luminance()` and `contrast()` on a string d3 refuses
capabilities.notes: This engine's CSS parser takes a **superset** of d3's — `rgb(120.5,30,50)` draws in a browser, so the renderer should accept it — but `luminance()` and `contrast()` are d3-color calls upstream and answer **NaN** for exactly those strings. They now go through `SceneColor.acceptedByD3`, d3's grammar transcribed, while the renderer keeps its own rule. The same fix retired **twelve** pinned "divergences" that were really the colour corpus comparing d3's parser against this engine's renderer parser — two functions never meant to agree

capabilities.feature: The seeded generator and the distribution functions
capabilities.notes: 9,708 of those vectors are `randomLCG()` drawn in sequence from one seed, and all of them reproduce **exactly**. The arithmetic is the point: `1103515245 * seed` reaches past 2^53, so JavaScript loses low bits and every later value is a property of that loss — computing it exactly gives a better generator and the wrong one, and a `sample` transform that draws a different subset draws a different chart. The engine had this right deliberately; it had never been checked. `densityNormal`, `cumulativeNormal`, `quantileNormal` and the log-normal and uniform families came with it — what a `density` transform draws a violin plot from

Not helpers: a band scale inverts a brush with `bisectRight(bandStarts, position) - 1`, and a crossfilter narrows a range with `bisectLeft` at both ends. A **`NaN` needle** was the fault — every comparison against a NaN is false, so the search converged on `low` and claimed the value belonged at the front, where d3 checks up front and answers `high`. For a band scale inverting a pointer position that is not a number, that is the first band instead of none

capabilities.feature: Time interval `ceil`, `round` and `count`; stepped-day tick grids
capabilities.notes: `TimeStepper` had only `floor`, `offset` and `range`. `count` carries a **daylight-saving correction** — a local day is not always 86,400,000 ms, so the day a clock springs forward would report 30 days in a 31-day March. The tick vectors found three faults: a stepped day ignored its step when flooring, so a two-day grid anchored to the domain start instead of the 1st, 3rd, 5th of the month; d3 has **two** day intervals and uses `unixDay` (days since 1970) for the UTC tick table where the local one uses `timeDay` (day of month), so the same step picks different days; and a zero-width domain drew **no** ticks because the increment is `NaN` and `coerceAtLeast(1.0)` does not rescue one

capabilities.feature: Polylinear domains on log, power and symlog scales
capabilities.notes: A transformed scale is upstream's `continuous()` wearing a transform and takes a domain of more than two stops just as a linear one does. `TransformedScale` read only the first and last, so a three-stop power scale over `[4, 2, 1] -> [1, 2, 4]` answered 3.5 for 1.5 where upstream answers 3. It also interpolated as `r0 + u(r1 - r0)` rather than d3's `r0(1 - u) + r1·u`, the last-bits difference `LinearScale` already documents. Separately, a range **longer** than its domain threw where d3 takes `min(domain, range)` stops and ignores the spare

With no projection upstream calls d3's **spherical** function, not the path generator. This engine ran the planar sinks over raw longitude and latitude, so a one-degree box measured `1` square degree instead of `0.000305` steradians. `SphericalMeasure` ports all three sinks; bounds is the hard one, because longitude wraps — two islands at ±179° are two degrees apart, so the box is the inverse of the largest gap between the merged per-line ranges. d3's winding sum uses `delta + (delta > 0 ? 360 : -360)`, which is not the wrap correction and had to be copied rather than reasoned about. Rotation and the `geoStream` walk replay too, both clean first time — the stream corpus is shapes rather than answers (unknown types, a null geometry, elevations), and all 22 walk without error. Of the rest, `geoContains`, `geoInterpolate` and `geoDistance` (55) are unreachable from Vega, the graticule replays in full once the recorded `chain` is read — it had been captured all along — and 16 `geoCircle` vectors have no generator here because Vega calls none

capabilities.feature: Scale references from a non-string literal
capabilities.notes: `geoArea(null, feature)` did not compile: the reference visitor treated only a *string* literal as naming a scale, so `null` read as "some scale, we cannot tell which" and made **every** scale a dependency of the dataset — a dependency cycle reported for a chart upstream compiles. Upstream branches on the node being a `Literal`, not on its type

capabilities.feature: Delimited text against d3-dsv's own corpus
capabilities.notes: The code between a `"url"` and the first datum. Two real faults: a lone `\r` was treated as nothing rather than as a row terminator, so a classic-Mac file came back as **one row**; and a blank line was dropped where upstream reads it as a record of empty fields. `parseRows` and the formatting side were missing and are now present. Of the 39 not replayed, **32 are `autoType`, which `vega-loader` does not use** — Vega has its own `inferTypes` — six pass a row-conversion function a vector cannot record, and one is the constructor. Separately, `format.header` is quoted with `JSON.stringify`, not DSV quoting, which this file had wrong: `a\b` comes back as `a\\b` and a name holding a quote yields no columns at all

capabilities.feature: `formatSpan`: an axis format resolved against its span
capabilities.notes: `"format": "s"` does not format each label on its own — upstream calls `formatPrefix`, which fixes **one** SI prefix for the whole span, so an axis over two million reads `0.5M \| 1.0M \| 1.5M \| 2.0M` where this engine read `500k \| 1M \| 1.5M \| 2M`. The four helpers behind it (`precisionFixed`, `precisionRound`, `precisionPrefix`, `formatPrefix`) are ported. `precisionRound` **subtracts the step from the bound** — `precisionRound(0.01, 1)` is 2, the digits for 0.99 — which `Ticks` also missed, costing an extra decimal on every `g`/`p`/`r`/`e` axis; and the prefix goes in the *suffix* slot, so it pads and parenthesises with the number: `($1k)`, not `($1)k`

capabilities.feature: `String(x)` — the shortest decimal that names a double
capabilities.notes: The conversion behind every number a chart writes as text, and the only one never told how many digits to write. Kotlin's `Double.toString` is not it: **91 of 7,957** disagreed. It goes exponential at 10^7 where JavaScript goes at 10^21, so `1777860673.6878662` printed as `1.7778606736878662e+9`; the integer fast path saturated `toLong` at 9.2×10^18, so larger integral doubles printed as `-9223372036854775808`; and past 2^53 the shortest decimal is not the exact one, so `319615008869810176` must print as `319615008869810200`. `Decimals.shortest` now binary-searches the digit count against a round-trip, which is exact and terminates in five tries. `String(x)` also breaks a tie towards the **even** digit where `toFixed` rounds away from zero

A `VegaLocale` given to `SpecCompiler` or `VegaChartController` beside the text engine, and for the same reason: the platform knows a language's names and common Kotlin cannot reach them. Its fields are d3's own — `d3-time-format`'s six and `d3-format`'s four — so a host with a d3 locale JSON copies it across. It reaches every generated string: temporal tick labels and the multi-format an axis falls back to, an axis's or legend's stated `format`, `timeunit` bucket labels, the `monthFormat`, `dayFormat`, `timeFormat`, `utcFormat` and `format` expression functions, number separators and grouping, the typographic minus, and the spoken captions. The captions are an **interface** rather than a table, because they are grammar — a plural agreed with a number, a list joined with a conjunction — and `VegaCaptions.English` is upstream's own wording and the default. **Parsing is not localised**: d3's parsing is part of the wire format, so a specification writing `"Jan 5 2026"` in its data means January in every language, and `TimeFormat.MONTHS` stays English. What it could **not** reach was the *order* of a date's fields: `%b` resolved to the reader's month abbreviation, so a Dutch axis said `mei` and said `mei 21, 2026`, because the pattern came from tables with no locale in them. It is derived now, from the locale's own `date` (d3's `%x`) and `time` (`%X`) — a **deliberate divergence**, upstream's `timeUnitSpecifier` taking no locale at all. Two derivations, because there are two tables: `TimeUnits`'s entries are numeric so the whole pattern transfers, as `%x` with fields *dropped* (which keeps prose — `%e de %B de %Y` yields `%B de %Y`); Vega-Lite's spell the month as a **name**, so only the order transfers and the directives stay `%b %d %Y`, a name in a numeric pattern being `21-mei-2026`. `VegaLocale.EnglishUS` is pinned to upstream's answers — upstream is internally inconsistent, `%x` being `%-m/%-d/%Y` where its specifier table is `%Y-%m-%d` — and is the locale every differential comparison runs under, which `LocaleDefaultsTest`, the upstream vector replay and the three fixture gates all name at the call site. `timeUnitSpecifierOverrides` and `timeTickFormatOverrides` state a table where derivation is not wanted. The pattern is written on the Vega-Lite side, so `VegaLiteInput.toVega` takes a locale too and wants the *same* one the runtime gets. Everything above is a **table**, and `VegaLocale.rules` is the one seam that is behaviour: what a name-bearing directive says and what digits a number is written with — a contextual name (Polish `stycznia` beside a day number) and a numbering system being the two things no table can hold, the engine having written `value.toString()`. The precedence is that a **specification's format decides the shape and a host decides the details inside it**, so a rule cannot reorder a date, drop a field, change a width or replace a pattern; literal text a document typed never reaches one. Every method may answer null and `EnglishUS` carries no rules, so the fixtures are untouched. Out of reach on purpose: the day a week starts on, calendars and eras, and any format a platform composes rather than names

Upstream has two zones — the browser's own and UTC — and needs no more, because a browser is always on the device it draws for. An app is not, so a `timeZone` given to `SpecCompiler`, `VegaChartController`, `VegaLiteInput.toVega` or `ChartSession` says which zone **local** is; null is the device's own, read when it is needed rather than captured, which is exactly what every host had before. It reaches a `time` scale's ticks, `timeunit`'s buckets, the local expression functions, and `format.parse` — the last because a timestamp with no offset names a different instant in every zone and `Date.parse` reads it in local time, so this settles what local *is* rather than whether it applies. The `utc` forms are untouched; one upstream rule looks like a defect and is pinned as a test — `utchours` **parses** a bare string in local time and only then reads the hour in UTC, so its answer moves with this too. `VegaTimeZones.of` answers null for an identifier the platform does not carry rather than throwing, because that string usually comes from a server and a Kotlin throw at a host boundary ends the process

Upstream's `view.data(name, rows)`: a dataset with no `values`, no `url` and no `source` is an **input**, and a host fills it — which is how a chart is drawn from data the app holds rather than data a payload carried. `SpecCompiler(hostData = …)`, `VegaChartController.setData(name, rows)`, `ChartSession.setData(_:rows:)`. In Vega-Lite the name from `data: {"name": …}` survives compilation — checked against `vega-lite@6.4.3` — so a host uses the name it wrote and never has to know about `source_0`. The rows go in **where inline values would**, before anything else reads the dataset, so `format.parse` and every transform run over them unchanged; `ForeignData.instant` hands a date over as a date, so a host holding one does not format it for the engine to parse back. Setting data recompiles, which is how any compile input changes here. Three refusals, each a diagnostic rather than a silence: a name no dataset carries, a **derived** dataset — filling one would discard the transforms it exists for — and a `url`, which is *not fetched* when the host supplied the table

capabilities.feature: The host's own font, and the reader's text size
capabilities.notes: Three renderers, and until this each had a different half of it. **Fonts:** Compose takes a `fontFamilyResolver` and, since the default one matched the generic CSS keywords and nothing else, a `namedFontFamily` registry behind `rememberVegaTextEngine(fontFamilies)` — a `FontFamily` comes from a resource or a loaded typeface, so only a host that holds one can map a name to it, where the other two renderers resolve a device family from their platforms. A family nothing resolves is drawn in the default face and named in `ComposeTextEngine.unresolvedFontFamilies`, a text engine having no diagnostics channel of its own. The Android View takes `fontResolver`, because Android resolves a family name against the *system's* families so a bundled face — which most design systems ship — silently could not reach a chart; on iOS a family the app registered resolves by name. Weight and slant are applied to the **supplied** face rather than asked of the platform, or a bold label arrives in a face nothing in the chart mentions. **Text size:** Android scales by the device's `fontScale` and Compose by measuring in `sp`; `CoreTextTextEngine(textScale:)` and `ChartSession(textScale:)` are that on iOS, applied to measuring **and** drawing from one source — a scaled layout drawn unscaled is small text in a big box. `DynamicTypeSize.chartTextScale` maps the reader's setting for a SwiftUI host, from Apple's own body-size ratios rather than `UIFontMetrics`, which is UIKit-only and would tie a chart to one text style. Uncapped: a ceiling is a decision about a particular chart, and a host passes one

capabilities.feature: Time formatting against d3-time-format's own corpus
capabilities.notes: The package was **missing from the recording list** — the one that formats every label on every time axis — and adding it found nine directives absent and all three padding modifiers unimplemented. `%-I` came out as the literal text `%-I` where a specification asked for "9am"; `%c`, `%x` and `%X` (the locale's date, time and both), the ISO week trio `%G`/`%g`/`%V`, `%u`, `%Q`, `%s` and `%Z` were simply not there. Two details came from reading d3's `pad`: the **sign sits outside the width**, so the year -2 is `-0002`, and `%Y` is `year % 10000`, so the year 10002 is `0002`. And `%Q` could not **parse** any real timestamp: the reader took an `Int` and an epoch in milliseconds is thirteen digits, so it threw for every date since 1970

capabilities.feature: Number formatting against d3-format's own corpus
capabilities.notes: The package recorded **nothing** until the recorder learned **vitest** — a third runner beside Vega's `tape` and d3's `mocha` — and then yielded 774 vectors. Three real bugs on the path every axis label takes: `format(",d")` of 1e21 printed `9,223,372,036,854,775,807` because it went through a `Long`, and the fix is not exact expansion either — d3 hands anything from 1e21 up to `toLocaleString`, which writes the *shortest* representation, so 1.3e27 is `1300000000000000000000000000` where the double's exact value is `1300000000000000044761612288`; precision was not clamped to d3's 20, so `.30f` wrote thirty decimals; and `%` defaulted to no decimals where d3 defaults to six, with the sign appended *after* trimming so `~%` can see the zeros it is asked to trim. 122 vectors ask for `s` and 71 for `d` variants this subset does not accept, which is the honest size of the remaining gap

d3's `clamp` works in **both** directions and this clamped only the forward one, so inverting a position past the end of the range — every pointer event past the end of an axis — returned a value outside the domain: with domain `[0, 1]` and range `[10, 20]`, `invert(30)` read **2** where upstream reads 1. A brush or tooltip built on that selects data the scale says is not there. Found once the recorder could follow a **builder chain**, which took `d3-scale` from 55 recorded vectors to 1,129

capabilities.feature: The five transform bugs the harness found
