capabilities.notes: Each was invisible to the 178 differential fixtures. `window` ranked every row **1** without a `sort`, because the peer scan tested for a comparator before treating each row as its own peer group. `timeunit` never inferred units at all — `inferUnits` has its own algorithm upstream, a table of grains tested for *alignment*, and this fell through to extent-binning, so a year of month starts bucketed by **day**; `TimeUnits.detect` transcribes it, skippable weekly grain included, and `inferUnits` now overrides `units`/`step`/`maxbins`/`extent` as upstream says it does. `impute` did not mark a row it invented (`_impute: true`) and lost one wherever a group was missing an observed key, because the key domain is `keyvals` **and then** the data's keys. `aggregate` ignored `cross`, so empty cells were dropped instead of emitted with a zero count. `bin` and `timeunit` ignored `interval: false`, writing an end nobody asked for

capabilities.feature: Vega's and d3's own test suites as a harness
capabilities.notes: Upstream has ~3,700 assertions over ~30 packages. They are **recorded, not transcribed**: their test files are run against the installed 6.3.1 with the package's exports wrapped, and every call — arguments and upstream's actual answer — becomes a vector in `test-fixtures/upstream-vectors/`. The vectors are **not committed**: `scripts/record-upstream-vectors.sh` rebuilds them byte-identically from the pinned version, so the repository carries the recipe rather than 5 MB of derived data, and the replays skip *loudly* when they are absent. Their assertions are never read, which matters twice: several are deliberately loose (`t.ok(x > 0)`) where a port needs the exact value, and on a version upgrade the diff is *data* rather than a hand-edit across Kotlin files. Imports are rewritten by AST (`acorn`) — the regex version missed `import * as vega`, the form 55 files use. **15,220 vectors** recorded so far — the jump came from wrapping a **returned function**: d3's interpolators, its scales and a regression's `predict` are built and then called, so recording only the construction recorded `{$: 'function'}` and nothing else. Each call on the returned function is now a vector carrying the arguments it was built with. The largest are `d3-array` (1,538) and `d3-time` (1,047) — most of the *arithmetic* this engine ports is d3's, and d3 tests it far more thoroughly than a chart-level fixture can — then `vega-transforms` (548), `vega-time` (460), `d3-interpolate` (253), `d3-color` (216), `vega-scenegraph` (190) and `vega-expression` (149). d3 needed five accommodations, all in the same recorder: mocha's globally-injected `it` rather than an imported `tape`, `../src/index.js` rather than `../index.js`, one repository per package tagged from the installed version, each package's **own timezone** (d3-time's suite runs in `America/Los_Angeles`, recorded into the vector file so a replay knows), and a replaced `Date` **constructor**, since pinning `Date.now` leaves `new Date()` moving. The transform packages needed a second seam: they export operator *classes* driven through a dataflow, so nothing crosses the export boundary with plain arguments, and the recorder hooks `prototype.transform(_, pulse)` instead — parameters, tuples in, tuples out, and the operator's own value. Four things had to be right there: a comparator carries `fields` like an accessor does (and `orders`, which is how they are told apart), a single `facet` tuple can be 52 MB, an operator is **stateful** so only its first call is replayable, and an `expr` recorded as an accessor was a JavaScript function whose arithmetic is gone. The Kotlin side is an adapter per package with a **coverage floor**, so a harness cannot shrink into a pass: 281 of 460 time vectors replay, and the unmapped ones are named in the output. It has found **six** gaps so far, none of them visible to the 178 differential fixtures: an override of `null` in `timeUnitSpecifier` *removes* an entry rather than falling back, which a `Map<String, String>` could not express; `window` ignores peer rows, so `rank`/`dense_rank`/`percent_rank` are computed as if every row were unique; `timeunit` with `inferUnits` picks day where upstream picks month; `impute` does not set `_impute` on a row it invented, and misses one combination; `aggregate` ignores `cross`; and `bin` ignores `interval: false`. The last five are pinned **exactly** in `known-divergences.json` — a new divergence fails the build, and so does fixing one without deleting its entry

limit.test: UpstreamTransformVectorsTest.upstream's own transform vectors replay against these transforms
limit.claim: Coverage is partial and the divergences it has found are pinned exactly in `known-divergences.json` — a new one fails the build, and so does fixing one without deleting its entry. Each is a bug to fix rather than an accepted difference.

capabilities.feature: CSS colour parsing, against d3-color's own corpus
capabilities.notes: 34 of d3's `color()` vectors replay against `SceneColor.parse`, and **nineteen expect null** — rejecting a malformed colour is half the corpus and the half a hand-written test skips. Two findings, neither a parser bug: channels are 0..1 here and 0..255 in d3, so the comparison scales; and this parser accepts a **superset** — d3's regular expressions require integers and reject `rgb(120.5,30,50)`, `rgb(120.,…)` and an alpha of `1.`, all of which a browser accepts. That is right for rendering, where a `fill` goes to a renderer rather than to d3, and wrong for `luminance()`/`contrast()`, which are d3-color calls upstream and answer NaN for them. Thirteen signatures pinned in `known-divergences.json`. `hsl`, `hcl`, `lab`, `lch`, `cubehelix` and `gray` are colour spaces this engine does not model as objects

capabilities.feature: d3-array 3.2's tick algorithm, including the retry
capabilities.notes: This engine had the *older* algorithm. d3-array 3.2 rewrote it: `tickSpec` returns the first and last tick indices with the increment, and **retries with twice the count** when the interval is empty and the count is between a half and two — so `ticks(1, 364, 1)` is `[200]` upstream and was nothing here, meaning `"tickCount": 1` produced an axis with no ticks. The count is a `Double` now, because the retry passes `count * 2` and the condition is fractional. Two more from the same corpus: a **NaN bound** returned -Infinity through an early guard d3 does not have, and `nice` multiplied it out into a `[NaN, NaN]` domain — a chart that does not draw — where upstream leaves the domain alone; and `tickStep` is d3's own function rather than `stepFrom(tickIncrement(...))`, which loses the sign of a reversed span and answers NaN where d3 answers 0. Separately, `resolveInt` mapped a non-finite count through Kotlin's `toInt`, so `"tickCount": {"signal": "1/0"}` became `Int.MAX_VALUE` and exhausted the heap; it is zero now, which is upstream's answer

capabilities.feature: Flooring an hour across a daylight-saving fall-back
capabilities.notes: The sub-day intervals rebuilt a local time to floor it, and a local time is **ambiguous** across a fall-back: 01:30 happens twice in Los Angeles on 6 November 2011, so reconstructing resolved to the first occurrence and moved any instant in the second hour an hour backwards. d3 subtracts the local sub-fields from the instant instead, keeping the offset it already had, so each of the two 01:00s floors to itself. `second`, `minute` and `hour` now subtract at step 1; a larger step still snaps the field, which is `every(step)` behaviour and what Vega's own vectors expect. A non-positive step also enumerates nothing now, as d3 does. Found by replaying d3's suite, which is the only corpus that tests an hour boundary inside a DST transition

capabilities.feature: An arc whose radii are inverted, zero or negative
capabilities.notes: d3 *swaps* the radii rather than refusing them, so an arc written inside-out draws the identical ring — and an arc given only an `innerRadius` becomes a solid **wedge**, because its defaulted zero outer radius swaps to the inside. `ArcPath` had always carried that rule; `MarkEncoder` opened with `if (outerRadius <= 0.0 || startAngle == endAngle) return null` and never let the geometry see the values, so three of upstream's five items were dropped. Where a shape really does collapse — a non-positive outer radius, an angle of nothing — upstream still **emits the item**, as a point or a degenerate line; dropping it shifts every later item up an index and puts the mark's container out of step, which is a wider error than drawing the wrong shape

Compiling for five targets proved the core *links* off the JVM; it did not prove it agrees. 23 tests in `commonTest` now execute on Kotlin/Native as well as on the JVM, chosen for where a platform could plausibly differ rather than for coverage: the decimal expansion (`toRawBits`, 64-bit multiply, shifts), a specification's own regular expressions (which also exercises `ktecma262`'s native artifacts — this repository is one of its first consumers), d3's tick algorithm (`kotlin.math` is backed by each platform's own library), and the two LRU caches that exist in their present form only because `LinkedHashMap`'s access-order mode is JVM-only. Expectations come from the same oracles as the JVM suites — `BigDecimal` for the 60 decimal vectors, `eval-probe.js` and `d3-array` for the rest — so a native run is checked against upstream rather than against this implementation. It caught a wrong expectation on its first outing: `tickIncrement(0, 1, 2)` is **-2**, a negative divisor, not 0.5. Two limits: a backtick test name may not contain a comma on native (it becomes a symbol), and `iosSimulatorArm64Test` needs a simulator runtime this machine does not have, so the Apple targets are compiled but not run

capabilities.feature: The core, actually compiled for Kotlin Multiplatform
capabilities.notes: Six modules — `vega-model`, `-expression`, `-dataflow`, `-scene`, `-runtime`, `-svg` — are `kotlin("multiplatform")` with a JVM target and four native ones. "Portable" had been a **claim** enforced by a grep for `java.`; compiling it found two things the grep could not, both of which had been there since Milestone 1. `LinkedHashMap` is common Kotlin, so a text-layout cache and an expression cache that **subclassed** it for `removeEldestEntry` and its access-order constructor — neither of which exists off the JVM, where the class is final — read as portable and were not. Both are now four lines of explicit LRU: remove-and-reinsert on a hit, drop `keys.first()` when over capacity. `Character.digit` went the same way, replaced by the ASCII digit rule, which is also what `parseInt` actually does. Sources stay in `src/main/kotlin` and `src/test/kotlin` rather than moving to `commonMain`, so the change is legible as a build change. `vega-loader` (a socket and a file) and `test-fixtures` (test scaffolding) stay JVM by design — they *are* the platform seam. The tests stay JVM too, which is honest rather than ideal: they exercise common code, but on one target. One trap came with it and is worth knowing before writing a script — the multiplatform plugin has **no `test` task**, only `jvmTest`, so `./gradlew test` matched nothing in these modules and reported success. The gate went green once without running 4,939 tests. There is now a `test` alias in every module, and `oracle.sh` names `jvmTest` outright

capabilities.feature: Exact decimal formatting, with no platform seam
capabilities.notes: The core's **last** JVM-only file is gone, and removing it fixed a bug it had been hiding. The argument for `java.math.BigDecimal` was that rounding a double at N places must round its *exact* binary value — true — and that common Kotlin cannot: false. A finite double is `m × 2^e`, so `m × 2^-k` is `(m × 5^k) × 10^-k`: the expansion is **finite**, at most ~767 digits, and producing it needs multiply-by-a-word and a shift. Rounding half-up then reduces to one bit test, because the discarded part is a run of bits and the remainder reaches half exactly when the top one is set. What the seam had hidden: `exponential` went through Java's `String.format("%.Ne")`, which rounds the *shortest printable form* rather than the exact value — so `format('.2e', 2.675)` answered `2.68e+0` where upstream answers `2.67e+0`, and `.17e` padded with zeros where upstream keeps expanding. Both wrong for as long as the engine has had a formatter, and both invisible until the replacement disagreed with it. `BigDecimal` survives as the **oracle in the test**, which is where it belonged: 150,000 random bit patterns plus every awkward value, all four functions

`$` is a slot of its own in d3's grammar — before the zero-pad flag and the grouping comma, so `$,.2f` parses and `,$` does not — and the symbol goes *inside* the sign, so a negative price reads `−$1.50` rather than `$−1.50`

WCAG relative luminance, the number `contrast()` is built from. Three things about it are easy to get plausibly wrong and only a comparison against upstream catches: the gamma knee is WCAG's **0.03928**, not the 0.04045 the Lab conversion in `ColorSpaces` uses — for a whole 8-bit channel the two never disagree, but an `hsl()` colour's fractional channel can; the arithmetic is on the channel already divided by 255, so nothing round-trips through bytes; and nothing rounds or clamps, so `rgb(300, 0, 0)` is brighter than white here as it is upstream. A colour that cannot be read is NaN rather than 0, and so is a fully transparent one — d3 blanks the channels at zero opacity, so `luminance('transparent')` is not black's answer

Returns the **count** of matching rows, not a boolean, and the comparison is by **string coercion** rather than `===` — upstream indexes the dataset with a plain JavaScript object, so `indata('t', 'k', 1)` finds a row whose `k` is the string `"1"` and `true` finds `"true"`. Absent is `undefined`, as upstream's is. Upstream requires the dataset and field names to be string literals because it resolves them into an index while parsing; nothing here needs them that early, so a computed name works. A name no dataset has is reported rather than quietly matching nothing

There is no DOM, so this is upstream's own headless answer rather than an invented one: `[undefined, undefined]` — two absent values, not `[0, 0]` and not an empty array. A specification that sizes itself from its container therefore falls back, exactly as it does against upstream outside a browser. Reporting the view's width and height instead would draw a different chart from the one upstream draws

The WCAG ratio, `(lighter + 0.05) / (darker + 0.05)` over two `luminance()` values. Symmetric — the brighter colour always goes on top — which is what lets the standard idiom work: `contrast('white', datum.fill) > contrast('black', datum.fill)` picks a readable label colour without knowing which way round the two are. The margin can be under 1%, so an approximation right to two digits still picks the wrong colour. An unreadable or fully transparent colour makes its luminance NaN, so the ratio is NaN and every comparison against it is false, as upstream

capabilities.feature: The colour constructors, and the geo and selection helpers
capabilities.notes: `rgb`, `hsl`, `lab` and `hcl` build colours an expression can read components off, and the geo helpers — `geoArea`, `geoBounds`, `geoCentroid`, `geoScale`, `geoShape` — and the `vlSelection*` family are registered. The row said these "belong to subsystems that do not exist yet".
`update` beats `init` beats `value`; dependency-ordered; `width`, `height` and `padding` implicit; cycles reported by name
Was "Reported; needs the interaction system". The interaction system exists; see the `on` rows below

Was "Not planned: input widgets have no equivalent here", which was the wrong conclusion — a binding *describes* a control and only the widget is a browser's. See "Signal `bind` — the controls a chart asks for" below

capabilities.feature: A transform's **expression** parameter as a dependency
capabilities.notes: `filter`'s `expr`, `formula`'s `expr` and `cross`'s `filter` are per-row expressions rather than `{"signal":...}` references, which makes it tempting to conclude they cannot be edges. Upstream's `parseExpression` says otherwise: it walks every expression's AST and lets the `scale`, `data` and `indata` visitors register what they find as operator **parameters**, so a `formula` calling `scale('x', datum.v)` waits for that scale exactly as a signal-valued parameter would
How a timeline offers to run right-to-left; there is nothing constant to write down. Resolved when the scale is built, like every other signal-valued scale property

A halo under a label on a busy background. Dropped entirely before, and invisible to the comparison besides — `textMark` emitted a fill and never a stroke, which is the seventh channel to have been blind here

`{"signal":...}` anywhere in a transform's parameters — which operation an aggregate computes, which field it reads, how many rows a filter keeps. Each such reference is an edge in the dependency order, so the dataset waits for the signal — and for the scale, when the expression reads one, which is how `{"extent": {"signal": "domain('xscale')"}}` computes a density over exactly the span an axis will show
`padding`, `align`, `tickCount`, `tickSize`, `labelPadding`, `labelFontSize`, `offset`

Which scale a channel uses, when the specification does not name it outright. Takes the same four forms a `field` does and resolves through the same code: `signal` is a control switching an axis between linear and log, `parent` is a faceted cell using the scale its enclosing group chose, and `datum` is a parallel-coordinates plot picking a different scale per row. An object naming none of the four is reported rather than read as a scale called nothing

Orders a mark's *items* — which is what is drawn where, and the order they are painted in — after they are encoded, because the fields are a path into the **item** rather than a column of the data. `{"field": "y"}` sorts by where the item ended up and `{"field": "datum.year"}` reaches through it to the row that produced it; upstream has no special case for either, `vega-util`'s `field` simply walks the path. A path this scene graph cannot follow is reported rather than treated as a tie, because a tie leaves the declaration order and looks exactly like a sort that worked. Only `"descending"` descends, as upstream tests it — `"desc"` ascends

Upstream's `adjustSpatial`, in its own order, which matters twice. An end without a start puts the mark's *far* edge there and lets the extent run back from it. A centre is applied **last**, overriding whatever the other channels worked out, so `xc` beside a `width` centres the mark rather than starting it. Group, image and rect read a start beyond its end as the pair written the other way round; a line or an area keeps the sign, because there the two ends are a direction and not a box. A `rule` is skipped entirely, as upstream skips it
The `[{test,...}, {...}]` array form, for every channel kind
Explicitly forbidden

limit.test: ForbiddenFunctionsTest.naming a host object reaches nothing
limit.claim: No general evaluator is reachable: a call to `eval` and its family is refused by a closed function registry, and a bare name like `globalThis` resolves to nothing rather than to a host object. A specification is data somebody else wrote, so this is a security boundary rather than a missing feature.

capabilities.notes: What a Vega-Lite selection compiles *into*: the predicate a filter or a conditional encoding calls to ask whether a datum is in a named selection, the identity form for point selections keyed on a field, and the tuple list a selection's store holds. A specification never writes these — Vega-Lite emits them — which is why they went unnamed here for six milestones while being exercised by every selection fixture

The arithmetic an interactive specification does inside an event handler: appending a point to a lasso with a minimum separation, turning the accumulated points into an SVG path, and the distance and angle between two touches. They are pure functions over numbers, so they are testable without a device, which is what the reference vectors do
Padding and `autosize` come with spec parsing

All three alignments and both bounds. `each` gives every column the widest lead-in in that column, `all` the widest anywhere, and `none` lets each cell keep its own overhang so nothing lines up and no space is wasted. `bounds: "flush"` measures a cell by its **declared** extent rather than by how far its contents reach, so an axis label hanging off to the left is allowed to collide instead of pushing the next cell across. Ported from upstream's `gridLayout` rather than derived: the three alignments differ only in how the per-cell lead-in is pooled, which is easy to get subtly wrong

`cell`, `view`, `point`, `circle` and `square`, which a specification can override but rarely defines. Not decoration: `cell` is `{fill: "transparent", stroke: "#ddd"}`, and it is what makes a `style: "cell"` group **painted** — a group that paints nothing is not a mark at all, so a chart laid out from styled cells came out two marks short of upstream's. The symbol styles carry a size of **30** where a bare symbol's is 100

`width` and `height` come from the **enclosing group item**, not from the `width` signal. Upstream compiles the reference to `item.mark.group.width`, the size the group item was encoded with; the two agree at the top level, which is why reading the signal survived so long, and they part company inside a cell that declares a width of its own

Ticks, labels, gridlines, domain line and title for all four orientations, plus `offset`, `zindex`, and switching any of the four parts off. A gridline runs back across the plot away from its own side, and an axis with its ticks off pulls its labels in by the tick size

The `{part}Color`, `Width`, `Dash`, `Opacity`, `Font`, `FontWeight` and `FontStyle` family, for all five parts — label, tick, grid, domain and title. Upstream spells them the same way with a different prefix, and they are read the same way here. A label's colour is a **fill** and every other part's is a stroke, so `labelOpacity` lands on a fill opacity where `gridOpacity` lands on a stroke opacity. A tick's stroke width counts towards the chart's size and a gridline's does not, because an axis is measured by its ticks and labels

`labelAngle` turns each label about its own anchor and changes nothing else — upstream leaves the alignment and baseline at whatever the orientation gave them, so a 45-degree label on a bottom axis stays centred and top-baselined and hangs off to the left of its tick. `labelAlign` and `labelBaseline` are how that is corrected, and are what Vega-Lite emits alongside an angle. A turned label's rotated extent is what the axis is measured by, so the chart grows to fit it

Replaces the scale's own ticks, and the gridlines follow. A value outside the scale's **range** is dropped rather than clamped; the survivors are ordered by where they land, so a list written out of order comes out in order and backwards on a reversed range; too many for `tickCount` are thinned by repeated halving, falling back to the two ends below three, so five values under `tickCount: 4` give three. Labels are formatted at the precision the *number of values* implies, not the values' own — `[0.5, 1.5]` on a `[0, 2]` domain reads "1" and "2", which is upstream's answer and rarely the intended one

Every one of the 79 properties upstream's schema documents for an axis is consumed, and the same for a legend's 72 — measured by `UpstreamPropertyCoverageTest` and published in `docs/upstream-coverage.md`. This row said "the forty-odd this engine does not honour", which was true when written and is now zero.

A gridline spans a **second** scale's range instead of the plotting area, which is how a grid is drawn across a cell that is not the size of its own plot. It takes the two ends in that scale's own order — `range(gridScale)[0]` then `[1]` — so a descending range gives a gridline whose start is the far end, which the plain form never does

A label within the threshold of an end of the range is aligned *to* that end rather than centred, so the first and last sit inside the plot instead of hanging off its corners. `true` means one pixel, and **zero is not off**: upstream's test is `flush === 0 or !!flush`, so a zero threshold still flushes a label landing exactly on an end. It moves the alignment on the axis's own dimension, so a bottom axis flushes its `align` and a left one its `baseline`; an explicit `labelAlign` still wins. `labelFlushOffset` is still reported
How deep the axis may be, whatever its contents measure. Upstream's defaults are 0 and 200

`tickOffset` nudges a tick along the axis after `bandPosition` has placed it, and its default is **not** zero: upstream's `config.axisBand` carries a `-0.5` correcting the half-pixel an axis group's translation adds, and applies it to a band scale only. A specification aiming its ticks at the band boundaries sets `bandPosition: 1` *and* `tickOffset: 0`. `tickExtra` adds one more tick at the **start** of the first tick's band, from a datum carrying no value of its own — so its label scales an absent value, and the three consequences all have to be reproduced together: upstream's scene records a `NaN` position, its `anchorPoint` reads `item.y \|\| 0` so the *bounds* are the box an empty string occupies at the origin, and its SVG contains no element for it at all

The band's **centre**, whatever the ticks do. Upstream's label mark hard-codes `band: 0.5` and takes only the offset from the shared band settings, so `bandPosition: 1` moves the ticks to the edges and leaves the labels where they were

Where a tick and its gridline sit along a band, as a fraction: 0 the start, 0.5 the centre. Ticks and gridlines only — a *label* is always at the band's centre upstream, which writes `band: 0.5` outright, so a chart that wants its labels moved says so in an `encode` block

capabilities.feature: A scaled channel taking its value from a signal
capabilities.notes: `{"scale": "x", "signal": "currentYear"}`, which is how a mark is placed where a *control* says rather than where a datum says. Upstream builds the base value from `signal`, `field` or `value` and *then* wraps it in the scale, so the scale must be read before the signal; reading the signal first drops the scale and puts the mark at the raw domain value — 2010 pixels from the left, on a scale of years

A rule over the tick's own value deciding whether the label is drawn — a calendar names the first week of each month and blanks the other forty-eight. No axis property can say it. A label hidden this way still contributes to the axis's measurement, unlike one dropped by overlap removal, which is upstream's distinction

The title stands beside the entries rather than above them, and the anchoring changes with it: upstream reads a left or right title as `middle`-anchored where a top one is `start`-anchored, and a gradient's title is centred against the **bar alone**, not against the labels beneath it. `right` and `bottom` are reported — each needs its own anchoring rule. The legend's `titleLimit` (180 by default, and nothing has to ask for it) is honoured with it, because the title's width is what pushes the entries across

A legend measures as its **box**, not as the union of what it drew: upstream's `legendBounds` anchors the aggregate at the legend's padding and then sets the item's bounds to the resulting rectangle. A vertically centred title reaches three quarters of a unit above the legend's top edge, and measuring it there makes the whole chart a unit taller

`number`, `time` or `utc`, deciding which grammar the label `format` is written in. Upstream's `tickFormat` checks it **before** the scale type, so `time` wins over every scale including the discrete ones whose labels would otherwise be their own values — which is the only thing that makes a band scale of instants read as `Sun, Mon, Tue` rather than as epoch milliseconds, there being no temporal scale to infer it from. With no specifier it falls back to the multi-format that picks a granularity per value. A screen reader hears the domain with `%a` expanded to `%A` and `%b` to `%B`, as upstream expands them, so an axis labelled "Sun" is announced "Sunday". A `formatType` chosen by a signal is reported rather than guessed at

capabilities.feature: A property computed by a parameter
capabilities.notes: `{"expr": …}` on a guide, a **mark** property or a **scale** property is a signal, and a signal is a *reference* — it replaces the whole entry rather than sitting inside a `value`. `{"expr": …}` is Vega-Lite's way of writing a signal and Vega's is `{"signal": …}`; passed through, the property was unread and the guide stayed at its default. A **`labelAngle`** supplied that way also moves its own align and baseline onto the labels' `encode`, the comparison being one Vega has to make: an axis property takes a constant, not a rule

`{"format": {"signal": "timeUnitSpecifier(tbin.units)"}}` — a chart whose granularity is bound to a control has no constant specifier to write down. It had been parsed and dropped, which is the failure mode `zindex` showed: read into the model, never used, never reported

Upstream's `formatSpan`, and it applies to axis labels, legend labels and the spoken caption alike. A specifier naming no precision does not mean "no decimals" — it means as many as the tick step over the span being labelled needs, so `"%"` over a `[-0.06, 0.06]` ramp reads `−6%` where d3's fixed six decimals would give `−6.000000%`. A percent format takes two fewer, because the value is multiplied by a hundred first, and the result is clamped into `[0, 20]` as d3's `FormatSpecifier` clamps it

A d3-format specifier on the tick labels, which is how a price axis reads `$1.50`. It also changes what a screen reader is told: upstream describes the domain the way the labels read it, **per axis** — two axes over one scale, one formatted as currency, are announced differently. Ignored on a discrete scale, where upstream coerces the domain's own values to strings and never consults it
Placed a padding beyond however far the ticks and labels reach — gridlines excluded, as upstream excludes them — anchored along the scale's range, and turned a quarter turn on a vertical axis

One swatch and label per entry, filled from the scale. Row heights, label offsets and the legend's own size match upstream exactly. A legend that maps no colour gets grey outlined swatches, as upstream does
Sampled at the scale's own ticks plus the domain ends, so a multi-stop ramp bends where upstream's does. Vertical and horizontal, with end labels baselined inside the swatch

All four edges, all four corners, `orient: none` with `legendX`/`legendY`, and stacking for legends that share an orientation. A vertical axis pushes out a side legend and a horizontal one an edge legend, kept separate as upstream does

Each entry advances by the previous cell's far edge rounded up, plus however far the next one overhangs backwards, plus the padding. With uniform swatches any reasonable rule agrees; with a size legend, where each swatch outgrows the last, they diverge by several units a row

The right colours against the right cut points, drawn as ordinary symbol swatches. Upstream draws a **stacked colour bar** instead — `legend-band` rects of `gradientLength / buckets` each, bottom upwards, with labels at the boundaries between them — so this is not the same picture and says so. Label precision is taken from the cut points themselves rather than from a tick step, since quartiles land wherever the data puts them and `2.5` beside a `5` must not print as `2`

An undeclared ordinal value **joins** the domain instead of being unknown, so the domain grows as the scale is used and each new value takes the range entry after the last one claimed. Off by default because order of use then decides which colour a value gets — a chart that reordered its rows would repaint itself

A **bypass**, not an override: upstream reads it first in `configureDomain` and returns before it looks at `zero`, `domainMin`, `domainMax` or `domainMid`. `nice` is the one that catches you — it is applied by the caller at six sites, one per scale family, so returning early from the domain resolution still leaves it to widen `[17, 43]` back out to `[16, 44]`. A raw domain of fewer than two values is *not* an override, which is what lets a brush signal be null until a reader touches the chart

`formatType` is the only thing that can make a gradient legend's labels read as dates: its scale is a colour ramp, so there is nothing temporal to infer from. Both come from `GuideFormat`, shared with the axis rather than reimplemented. The **caption** formats the same domain differently from the labels — upstream expands the abbreviating directives before reading one out, so a ramp labelled `%b %Y` is described as "January 2024" — and a caption with no format at all carries its zone, because one that reads out a whole timestamp should say which clock it is on
A fixed row height for a symbol legend. Implemented since that fixture, and until now missing from `LEGEND_CONSUMED` — so every legend using it was told it had been ignored

Not a truncation: upstream keeps `limit - 1` entries and spends the last row on a summary — `…7 entries` — where the number counts what was *not* shown and the swatch beside it takes the next value's own size, so a size legend's summary row is drawn at the size of the first thing it stands for. A limit the entries already fit inside does nothing

An `href` makes an item a link, and upstream's renderer wraps whatever it drew in an `<a xlink:href>`. It was missing on **marks** as well as guides — the one remaining channel that was, rather than a guide-only gap. Kept on the item rather than turned into a click handler, because a renderer that knows how to draw a link knows how to make it navigable and one that does not can ignore it; the wrapper is emitted once at the renderer's single dispatch point rather than in each of the seven shapes. Unlike the other item channels this one **is** comparable — upstream carries it on the item — so the harness now checks it on every fixture, and adding that immediately caught text, rule and group marks recording it nowhere

`tooltip`, `cursor`, `zindex`, `aria` and `description` reach the **item** rather than its geometry or its paint. Every one is already a mark channel and none was reachable from a guide, so a hoverable axis label, a tick that says what it marks, a label raised over its neighbours and a decorative title kept out of the accessibility tree were all impossible to ask for. Resolved against the part's **own datum**, which is the point: a tooltip written `{"signal": "'at ' + datum.value"}` on an axis label reads that label's tick, so one axis gives one tooltip per label rather than one for the whole guide. Threaded through all ten parts — the axis's labels, ticks, gridlines, domain and title, and the legend's symbols, labels, title, gradient and its own group. Tested against upstream's items rather than by a fixture, because the differential harness reads coordinates, colours and text and can see none of these

Upstream's `DataJoin`, and it is not the hint about redraws it reads as: the join maps each key to **one** item, so two rows sharing a key are one mark rather than two. The item keeps the position its key first appeared in and takes the *last* such row's datum, so a repeated key draws the later row's values where the earlier row would have been — a shape no filtering or ordering produces, which is why it had to be honoured rather than treated as advice. A specification saying `key` was getting one bar per row: three bars where upstream draws two. Keys are compared as **text** because upstream's `fastmap` is an object and coerces them, so a numeric `1` and the string `"1"` are one key on both sides

capabilities.feature: A mark's `description`, and the container it is announced on
capabilities.notes: Upstream draws every item of a mark inside one element and hangs the mark's own announcement on it — `role`, an `aria-roledescription` naming the kind of thing in words, and the `aria-label` a mark-level `description` supplies — so a series is named **once** rather than on each of its fifty bars. It had nowhere to live: this scene has no mark level, a group's children being the items themselves. Two fields now travel on the items and the renderer rebuilds the container from a run that shares them, and one of them, `markOrdinal`, was needed for its own sake — two `rect` marks side by side read as a single run before it, so an item `zindex` in the second could paint among the first's items. The role is upstream's rule and not the obvious one: `graphics-object` for a group, a text mark, or a mark whose items say something **of their own**, which is why an `AccessibilityDescriptor` records whether its label was asked for or derived. Verified by harvesting upstream's rendered output, the way `zindex` had to be, and that immediately taught two things nobody would have guessed: a symbol legend's entries are announced as a group mark container and a gradient legend's are not, and `aria-roledescription` was missing from **every** guide and item this engine drew

A silent gap the differential harness *cannot* see, which is why it survived: the comparison reads the **scene**, and upstream keeps its items in data order and reorders inside `visit` at render time. So a chart using `zindex` drew in the wrong order here while every compared number agreed. The rule is not a sort — upstream paints every item whose `zindex` is zero first, in data order, then the ones that carry one, ordered by it. A negative `zindex` is still non-zero, so it joins the second pass and draws **on top**: `[0, -1, 0]` and `[0, 5, 0]` give the same order, which no sort would produce. Confined to each run of children from one mark, so a raised bar draws over its neighbours and still under the axis. The expectations are the left-to-right order of the rects in upstream's own SVG

capabilities.feature: Seven channels the harness could not see
capabilities.notes: The comparison looked at position, colour, width, opacity, dash, text and font — so `strokeCap`, `strokeJoin`, `strokeMiterLimit`, `blend`, `limit`, `ellipsis` and a group's `clip` went past it entirely. Each changes what is drawn: a round-capped rule is longer than a butt-capped one by its own width, a mitre limit decides whether a spike is pointed or cut flat, `limit` decides whether a label reads "September" or "Sep…" — and the item's `text` is the *untruncated* string on both sides, so a wrong limit changed the drawing and nothing else. All seven are now compared on every fixture, and all 156 passed unchanged: they were right, they were simply unverified

capabilities.feature: Guide `encode` channels with no property, and what "not implemented" should mean
capabilities.notes: Sweeping every channel against every guide part turned up about 150 reported as "not implemented", and most were not gaps at all: a tick is a **rule**, so `encode.ticks.update.text` is a channel a rule has no use for, and upstream agrees in the only way that counts — it writes the value onto the item and its renderer never reads it. Those now say what they are, naming the shape the part actually is, which left a short and actionable list of real ones. Closed from it: a label's `ellipsis` and `lineBreak`, and a title's `text`, `ellipsis`, `lineBreak`, `dx` and `dy` — none of which has a guide property behind it, so each is resolved against the item as a label's position already was. Two things fell out: a **multi-line** title sits further from the axis by the height of its extra lines (upstream's `axisTitleLayout` adds `multiLineOffset`), and the accessibility caption has to read the title the encode block produced rather than the one it replaced

`config.group` paints the chart's own **frame**, not its group marks — the name says otherwise and so does upstream's own comment, but probing it both ways shows the root item carrying the fill while an inner group mark does not, and reading it as a mark default put a tinted rectangle behind every group a specification wrote. `config.projection` merges under each projection the way `config.title` merges under the title. And `autosize`, `background`, `padding` and `description` were being **reported as the wrong shape** while being read perfectly well elsewhere — a diagnostic that sends a reader looking for a bug that is not there. `config.events` was what remained, and it is the row below

`sort: {"field": "value"}` on a `treemap`, `pack`, `partition` or `tree` sorts by the total the layout **computed** — the sum over each node's leaves — which is the whole reason to sort a hierarchy and is not a column anywhere in the data. It was read off the row instead, found nothing, and sorted nothing: a chart asking for its biggest group first got its groups in data order and a completely different picture. No fixture used `sort` on a layout, which is how it survived. `depth`, `height` and a `data.` path into the row are the others a node answers to, and a bare column name does nothing — upstream's accessor is on the node, and probing confirmed it ignores one

capabilities.feature: A domain `sort` whose direction is a signal
capabilities.notes: `{"order": {"signal": "order"}}` is what a control changes when a reader reverses a chart, and it was read with `asString()` — so the object stringified to something that did not begin with "desc" and **every such domain came out ascending**, in silence. Resolved where the signals are now. Found by building the demo's bound chart, which is the second thing that fixture pins: upstream shares one sort operator between two domains that differ *only* in the signal, so the second silently takes the first's order — which is why each question in the fixture is asked once

capabilities.feature: A chart loaded asynchronously answering anything
capabilities.notes: `setSpecAsync` recorded neither the specification's text nor a fresh set of overrides, so a chart loaded through it had nothing to recompile **from**: no signal change could redraw it, whether it came from a control, a handler or a tap on a mark. Every test used the synchronous path and the demo uses the other one, so every interactive specification in the demo was inert and nothing said so. Two lines, and the reason to build a demo at all

capabilities.feature: A guide `encode` block moving the geometry
capabilities.notes: `encode.ticks.update.y` is not decoration: upstream merges the block into the part's own encoders and applies it **last**, so a specification can lift every tick off its axis, pull a gridline in from both ends, or start a domain line short of its scale. Probed rather than assumed, because a guide that writes its own geometry on every pass could as easily have overwritten it. A published example reaches through a tick to mark a temperature, which no axis property can express

capabilities.feature: A guide stroke channel that reads `datum`
capabilities.notes: Folding a guide's encode channel into the property it duplicates — `encode.ticks.update.strokeWidth` *is* `tickWidth` — is right for a constant and for a signal over the chart's state, and cannot work for one that reads the **tick**: at parse time there is no tick, so `{"signal": "datum.value === marked ? 2 : 1"}` took the false branch on every one of them. The stroke channels are resolved again per tick, which costs nothing where they are constant and is the only way that form works at all

`{"parse": {"when": "date:%d/%m/%Y"}}` and its `utc:` twin, which is how a column of dates a `Date.parse` cannot guess gets read — most of the world writes them day-first. The pattern may be quoted and the split is on the **first** colon, since a time pattern contains its own. 406 rows of one published example were staying text and drawing an axis from strings. The parser it needed already existed, written for the expression `timeParse`, and was simply never wired to the loader

capabilities.feature: A guide number that goes through a scale
capabilities.notes: Upstream's `numberValue` is a **value reference**, not a number or a signal: `"offset": {"scale": "ord", "value": "Cylinders", "mult": -1}` on an axis is how parallel coordinates spaces its seven axes across the plot. Refusing it left every one of them at the same offset, stacked on top of each other. Resolved by the encoder's own channel code against the empty datum a guide has, so a guide number and a mark channel are read by exactly the same lines

capabilities.feature: A colour that resolves to nothing
capabilities.notes: `{"value": null}`, or a field a row has not got, means the channel is **unset** — the mark draws without a stroke, which is how a specification says "no outline on these rows". It was being stringified first, so every one became the word "null" and then a complaint: 318 across the published examples, every one of them on a chart that was already drawing correctly. The third diagnostic of this shape to be removed, and the reason to read what a warning says rather than count it

`conicConformal`, `conicEqualArea`, `conicEquidistant`, `azimuthalEqualArea`, `azimuthalEquidistant`, `gnomonic`, `orthographic`, `stereographic`, `transverseMercator`, `naturalEarth1`, `equalEarth` and `mollweide`, each drawn with the same graticule and the same four cities so nothing but the projection differs. All correct, including the clipping each family does — the gnomonic's 60-degree cap and the orthographic's hemisphere are what keep them from drawing the far side of the world folded over the near one

capabilities.feature: The unexercised shapes, curves and time units
capabilities.notes: Seven symbol shapes (`cross`, `triangle`, the left and right triangles, `arrow`, `wedge`, `stroke`), three curve families (`basis-open`, `catmull-rom-open`, `catmull-rom-closed`) and five `timeunit` units (`quarter`, `dayofyear`, `minutes`, `seconds`, `milliseconds`) had never been drawn or bucketed by anything. All correct, `dayofyear` included — which is the one worth having, since it maps a date onto a **reference year** and so answers "Mar 27" for a reading on 28 March

`rank`, `dense_rank`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist`, `ntile`, `first_value`, `last_value`, `nth_value`, `prev_value` and `next_value` — every one of them right, over a column built with **ties**, which is the only arrangement that separates the ranking family: `rank` leaves a gap after a tie where `dense_rank` does not, and `percent_rank` and `cume_dist` divide by different totals. Read out as text so the numbers are compared rather than a bar's height

capabilities.feature: `distinct`, and the six other unexercised aggregates
capabilities.notes: `argmax`, `distinct`, `missing`, `valid`, `variance`, `variancep` and `stdevp` had never been asked for by any fixture — they are named in an `ops` array rather than as a transform `type`, so the transform-coverage count misses them. Six were already right and `distinct` was not: it counts over **every** row rather than the readable ones, and by the string each value coerces to, so an absent field and an explicit `null` are two different answers and both count. A column of 4, 9, 4, `null` and nothing has **four** distinct values upstream where filtering the missing ones out first said two

Collects the **rows** of a group, not the column the schema makes you name — upstream pushes the tuple itself and ignores the field. The difference is the whole point of the operation: it carries a group's rows along so something downstream can read a *different* column out of them, which `donut-chart-labelled` does with `pluck(datum.shiftArray, 'shift')`. Against an array of one column's values that reads back nothing but nulls, and every label's shift came out zero. Invisible to the corpus because the array is only ever read by a **signal**: no fixture's scene could tell the difference, and the one specification that depends on it looks identical until its timer has run

capabilities.feature: The smoothing and text transforms' own options
capabilities.notes: `kde`'s `bandwidth`, `extent`, `steps`, `cumulative`, `counts`, `groupby` and `resolve: "independent"`; `loess`'s own `bandwidth` and `groupby`; `countpattern`'s `pattern`, `case` and `stopwords`; `identifier`'s `as`; and `voronoi`'s `extent` and `as`. Each of those transforms had exactly one fixture and each used only the defaults, so the options were implemented and unverified. All correct

`pack`'s `radius` column and `padding`, `partition`'s `round` and `padding`, `tree`'s `cluster` method and `separation: false`, and an `as` on all three that renames every output the layout writes. Each layout had exactly one fixture, and each of those used the defaults — so this says what was previously only hoped: all of it was already right

Three transforms with no fixture between them, all three already correct. `impute` fills the hole a stacked chart cannot draw around — a series missing one category — and `pivot` turns a long table wide, naming a column after a value in the data. `nest` builds the hierarchy a `treemap` needs from a table with no parent column, generating the interior nodes its keys stand for

capabilities.feature: A legend for a discretizing scale
capabilities.notes: The **stacked colour bar** was already right and nothing had ever verified it: one band per bucket, each as tall as the share of the domain its bucket covers, labels at the boundaries between them and none on the first, since nothing bounds it from below. The fixture pins all three scale types and both directions. What was wrong was the same scale asked for as **symbols**: each swatch was labelled with its lower edge, which does not say which side of the number the colour is on, and a diagnostic claimed the whole legend was an approximation of a colour bar. Upstream draws swatches there too and names the *interval* — `< 25`, `25 – 50`, `≥ 75`, with an en dash — and a bin scale's last bucket ends at its last edge rather than running to infinity. So the drawing was right, the labels were the gap, and the report was pointing at neither

All four — `quantize`, `threshold`, `quantile`, `bin-ordinal` — were skipped outright with "cannot generate ticks", which is a whole axis missing from a chart that asked for one. Each ticks at something different and upstream decides by what the scale *has*: bins first, then a `ticks` method, then the domain. So a quantize scale ticks over the domain it buckets (d3 builds it on a linear scale), a threshold scale at its own cut points, a quantile scale at **every sample** in its domain, and a bin-ordinal scale at its bin edges — the only one filtered, since the last edge bounds the topmost bucket rather than opening one and maps to nothing. Their labels are plain values rather than formatted: only `quantize` has a `tickFormat` upstream, so a `format` on the other three is *ignored* rather than applied, which is the faithful reading and not an omission. The axis is drawn between the first and last entries of the range, which is what centres its title

`{"interval": "hours", "step": 2}` on an axis or a legend is not a count at all: it names the calendar unit the ticks land on. It was dropped in silence — `numberOrSignal` saw a string or an object and had nothing to make a number of — so a night was labelled at whatever round number the count algorithm liked, 27 ticks where upstream draws 10. Snapped to the calendar rather than added to the start, which is what keeps the ticks on even hours across a daylight-saving change instead of drifting an hour after it. Writing the fixture also found that **every plural interval name matched nothing**: `TimeInterval` is spelled `HOUR` and Vega's units are `"hours"`, `"minutes"`, `"seconds"`, `"date"`, `"dayofyear"`, `"quarter"` — so `nice: "hours"` had been silently doing nothing too, and `"quarter"` is three months rather than an interval of its own

capabilities.feature: A `bin-ordinal` domain taken from a field
capabilities.notes: Distinct, unlike the other three discretizing scales: the domain of a bin-ordinal scale is the bin **edges**, so a column of a thousand rows in four bins has a domain of four. Keeping the duplicates put every edge at the wrong bucket — the bisection counts equal values, so the lowest bin was painted with the highest bucket's colour, a chart wrong in the most visible way it could be. Order is first appearance and not sorted: upstream sorts only when the domain says `"sort": true`, and a jumbled column really does give a jumbled scale there

capabilities.feature: Scale `nice` as a time interval, and a time axis's own format
capabilities.notes: `nice` takes three forms and they round to different things: a flag rounds out to whatever step the tick algorithm chose, a **count** changes that step, and a **time interval** — `"month"`, or `{"interval": "month", "step": 3}` — rounds out to a calendar boundary. Over 17 January to 9 May the flag gives the Sundays either side and `"month"` gives 1 January to 1 June, eleven days apart at one end: the difference between an axis labelled by months and one by weeks. The interval form was reported and treated as false. Writing the fixture then exposed a **separate bug** with a much wider reach: an axis `format` on a time scale was read as a *number* specifier, so `%b %d` printed the epoch milliseconds unchanged. Upstream asks the scale, and a temporal scale's own formatter is `timeFormat` — no `formatType` needed

capabilities.feature: A custom `symbolType`, and `format`/`formatType` from a signal
capabilities.notes: A legend's `symbolType` that is not one of the twelve names is an **SVG path**, exactly as a mark's `shape` channel is — the same rule, and now the same code path, so a swatch upstream does not ship draws rather than reporting. And both `format` and `formatType` may be chosen by a **signal** on either guide: `formatType` was reported and a legend's `format` was silently dropped, which mattered more than it sounds because the two travel together — the grammar decides how the string is read, so a control switching a column between a count and a date has to switch both. Resolved once at the top of each builder, like the styling signals, so nothing downstream knows the difference

`geoIdentity`: coordinates already on the page rather than on a globe, which is what a chart whose geometry is a floor plan — or a map projected somewhere else — hands over. Two things make it not just another projection, and the first draft got both wrong. There is **no spherical clipping**: put a five-sided polygon through the antimeridian clip and it measures as the whole world, which is how a fitted scale came out nine times too small. And the vertical axis is **not flipped** — a map projection negates `y` to put north up, an identity projection leaves the data as written. Everything else is shared with the spherical machinery, so `clipExtent`, `fitExtent`, `reflectY` and the plane rotation came for free

The last scale type upstream registers that this engine did not build, so `ScaleResolver`'s `when` no longer needs an `else` and the compiler now enforces that every type is handled. It maps the value itself, which is how a specification hands final coordinates to a channel that expects a scale; its `[0, 1]` domain is d3's and is never consulted, existing only so `domain('name')` answers something. A value that does not coerce maps to **nothing** rather than to NaN — d3's `unknown` — so the mark does not draw

The table of functions this engine deliberately did not have is now empty, and every excuse on it turned out softer than it read. "Needs a strptime" became a strptime. "A date is indistinguishable from a number" became `VegaValue.Timestamp` — and finding that out exposed `isNumber` lying about dates. "Selection helpers need the selection subsystem" became the observation that a selection is an ordinary dataset. The last one, `isTuple`, is answered from **origin** rather than identity: `datum`, anything reached through it, an element of `data('name')` and an item's `.datum` are tuples, literals are not — every form probed against upstream, with the one edge (a value laundered through a signal) stated rather than hidden. The table stays because it is the right shape for an answer; an empty map is now a claim, and a test checks it against upstream's own function table

Excused as "selection helpers require the signal and selection subsystems", which was never true: a selection is an ordinary **dataset** whose rows say `{unit, fields, values}`, and all four functions are arithmetic over those rows. The field types are the vocabulary — `E` enumerates, `R` is an inclusive range, `R-RE` is the binned form whose upper edge belongs to the *next* bin, and the `E-LT`/`E-GT` family are one-sided. A selection unions **within** a unit and intersects **across** units, which is why `vlSelectionResolve` needs two passes and why a value in one brush but not the other is inside the union and outside the intersection. One stated difference: over an id store, upstream resolves with `d3.union`, and a `Set` serializes as `{}` — its own answer is opaque to whatever reads it back, so this returns the ids as an array with the same membership

capabilities.feature: `modify`, and seven more functions off the excuse list
capabilities.notes: `modify(name, insert, remove, toggle)` is the interactive write — a click handler builds a selection with it — and it goes through the same sink `setdata` uses. `remove` matches an object **field by field**, not by identity, because the row a click hands back is a copy. Closing it exposed an ordering rule: a signal that *writes* a dataset has to run after that dataset exists, or its rows are laid down and then overwritten by the declaration. Beside it: `copy` (null, which is what `isValid` sees of upstream's unusable scale function), `isRegExp` (true for a `VegaValue.Pattern`, which `regexp()` and a `/pattern/flags` literal both build), `encode`, `inScope`, `intersect` and `intersectLasso`, each answering what upstream answers with no running view, which is the position every compiled scene is in

capabilities.feature: Gradient fills, written out or computed
capabilities.notes: A mark's `fill` or `stroke` may be a gradient **object** rather than a colour, and this stringified one into `gradient:linear,x1:0,…` and reported that it was not a colour — true, and useless. Both spellings work now: the literal object, whose coordinates are fractions of the mark's own box in both engines, and `gradient(scale, p0, p1[, count])`, which fills in the scale's own ticks as stops with each offset being the value's *fraction* of the domain, so a log scale's stops bunch up exactly as its colours do. Upstream's `Gradient` is a plain object, which is what lets the encoder take either without knowing where it came from

capabilities.feature: A signal in a guide's styling
capabilities.notes: The quietest gap in the parser, and the reason it was quiet is that half of it works: `labelFontSize: {"signal": "n"}` is honoured because that property is read through `numberOrSignal`, while `labelColor: {"signal": "c"}` was dropped without a word because the styling block takes only a literal — so a chart colouring its axis from a control drew black labels and looked finished. `GuideStroke` now carries a `signals` map beside its constants, and each builder substitutes a resolved copy of its styling blocks **once** before anything reads them — which is what kept the change from spreading to a hundred call sites. A value that is neither a constant nor a signal is still named: an array where a colour belongs is nothing anything can read. A guide `encode` channel carries a signal too, but only onto a property that can hold one — the fold into properties happens at parse time, where no signal has a value yet, so a channel aimed at a plain string property is named rather than stringified

capabilities.tests_text: `ExpressionReferenceTest` (`every upstream expression function is implemented or explained`)
capabilities.notes: The inventory is now closed the way the property tables are: each of upstream's `functionContext` names either works or carries a reason. Nineteen had neither, so an expression using one got a bare "unknown function" and no hint that the obstacle was a browser (`screen`, `windowSize`, the pinch and lasso geometry), a running view (`encode`, `modify`, `inScope`, `intersect`), a value model with no place for a function (`pathShape`, `geoShape`, `copy`, `gradient`) or a console (`debug`, `info`, `warn`). A function upstream adds later fails this test, which is the point

capabilities.feature: Sixteen more expression functions, and two time bugs behind them
capabilities.notes: The pan and zoom family (`panLinear`/`panLog`/`panPow`/`panSymlog` and the four `zoom` twins), which is what an interactive chart's `domainRaw` is written with — each lifts the interval into the space its gesture is linear in, so panning a log axis multiplies where a linear one adds. Plus the month and weekday **names** (`monthFormat` and the three beside it, whose indices wrap and whose non-integers give the empty string), `week` and `utcweek` (Sundays since the start of the year, not ISO weeks), `utcOffset` and `utcSequence`, `merge` and `flush`. Writing the vectors down found two real bugs neither the fixtures nor the tick generator could see: a **sequence** yields the unit *boundaries*, so a start at noon is ceiled to the next midnight rather than stepped from — the implementation walked from the start and carried a comment claiming that was upstream's rule — and a **month or year offset overflows** rather than clamping, because `Date.setMonth` does, so 31 January plus a month is 2 March and not 29 February. `isDate`, `isRegExp` and `isTuple` are **in**, each answered from this engine's own value model rather than from upstream's: `isDate` is `VegaValue.Timestamp` — an instant being its own type here, which is what makes it answerable at all — `isRegExp` is `VegaValue.Pattern`, and `isTuple` is answered from **origin** rather than identity, because upstream reads an id it attaches to every tuple and attaching one here would cost the whole value model for one predicate. A value laundered through a signal is the edge `isTuple` cannot see, and it is stated at the implementation. This row used to say all three stayed out, which contradicted both the code and the `regexp()` row below it

Reservoir sampling, transcribed rather than reimplemented, because the two differ where a fixture can see it. The reservoir fills with the first `size` rows in order; after that each row is offered slot `trunc((seen + 1) * random())` and taken only if that slot is inside the reservoir, **replacing** what was there — so the output is the reservoir's order and a row from the far end of the data can sit between two early ones. The counter advances for every row including the ones that filled the reservoir, which is what makes the acceptance probability `size / seen`. Verifiable at all only because both engines draw from the same seeded stream: upstream's `setRandom` installs one in the oracle and `RandomStream.DEFAULT_SEED` matches it. Input shorter than `size` passes straight through

capabilities.feature: `geojson` transform, and the ordering a fitted projection needs
capabilities.notes: The ordinary way to fit a map to point data: every row becomes a point of one `MultiPoint` feature, so the fit sees the cloud as a single geometry, and a column already holding a feature combines with it — features first, the `MultiPoint` appended after, which is upstream's order and matters because `fit` walks the collection in order. Two ordering rules had to follow it. A dataset that places rows through a projection now waits for whatever that projection's `fit` reads, including a signal another dataset's transform publishes; and the projections are rebuilt when a transform writes a signal, so a `geopoint` two lines below a `geojson` in the *same* list is fitted rather than falling back to the family's default. It also corrected `geopoint`: each coordinate is coerced the way `+value` is and the pair projected whatever comes out, so a **null** longitude lands on the prime meridian and `"west"` leaves `x` unusable while `y` still lands where the latitude says — rejecting the pair put both at the origin, drawing a point nothing asked for

capabilities.feature: Guide `encode` channels, and a legend title's overhang
capabilities.notes: The same schema subtraction, one level down. A tick's `strokeCap` and `strokeDashOffset`, a label's `lineHeight`, and an axis title's `align`, `baseline`, `angle`, `limit`, `x` and `y` were all reported as unimplemented while the properties behind them were being honoured — one entry each in the translation map. `encode.gradient` and `encode.legend` were whole blocks unread; the second is where a legend's background and placement live. A ramp label's `align` and `baseline` are deliberately **not** folded: upstream derives a gradient label's alignment from where along the bar it sits and reads no property for it, so the channel works and the property does not — probed both ways — which is why the mapping has to know what kind of legend it is. Closing it exposed a placement rule nothing had exercised: a title aligned away from its default reaches left of the legend's origin, and upstream drags the whole legend right by the overflow rather than letting it be cut off

Three blocks, not one: `group` for the group the heading sits in, `title` for its text, `subtitle` for the second line — plus upstream's **deprecated** form, where a block naming none of the three applies to the *text*, which is the form `encode.update.dx` is written in and the reason this engine had been reading `dx` out of an encode block without reading anything else. Each channel beats the matching property, which is upstream's order. The `group` block is the only way to paint a panel behind a chart's name, since a title has no `fillColor` — and it brought one scene-graph rule with it: `titleLayout` writes the union of the texts' bounds *over* the group's, discarding the half-unit `boundStroke` had added, so an outlined heading does not make the drawing wider. Channels a part cannot express are named one at a time rather than the block being written off

Not decoration: upstream builds the heading's text with `style: "group-title"` and a specification's `style` takes **that slot**, so naming one removes the 13-point bold rather than adding to it, and what the named block leaves unsaid falls through to the renderer's own 11 point and no weight. Implemented as two configuration layers beneath `config.title`, which keeps the ordinary precedence — the title's property beats the theme beats the style beats the renderer — and needs the names translated, since a style block says `fill` where a title says `color`. The subtitle keeps its 12 point: its slot is `group-subtitle`, which a title's `style` never takes

On a legend these two name **scales**, so a legend can be keyed to one and its swatches then vary in dash pattern or in outline width — the natural legend for a chart that tells its series apart by line style. They sit between `stroke` and `opacity` in the order that picks a legend's canonical scale. Two traps: the row-height expression reads the *scale*, not `symbolStrokeWidth`, so such a legend has rows of different heights; and the channel must be read from the legend's own object rather than the config-layered one, because `config.legend.strokeWidth` is the width of the border drawn round the legend and layering it in turns a themed border into a channel naming a scale called "2"

capabilities.feature: Legend `gridAlign`, and the entry grid's row centring
capabilities.notes: It looks like a dead letter — alignment only means anything to a multi-column grid — but `config.legend` defaults it to `each`, and the grid's row **centring** is conditional on being aligned at all. So the default was doing work no legend had noticed until one had entries of unequal height, and `none` both packs the columns against their own contents and stops a short entry being centred against a tall one. The centring is not symmetrical: `center: {row: true, column: false}`

The flush offset was a **stale** report: its explanation said it needed `labelFlush`, which had been implemented for some time. It nudges a flushed label along the axis and is signed *outwards* — a label flushed to the start moves back towards it — and applies only where the flush rule decided the alignment, since an explicit `labelAlign` on a horizontal axis or `labelBaseline` on a vertical one means the label is not being flushed at all. Beside it, a mark's `strokeDash` read through a **scale** was dropped without a word: the encoder resolved a constant or a field and returned nothing for a scaled one, so every line in a chart that distinguished its series by line style came out solid

capabilities.feature: Legend `titleAnchor` and all four `titleOrient`s, and array-valued guide titles
capabilities.notes: Upstream's `legendTitleOffset` measures along the **entries'** own extent, not the legend's, so the anchor slides the title against the thing it labels. Which extent depends on the legend: a ramp anchors along the bar alone, a symbol legend along the whole block of entries — the same distinction that decides where a left title is centred. A title above the entries carries the anchor in its **alignment** (`end` puts its right edge at theirs, so the two line up instead of the title starting there and running off); a title beside them carries it in its **baseline** and stays left-aligned. A multi-line one anchored `end` is placed by its *last* line, which is upstream's `multiLineOffset`. `titleOrient: "right"` and `"bottom"` were reported on the grounds that each needs its own anchoring rule; they do, and it is the same rule read the other way round — a bottom title anchors along the entries' width exactly as a top one does and is *placed* past their bottom edge, and a right title anchors down their height as a left one does and is placed past their far edge. Finding the anchor out took fixing a second thing: an array-valued `title` was accepted for the chart heading but dropped without a word on an axis or a legend, so a two-line legend title produced no title mark at all

capabilities.feature: Trellis footers, bands, anchors and offsets
capabilities.notes: `row-footer` and `column-footer` were not recognised roles, so they fell through to `CELL` and were **gridded among the cells**. With them added the whole `layout` block closes. Four details are upstream's: a band defaults to `null` for a header — the cell's own origin, not its middle — and to `0.5` for a title; a title is centred on the *cells* rather than on the grid plus its headers; `titleAnchor: "end"` measures from the footers; and more headers than rows is neither an error nor a reason to drop one — the first `limit` are laid out and the rest left where they were, where the limit is the row or column count and not the cell count

A cell narrower than its column sits in the middle of it. Upstream guards it twice and both guards matter: horizontally it needs more than one **row** and vertically more than one **column**, since a single row has nothing to centre against — every column is exactly as wide as its one cell. The correction is applied only when positive, so the widest cell in a column is not pulled backwards out of it

With no `units` the transform picks its own from a table of seventeen intervals, by which duration is nearest the span over `maxbins` — nearest **in ratio**, not in difference. `step` applies to the **finest** unit only, with a phase of 1 for the units counted from one: `3 * floor(month / 3)` would put January in a bucket starting at month zero, which is December of the year before. `step` had been published in the transform's own signal and never applied, so `step: 3` bucketed by month and announced quarters

capabilities.feature: An explicit `format` on a time axis
capabilities.notes: A time scale labels each tick at its own granularity — a January tick carries the year — *unless* the axis names a format, which then applies to every tick alike. The linear branch of the tick generator had always made that distinction and the time branch had not, so `%b` came back multi-formatted. The accessibility caption had the same hole one layer down

Upstream culls **nothing**: it applies the test as `boundRectangle.encloses(item.bounds)` inside `Overlap`, which runs *before* the label bounds exist, so every item still holds a cleared `Bounds` that any rectangle trivially encloses. Established by experiment — a label overflowing by 68 survives `labelBound: false`, `true` and `40` alike. Implementing the documented behaviour would make this engine differ from upstream on every chart that sets it

`{"type": "rgb", "gamma": y}`, the only interpolator d3 gives one. It bends the ramp's **middle** and leaves both ends where they were, which is why a chart that asked for one and got the plain ramp looks composed and is wrong exactly where nobody checks

A floor on the gap between ticks, which can only be applied by reducing the *count* — d3 chooses the step. Upstream caps the count at `floor((hi - lo) / minStep \|\| 1) + 1`, where the `\|\| 1` is JavaScript turning a zero into a one, so a floor wider than the domain leaves **two** ticks rather than none; then it walks the count down one at a time until `tickStep` reaches the minimum, because d3's steps grow monotonically as the count shrinks and there is no closed form to invert. The walk-down is skipped for log and time scales, whose steps are not linear in the count

Slides a label **along** the axis, which is the other direction from `labelPadding`. Applied after a band scale's own centring rather than inside it — the first attempt put it in the band rule, where a linear axis never sees it

On an axis and a legend. `aria: false` removes the guide from the accessibility tree; a `description` replaces the caption generated from the scale, and one that is only whitespace is not a description. Invisible to the differential harness — upstream carries both as properties of the guide group and nothing about the drawing changes — so they are pinned by a unit test instead

`tickBand` is a shorthand for three properties and only `"extent"` touches all three: it sets `bandPosition: 1`, `tickExtra: true` **and** `tickOffset: 0`, where `"center"` sets the first two back to their defaults and leaves `tickOffset` alone — which matters because `config.axisBand` gives a band axis a `-0.5` there. `position` slides the axis along its own direction, which is the other direction from the one `offset` moves it. `translate` replaces the half-pixel nudge onto the pixel grid, and that nudge is **excluded from the chart's measurement**: upstream bounds the axis at `x` and only then places the item at `x + delta`, so a `translate: 0` axis is not half a unit wider

capabilities.feature: Guide line caps and dash offsets
capabilities.notes: `tickCap`, `gridCap`, `domainCap`, `tickDashOffset`, `gridDashOffset`, `domainDashOffset`, and `symbolDashOffset` on a legend. All seven were reported as unimplemented while `Stroke` had carried both properties since it was written and both renderers had honoured them — nothing passed them on. `GuideStroke` now carries the whole family per part, which closed the legend's `labelAlign`/`labelBaseline`/`titleAlign`/`titleBaseline`/`titleLineHeight` and the axis's `labelLineHeight`/`titleLineHeight` in the same change. Note the one name that breaks the pattern: the legend's is `symbolDashOffset`, not `symbolStrokeDashOffset`, even though the colour is `symbolStrokeColor`

`symbolOffset` shifts a swatch **and its label**, since upstream builds the label's offset by extending the symbol's — the gap between them stays `labelOffset`. `symbolFillColor` is a *fallback*, not an override: upstream sets the channel from it and then overwrites it from the scale, so a `fill` scale always wins and only a `size` or `shape` legend takes the stated colour. `gradientStrokeColor`, `gradientStrokeWidth` and `gradientOpacity` style the ramp, the last fading the outline along with the colours because upstream puts it on the item
Truncates a long axis title with an ellipsis, as the labels have always been truncated

On the heading **and** its subtitle, because upstream builds them as two marks under one guide and either can be focused. `aria: false` is the only way to keep a decorative heading out of what a screen reader reads

`color`, `font`, `fontSize`, `fontWeight`, `fontStyle`, `lineHeight` and `limit`, and the subtitle's own `subtitleColor`, `subtitleFont`, `subtitleFontWeight`, `subtitleFontSize`, `subtitleFontStyle` and `subtitleLineHeight`. An explicit `align`, `angle` or `baseline` **overrides** what `anchor` and `orient` imply rather than being ignored — upstream writes the derived values into `enter` and these into `update` — which is how a left-hand title is made to read up the page. `font` had been listed as consumed and never read

capabilities.feature: A title written as an array of lines
capabilities.notes: `"text": ["two", "lines"]`, and the same for `subtitle`. Rejected outright before this: a two-line heading produced `A title needs a 'text'` and no chart. The accessibility caption joins the lines back with a space, which is upstream's `array(text).join(' ')`

The panel behind the entries: `fillColor`, `strokeColor`, `cornerRadius`. The outline's **width and dash come from `config.legend` alone**, which is upstream's rule and not a slip — a legend's own `strokeWidth` names a *scale*, as `fill` and `size` do, and writing `"strokeWidth": 2` on a legend makes upstream throw `Invalid field reference: 2`. An outlined legend also reaches half a stroke width past its declared box, which makes the chart a unit wider

The same `{part}Color`/`Width`/`Dash`/`Opacity`/`Font` family the axis has, for the label and the title, plus `symbolStrokeColor`, `symbolStrokeWidth` and `symbolDash`. `symbolOpacity` is the swatch's **overall** opacity upstream, not a fill or stroke opacity, so it fades the outline along with the inside. `symbolFillColor` is reported: upstream applies it only where the scale supplies no fill of its own, and the legend's own background — `strokeColor`, `cornerRadius` — has nothing drawing it yet

A `quantize`, `quantile`, `threshold` or `bin-ordinal` scale has buckets rather than a continuum, and its legend is the colour bar cut into them: one band per bucket, **equal** whatever the cut points are worth — the buckets are categories, and a quantile scale's uneven thresholds would otherwise make a band's size say something about the data that it does not — labelled at the joins between them. The first band has no lower bound and its label has no text; upstream's scene carries a literal `null` there, which its renderers draw as nothing. A stated `gradient` over such a scale is drawn as bands too, which is upstream's own substitution
`columns` wraps the entries, filling *down* each column before moving across — the order a reader scans a list — and the same grid code places a trellis
