`symbolLimit` is honoured with upstream's own arithmetic: it keeps `limit - 1` entries and spends the last slot on a summary — a limit of 3 over six entries draws `a`, `b` and `…4 entries` — and the summary's swatch takes the *next* value's size, so a size legend's summary row is drawn at the size of the first thing it stands for. A limit the entries already fit inside does nothing. `encode` overrides are still reported by name. `labelOverlap` is implemented — see Label collision handling. A group marked `row-header`, `column-header`, `row-title` or `column-title` is arranged around the grid rather than gridded into it. A header tracks the cell it labels on one axis and the grid's edge on the other; a title sits halfway along, outside the headers. Footers, `headerBand` and `titleBand` are reported
A `title` on a group mark, built in that group's own scope — which is how a trellis header gets its words, since its text is usually `{"signal": "parent.<field>"}`

All four orientations and all three anchors, verified against upstream in every combination. Placed against the whole drawing — axes and legends included — not the plotting area, unless `frame: "group"` says otherwise. `fontWeight`, `fontStyle` and `font`, and `subtitleFontStyle` beside them, are read rather than reported: an italic, lighter or narrower face is *measured* as well as drawn, so a chart whose subtitle is its widest line is a different size without them. A title's `style` names the `config.style` block behind it and **replaces** the `group-title` block a heading otherwise takes, which is upstream's `mark.style = extras.style || mark.style` — without it every caption in a trellis is set at a chart heading's thirteen points and in bold instead of a label's ten. `encode` overrides and explicit align, angle and limit are reported

A label produced by a *format string* — every continuous axis tick, every gradient legend entry — is grouped in threes and signed with **U+2212 MINUS SIGN**, which is what d3-format writes. A label produced by JavaScript's own stringification — a discrete axis or legend label, whose text is the domain value itself — is neither grouped nor re-signed, so upstream draws `-1200` on a band axis and `−1,200` on a linear one. Two different characters of two different widths, following the scale type rather than the number

`labelLimit` on an axis and a legend, and it is a **default** rather than an option — upstream's config carries 180 and 160, so a long label is already being shortened on every chart drawn against upstream. The scene graph keeps the whole string on the text run and only the drawn lines and the measured width shrink, matching upstream, so a truncated label still reports the value it came from. Both of upstream's comparisons are strict, which takes one more character off than "fits within the limit" would

`labelOverlap` with `parity` and `greedy`, plus `labelSeparation`. A **legend** removes overlapping labels by default and an **axis** does not: `labelOverlap: true` is in the `legend` block of upstream's config and the `axis` block has no entry, so a dense axis prints every label unless asked otherwise. A hidden label stays in the scene at zero opacity rather than being removed, so a chart's mark count does not change with its width; only the guide's measured extent shrinks

capabilities.feature: A signal calling `scale()` at the top level
capabilities.notes: Ordered rather than special-cased: a scale is built before every signal that reads it and after every signal it reads. `scale('x', step) - scale('x', 0)` turns a step in data units into a size in pixels, which is how Vega's dot plot sizes its marks — and a scale whose own domain comes from *another* signal now works too, which the phased version refused. A `"width"` or `"height"` range is an edge to the same-named signal when the specification declares one, which a chart sizing itself from its own contents does. Only a genuine cycle is refused

`"source": ["a", "b"]` concatenates both, in the order written, and everything after it — a transform pipeline, a scale domain — sees the whole. A single source is the same path. Only a single source passes on a `stratify` tree: concatenating two would leave the structure describing rows that are no longer all there

`"values": [6.3, 2.1,...]` — a row that is not an object is wrapped as `{"data": value}`, upstream's `ingest`. Every transform downstream reads *fields*, so there has to be a field to read, and `data` is the name upstream gives it — which is why Vega's dot plot writes `"field": "data"` over data that appears to have no such column. Applies to a loaded document too

`{"type": "extent", "field": "v", "signal": "vals"}` writes `vals`; `{"type": "bin", "signal": "bins"}` writes the bin settings it chose. Nothing declares the name, so reading one is an edge to the **dataset** whose pipeline writes it — which is what upstream gets from `scope.addSignal(spec.signal, scope.proxy(t))`, where the published name is an operator standing in for the transform. `extent` publishes its `[min, max]` and `bin` publishes `{start, stop, step, fields}` — upstream hangs those three off the binning *function* it publishes, and nothing here can call a function from an expression. Every other transform's `signal` output is **not implemented** and is reported by name, since upstream publishes the operator's own value and most operators' value is their tuples

capabilities.feature: Datasets, scales and signals ordered by dependency
capabilities.notes: One dependency ranking over all three kinds instead of three fixed phases, which is what upstream gets from putting every operator into a single dataflow. `probability-density` is the case that needs it: `xscale`'s domain names a dataset and the `density` dataset's `extent` is `{"signal": "domain('xscale')"}`, so a scale waits on data and data waits on that scale. Edges come from where upstream's come from — the string literal a `data()`, `scale()`, `domain()` or `bandwidth()` is handed, a dataset's `source`, a scale's domain and every signal-valued property, including one element of a range array. Ties break towards signals, then datasets, then scales, so every signal that has become resolvable resolves before the next dataset runs: `clamp(handleYear, 1980, 2010)` filtering rows by a draggable year sees its number, and so does a signal computed from an *earlier* dataset. A cycle is reported as the path that closed it and one operator on it is placed anyway, so the chart draws and says it is wrong

capabilities.feature: A transform reading a signal it cannot see
capabilities.notes: A signal read through a transform's **expression** parameter — `filter`'s `expr`, `formula`'s `expr`, `cross`'s `filter`, the only three upstream declares as `type: 'expr'` — is not an edge in the graph, because those are per-row expressions rather than `{"signal":...}` references. It resolves whenever the ordering happens to put the signal first, which it usually does; when it does not, the read comes back null, and null is zero to arithmetic. Vega's own radial tree example fails that way — every node placed at `originX + radius * cos(...)`, the whole diagram on the origin — so it is **reported by name** rather than left silent

Produces **no rows**, not a row of nulls — upstream never invents a group it saw no tuples for, with or without a `groupby`. It shows wherever a filter can empty a dataset, which is every tooltip and every brush: a row of nulls there draws the tooltip's frame at the origin over a chart nobody is pointing at

capabilities.feature: A chart sized by a signal
capabilities.notes: `width` and `height` are signals as well as top-level properties, and a specification may declare either as a signal instead — a trellis whose height is `6 * (offset + cellHeight)` has no number to write down. Upstream merges such a declaration into the built-in signal, so the property is only a seed. A scale with a `"width"` or `"height"` range is an edge to that signal, so it is built from the computed size rather than from the seed. A specification that declares **neither** gets a plotting area of zero, which is upstream's `spec.width || 0` and not a missing default: such a chart is measured entirely by what it draws, which is how every faceted Vega-Lite chart is written. It is said once, at `info`

All five types. `contains: "padding"` measures the declared size to the *outside* of the padding and shrinks the `width`/`height` signals with it — so a 400-wide chart with 40 padding has a 320-wide plotting area and a `width / 2` radius of 160. Upstream applies that subtraction for every type and then overwrites it for `pad`, where the surface grows anyway, so the setting only bites on the others. A `none` chart is inset by its padding and never grows for what overflows. `fit` compiles the chart **twice**: once to measure how far it reaches, then again with `width` and `height` seeded to what is left, which is upstream's own arrangement — it measures once, sets the size signals and re-runs with the layout step short-circuited. The overhang is rounded outward before it is subtracted, and the origin comes from the first pass; the surface is then measured like `pad`, so a fitted chart lands a fraction *under* the declared size rather than exactly on it

The chart's own group item, encoded like any other group mark over two defaults upstream supplies: an origin at (0,0) and an extent of the plotting area. Overriding the origin moves every coordinate in the chart with it, which is how a polar plot puts its centre in the middle of the surface — without it a radar chart draws around (0,0) with three quadrants off the edge

Grid, not R-tree; the two agree by test. A **group** is picked only where it paints, as upstream's `marks/group.js` does — its fill, or a stroke that is not drawn in the foreground, over its declared extent rather than over the bounds its children reach — so a tap on blank space inside a chart finds nothing rather than the frame. A clip is a hard boundary: what it hid cannot be tapped, which is upstream returning from `pick` before testing a clipped group's contents. A **rect** is picked over the path it draws rather than its box, so a rounded bar's cut corner is not part of it and an unfilled frame is picked on its edge; a **rotated label** is picked by turning the point back about its anchor, as `marks/text.js` does. A fill of zero opacity is still a target, because upstream's `isPointInPath` never reads alpha and `"fill": "transparent"` is the idiom for an invisible one
Tolerance never changes visual bounds
The host must publish `contentScale`, otherwise taps miss by the fit factor

Superseded by the two **Tooltips** rows below, which describe what this one said was missing: `TooltipContent` turns the dataflow's value into rows and a line of text in the chart's own locale, `interactionState.tooltipAnchor` says where to put it, and `VegaChartView` draws one. This row said "no tooltip rendering yet" while two rows in the same file said the opposite — the file disagreeing with itself, which is the failure the generated status column exists to catch and could not, because a status is checked against a run and prose is not.

Press, move, release, through the controller and into the signals a brush is built from — including the backwards drag, where a reader pulls right to left and the extent has to come out in order. This row said "no drag-to-select gesture yet", which was a line left from the original roadmap sitting above the rows that describe the dispatch, the event-selector language and the signal handlers; a brush is made of those three and all three had been supported for some time. There is no `interval` primitive here and upstream has none either: a brush in Vega is a rect mark whose corners are signals.

The value comes from the dataflow — `"tooltip": true` compiles to the row itself — and `TooltipContent` turns it into **rows** and a line of text in the chart's own locale, with `interactionState.tooltipAnchor` saying where to put it in the host's own pixels. No renderer draws a bubble, deliberately: that is a design-system decision, and rows rather than markup is what lets an app lay one out. Three details it handles that each host was improvising: a mark with no tooltip channel produces an **empty object**, which is not a tooltip and used to mean an empty bubble on every mark; a number is formatted the way the axis beside it formats one, so a chart never disagrees with itself in front of a reader; an instant takes the locale's own date-and-time format. The **shape** is `vega-tooltip`'s — an object becomes a row per field, in order — and byte-fidelity with its HTML is not claimed, that package not being one this repository pins

View transform; axes do not rescale. The controller accumulates the offset in **pixels** and every renderer now draws through it — the Android View always did, while the Compose Multiplatform and Swift renderers accumulated the state and left the chart where it was, so a pan made `canReset` true and moved nothing. The drawing, the touch target and the accessibility frames go through one placement, so a reader's finger and a screen reader's frame land on the mark where it is now

As above; clamped to 0.1×–50×, with the anchor kept stationary by the controller. A host reports the factor and the anchor in the controller's own space — pixels with the chart's centring removed, the fit scale left on, since `toSceneSpace` divides by `contentScale` itself; dividing twice is the defect this contract is written down to prevent

The whole grammar, ported from `vega-event-selector`: comma-separated streams, `source:type` prefixes, `@name` for a named mark, stacked `[filter]` expressions, `{throttle, debounce}` read from the end, a trailing `!` to consume, and the `[a, b] > c` pair a drag is written as. A word before the colon is a **mark type** if it happens to be one and an event source otherwise, so a mark named `rect` cannot be reached without the `@` — upstream's rule, matched. A pair wrapping a stream that already has one nests rather than merging

capabilities.feature: Signal `bind` — the controls a chart asks for
capabilities.notes: **149** of the diagnostics Vega's own examples produced said bindings had no equivalent here, which was half true and the wrong conclusion: upstream's binding is a *description* of a control bolted to a DOM implementation of it, and only the second half is a browser's. The description is grammar, so it is parsed like grammar — `SignalBind` names the five shapes `bind.js` generates — and the runtime turns it into `controller.inputs`, a list of controls with the value each currently holds, republished on every compile so a signal moved by a tap or a timer moves the control that shows it. `controller.setSignal` is the way back, and it is the same path a fired handler takes: pin, cascade, recompile. So a slider bound to `size` reaches a signal derived from it and a scale built on that. A slider's unstated bounds are filled in as upstream fills them — `max` the larger of 100 and the value, `min` the smaller of 0 and that, `step` the tick step for a hundred divisions — because a slider whose bounds differ puts the same gesture at a different value. Nothing about widgets is in the engine: the demo draws Material controls from that list in 170 lines, and a host with other widgets writes its own. A generic input carries **every** remaining property in `Field.attributes` rather than reporting it, which is upstream twice over: its generic generator copies all of them onto the element as attributes, and its schema marks that one variant of the five `additionalProperties: true`. So `job-voyager`'s `placeholder` is grammar, and the demo shows it as the hint in its empty field; `autocomplete` is carried and deliberately ignored, because it offers a value a browser saved from a form and there is no form here. The four structured kinds went the other way and are now checked **per shape** — upstream closes each with `additionalProperties: false` and builds a fixed control — so `{"input": "checkbox", "min": 0}` is reported as the mistake it is rather than as something unimplemented. Across the 93 examples that is two fewer false gaps and no new ones

Parsed, matched, applied and redrawn. `update` in all four forms (bare expression, `expr`, `value`, `signal`), with `event` and the mark's `datum` in scope. A `merge` stream object is reported and asks for the equivalent comma-separated string

`{"events": {"signal": "brush"}}` — how one signal is derived from another, and the shape every pan, zoom and brush in Vega's gallery is built out of: **79** handlers across twenty of the 93 published examples use it, against none for the scale form. It fires when the source changes and cascades, which was probed both ways — a chain two deep took `a = 5` to `b = 10` and `c = 11` in one run, and at **initialization** nothing fires at all, so every signal keeps its declared value. That second half is why no differential fixture can cover this and why nothing was visibly wrong: the scene the harness compares is the one before anything has changed, and a pan that did nothing looked like a chart with no pan. Dependency order falls out of the loop rather than needing a sort, since each round fires only what the round before changed. A **cycle** never settles, so it is capped and reported, which is what `DataflowOrder` does with a cycle among `update` expressions; upstream refuses the whole specification instead

`{"events": {"scale": "x"}}` fires when the scale is rebuilt. Upstream knows which one that is because a scale is an operator in its dataflow; here a changed signal recompiles the whole specification, so every scale is rebuilt every time and firing on all of them would run the handler when nothing about the scale had changed. So "rebuilt" is answered as **"resolves differently"** — each watched scale is asked to map a fixed set of probes and the answers are compared against the previous compile's, which needs no incremental dataflow and gets the case the refusal was about: a recompile that rebuilds every scale and moves none of them fires nothing. A handler that moves the scale it watches is a cycle, reported and stopped at the round bound the signal cascade uses. A specification with no scale source fingerprints nothing, which is nearly all of them: not one of the 93 published examples uses this source

capabilities.feature: Matching an event to its handlers
capabilities.notes: `EventDispatcher` takes an `InputEvent` — a portable record, not a `MotionEvent` — and returns the handlers it fired. Type, source, mark type and mark name all narrow the match; `[filter]` expressions are evaluated with `event` in scope; a `between` pair is a **latch** opened by the first stream and closed by the second, so a lost `mouseup` leaves a drag stuck exactly as upstream does; a `!` stops every stream behind it. Gates are updated before the streams they gate, which upstream leaves to registration order and this fixes. A filter that cannot be read **suppresses** the event rather than being ignored, since ignoring it would fire on every event of that type
Events arriving sooner than the interval since the last firing are dropped. Time is passed in rather than read from a clock, so it is testable and the core stays portable

The last config block that was reported rather than read, and the only one that is not a drawing instruction: it decides which listeners a view may attach. A specification asking for `window:mousemove` is asking to watch the pointer across the whole page, and `{"events": {"window": false}}` is how a host that embeds a chart it did not write says no — so a block that was parsed and dropped meant the refusal was silently ignored, which is the opposite of what a policy is for. Enforced where the listeners are **made** rather than where events arrive, which is upstream's `permit`: the stream never registers, a warning names it, and the rest of the chart still draws. Four keys govern four sources, and a `scope` stream is a view listener as far as the policy goes because upstream rewrites it to one before testing. A list is an **allow-list** — `{"window": ["mousemove"]}` blocks every other window event — and an object naming types is the same list written out, with a key set to `false` a refusal. `timer` is the one key upstream leaves un-unpacked, so an array there matches nothing and permits nothing; that is carried through rather than corrected, because a host copying a theme should behave as upstream does with it. `defaults.prevent`/`allow`, `bind` and `globalCursor` are read and carried for the host, which is what lets it obey the specification instead of guessing. Enforcing it also fixed a hole beside it: the dispatcher had always reported as it registered — a blocked stream, a debounce nothing can schedule — into a collector `VegaChartController` threw away, so a host reading the diagnostics saw only the compiler's. A policy whose enforcement is invisible is indistinguishable from one that was ignored

Fires on its own with nothing to prompt it, at the interval it asked for, carrying the two fields upstream's timer event does: a wall-clock `timestamp` and the `elapsed` since the timer started, which is what an animation reads to know where it is. Started per specification and **left alone by a redraw** — restarting them on every publish cancelled the running ones mid-flight, reset every `elapsed` and dropped the ticks in between, which a test with virtual time makes visible immediately. `stop()` cancels them, and a host with a scheduler has to call it: a timer that outlives the view it draws into is a leak with a repaint attached. Reported by name, as before, when no scheduler was given

capabilities.feature: A timer standing in for a `for` loop
capabilities.notes: `donut-chart-labelled` passes the differential comparison and still looks wrong in the demo: its three most crowded labels are drawn on top of each other. The fixture is not lying — upstream's static scene stacks them too, because the gallery shows a *later frame* — and the reason there are frames at all is that the timer is standing in for a loop the expression language cannot express: `counter` walks the labels one per tick and `p1`/`p2` accumulate a running shift, building an array by joining strings because there is no append either. With a scheduler the loop runs to its own fixed point and the labels spread, and running the clock on further changes nothing, which is what makes it a loop rather than an animation. Not verifiable against upstream — `runAsync` never returns for a specification with a timer, so there is no settled reference — which is why it is pinned by a test rather than assumed in a note

`"timer{500}"`, where the selector grammar cannot tell a source from a type, and `{"type": "timer", "throttle": 500}`. Both are folded onto a `timer` source with the interval as the type — which is also the key `config.events.timer` tests — so nothing downstream has to know that one type name is secretly a source. Before that they read as a view event of type `timer` that nothing ever raises: a signal that silently never changed and said nothing about why

Fires *after* a quiet period, so it needs something that can wake up later — which a compiler that is a pure function of its specification has no business owning. A host hands one in (`Scheduler`, one method, with a coroutine implementation shipped beside it), and then a debounce is upstream's exactly: each event cancels the pending run and schedules another with itself, so four hundred moves during a drag produce **one** update at the end. Without a scheduler nothing changes from before — the stream fires on every matching event and says why — which keeps a chart a pure function of its specification unless a host asks otherwise, and that is what makes the corpus comparable at all. Tested against **virtual** time rather than a real clock, which is the other reason the capability is handed in: the result is exact instead of slow and flaky

`SignalUpdater` evaluates the update — a bare expression, `expr`, `value` or `signal` — with `event` and the event's `datum` in scope, which is what makes `{"events": "rect:click", "update": "datum.category"}` work. It returns only the signals that actually changed, so an unchanged value costs nothing; `force` reports a change either way, for a value mutated in place. Handlers earlier in the same batch are visible to later ones

The changed signals are **pinned** and the whole specification is compiled again. That is a measured decision rather than a shortcut: a full recompile of the heaviest fixture is 366 microseconds against a 16,600 microsecond frame (STATUS.md, Performance observations), so an incremental dataflow buys nothing. A pinned signal that also has an `update` expression keeps the handler's value and does not re-run the expression — upstream would re-run it when a dependency moved, and that difference is reported

Missing entirely, and `x()` is the commonest expression in an interactive specification after `datum` — **forty** of the uses across Vega's 93 examples, in every brush and every pan. They read the event rather than the data, which is why upstream generates them as `event.vega.<name>` rather than as ordinary functions. `x()` is **not** `event.x`: the chart's padding and autosize origin come off first — upstream's `offset(view)`, which is exactly what the root group carries as its translation — so the answer is in the space the marks are placed in. A chart with no padding would have hidden that. The **argument** forms, `x(item)` and `group()`, are refused by name: both walk the chain of groups above an item, which a live view's event carries and this one does not, and five uses across the corpus are in one example

`{"events": "*:mousedown", "encode": "select"}` overlays one of the mark's named blocks on the **event's own item**. Upstream rewrites it into `encode(item(), 'select')`, and doing the same here means one code path serves both spellings and a specification that writes the call out by hand behaves identically. Three things had to be true and each was probed rather than assumed. Blocks under any other name were being **reported as unknown sets and dropped**, so a chart whose press styling lived in a `select` block lost it at parse time. The overlay beats the mark's `update` on the pass that applies it and loses to it on every pass after — a `select` setting `fill` red wins immediately and a later signal change returns the item to green, which is reproduced by putting the block after `update` while it is fresh and before it once it is not, with no per-channel state. And a handler whose whole effect is an overlay changes **no signal value**, since the call returns the item it was handed, so a fresh overlay is a reason to redraw in its own right; testing only the signals meant a press styled nothing

capabilities.feature: Binding an Android gesture to a stream
capabilities.notes: `VegaChartController.dispatch` turns a gesture into the Vega events a selector is written against, resolves the mark under the pointer by hit testing, and recompiles if a handler changed a signal. One gesture emits **several** names — pointer, then touch, then mouse, then `click` — because that is what a browser does on a touch screen, and almost every specification in the wild is written against `click` or `mousedown`. Single page; unsupported operations surface as warnings
Compares mark count, type, role, coordinates, extents and scale outputs in absolute content space
References are checked in, so JVM tests need no Node and no network

The reference records only top-level scales, because a faceted group resolves its scales once per cell and there is no single scale of that name to compare. The cells' geometry is compared in full, which is what those scales produce

Vega emits one item per datum for a line or area; this engine builds one path. Both sides collapse to an outline point list, compared numerically. An interpolated curve puts corners and control points between the data points, so the item list is no longer the outline — the normalizer asks `d3-shape` itself for them rather than reconstructing them, through a recording context because `d3-path` rounds its string output to three decimals. A cubic's control points are compared as well as its anchors, since two curves through the same anchors are different shapes, and the method is compared alongside them. Whether the outline **closes** is compared separately, because no point list can express it: `linear-closed` emits exactly the points `linear` does and draws a polygon rather than a polyline. Marks are compared in the order they are **painted**, not the order they are declared, because the comparison matches them positionally within each type — a chart whose grid lines paint over its data would otherwise match a reference where they do not. An `hsl` colour keeps **fractional** 8-bit channels, as d3 does, and a lightness at or outside `0%..100%` drops the saturation, so `hsl(210, 50%, 100%)` is white rather than a pale blue. capabilities.feature: Text measured by the font that draws it
capabilities.notes: On every renderer, through one layout: all three engines are `MeasuredTextEngine` subclasses that answer three questions — an advance, an ascent, a descent — and inherit everything else. `ComposeTextEngine` was the gap: the Compose Multiplatform module had no engine, so it fell back to `MetricTextEngine` — an advance that is a ratio of the font size and matches no real font — while Compose drew real glyphs, which is the mismatch whose visible form is a right-aligned axis label over the domain line. It measures with the composition's density **and font scale**, so a reader who has asked for larger text gets a larger reserved box rather than overlapping labels

The setting Android calls `fontScale` reaches the **layout** on both Android renderers and on Compose Multiplatform, which is the only place it can do any good: an axis reserves its label box from a measurement, so text drawn larger inside a box measured smaller is what makes labels overlap. `AndroidTextEngine` had the parameter and nothing ever set it; `VegaChartView` now passes the device's own scale, and `newCompatibleTextEngine()` passes the same one so a controller compiling off the main thread measures as the view draws. A change to the setting restarts the activity unless an app declares `android:configChanges="fontScale"`, and an app that does declare it rebuilds the engine itself

capabilities.feature: Where a Compose chart's size comes from
capabilities.notes: A chart takes the scene's own size — one scene unit per dp — wherever `modifier` leaves a dimension free, which is what a specification asked for and is the default. The trap that made this a feature: it happened whatever `fit` said, so a caller that bounded neither dimension got a slot the same size as the scene and `fit` had nothing to place — about 300 units plus axes for a `width: "container"` chart, in however much room was going, with nothing saying so. `SceneSizing.Fill` puts `fillMaxSize` in front of the same `size` modifier, so it takes a bounded slot and falls back to the scene's size in an unbounded one, which is the only thing it can do inside a scrolling column. The caller's modifier is applied first, so a bound it states wins over both — that order is now a test rather than a comment

Two arithmetic slips in the Compose renderer, neither visible at density 1 and both found once a test ran at 3x. Glyphs were sized in `sp` — pixels times the density times the font scale — inside a scope the density had already scaled, so every label came out three times the size of the box reserved for it; and `SceneFit.None` drew at a scale of 1 where a scene unit is a `dp`, so the geometry came out at a third of its size. The engine's units are stated once, in `composeStyleOf`, as how many `sp` a scene unit is
